Boundary: Ignore this when the task is free-response or when options are intentionally equivalent and require extra interpretation beyond direct value matching.

Transfer rule: If amounts are given in a ratio and the same fixed amount is added to or subtracted from each share, then convert ratio parts to actual amounts first, adjust each equally, and only then reduce to a new ratio.
Error pattern: Success came from not treating equal subtraction as preserving the original ratio.
Diagnostic check: Compute one-part value from total ÷ sum of ratio parts, form each share, apply the equal change, then divide all adjusted shares by their greatest common factor.
Use when: This applies to ratio-distribution problems with a known total and an identical additive or deductive change to every person’s share.
Boundary: Ignore when changes are proportional, unequal, percentage-based, or when no total amount is given.

Transfer rule: If asked how much a growth rate increased between equal-length periods, then compute each period’s percent growth from its own starting value, then percent-change the second rate relative to the first.
Error pattern: Success came from separating “growth in amount” from “increase in the growth rate” and using a two-stage comparison.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write r1=(change1/start1), r2=(change2/start2), then verify the target is ((r2−r1)/r1)×100, not r2−r1 alone.
Use when: Apply this to consecutive time intervals, especially when durations match and the prompt compares rates or percent increases of rates.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks only for absolute change, final-minus-initial percent, or intervals with unequal lengths requiring normalization.

Transfer rule: If multiple listed points share the same x-coordinate on a nonvertical line, then set their y-values equal to extract a relation before solving for slope.
Error pattern: Success came from exploiting repeated structure instead of treating every point as an independent full equation.
Diagnostic check: Scan the coordinates for any repeated x or repeated y; if found, write the implied equality and simplify it first, then substitute once into the line formula.
Use when: Coordinate-geometry problems give several points on one line and some coordinates are symbolic or partially repeated across points.
Boundary: Ignore this when the line could be vertical or when no coordinates repeat, since the shortcut equality gives no new constraint.

Transfer rule: If groups must be equal-sized, single-category, and total sections are asked, then first use the greatest common divisor as section size, then divide each category and add the quotients.
Error pattern: Success comes from translating “equal sections” into a common divisor optimization instead of combining counts or using a ratio shortcut.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify the chosen section size divides every category count with no remainder, then compute each section count separately and sum them.
Use when: Apply this to partitioning problems with multiple separate counts, same section size, and no mixing between categories.
Boundary: Ignore this when groups may mix categories, section sizes may differ, or the task asks for size rather than number of sections.

Transfer rule: If the same job is done with different worker counts and times, then equate worker×time across scenarios before solving.
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing inverse proportion in fixed-work problems and translating it into a single linear equation.
Diagnostic check: Compute both worker-days expressions from the setup and verify they represent the same total work quantity.
Use when: Apply this to fixed-output rate problems where adding or removing identical workers changes completion time.
Boundary: Ignore when worker efficiency varies, total work changes, or rates are nonconstant across time or people.

Transfer rule: If one quantity is x% more than another, then rewrite it as (1 + x/100) times the base quantity before forming the ratio.
Error pattern: Success came from translating comparative-percent language into a multiplicative relationship and simplifying the resulting ratio.
Diagnostic check: Let the base be 2 or 100; compute the increased amount and verify the ratio matches the simplified multiplier.
Use when: A problem states one group is some percent more or less than another and asks for a ratio or relative size.
Boundary: Ignore this when the percent is of a total, the comparison direction is reversed, or extra constraints change the base.

Transfer rule: If your computed value matches an option’s content, then verify the chosen letter matches that exact content before submitting.
Error pattern: Correct quantitative work but a transcription/option-mapping failure between the derived result and the selected choice.
Diagnostic check: After solving, point to the final value, scan choices for an exact match, then read back “value ↔ label” once before commit.
Use when: Relevant in multiple-choice questions with close numerical alternatives, mixed numbers/fractions, or any step where you convert units and then select a labeled option.
Boundary: Ignore when there are no labeled choices or when the task asks for a free-response value rather than an option selection.

Transfer rule: If a question gives lower bounds for three set sizes and asks the minimum in all three, then use max(0, sum of minima − 2×whole) for the triple overlap.
Error pattern: Misapplied inclusion-exclusion by stopping with an inequality instead of converting it into a sharp lower bound on the three-way intersection.
Diagnostic check: Add the three percentages; subtract 200% of the population total; if positive, that value is the forced minimum common to all three.
Use when: Three groups lie inside one universal population, each has an “at least” percentage, and the task asks for the smallest guaranteed overlap of all three.
Boundary: Ignore when there are only two sets, “at most” bounds, exact pairwise overlaps, or totals not measured against the same whole.

Transfer rule: If two movers start with an initial gap, then update separation as initial gap minus relative-speed gain times elapsed time, not by comparing only distances traveled.
Error pattern: Ignored the starting separation and treated the chase as if both began together.
Diagnostic check: Compute relative speed, convert time and units consistently, then test: new gap = initial gap ± (relative speed × time); confirm sign by asking whether the faster runner can fully close it.
Use when: Pursuit, catch-up, head start, or separation-after-time problems with both speeds given.
Boundary: Ignore when both start from the same point or when the question asks total distance traveled rather than remaining separation.

Transfer rule: If two fractions/percents of different quantities are equal, then write the equation and isolate the requested ratio by dividing by the coefficient on that quantity.
Error pattern: Success came from translating words into an algebraic relation and inverting the percent/fraction correctly instead of comparing coefficients directly.
Diagnostic check: Convert every percent to a fraction, solve symbolically for first/second, then substitute easy values to verify both sides of the original equality match.
Use when: The prompt states one part of one quantity equals another fractional part of a second quantity and asks for their ratio.
Boundary: Ignore this when quantities are not linked by equality or when extra constraints make direct proportional reasoning invalid.

Transfer rule: If combining groups with different averages, then compute each group’s total (count × average), add totals and counts, and divide once at the end.
Error pattern: Success came from using a weighted average instead of averaging the two means directly.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write totals for each group, verify units stay “weight,” then confirm combined average lies between the two group averages.
Use when: This applies to multi-group average problems where each group has its own size and mean, especially with fractions or mixed numbers.
Boundary: Ignore this when groups are equal-sized or when the question asks for a total, difference, or a single group’s value rather than a combined mean.

Transfer rule: If quantities are sold in stages at different profit rates, then compute each stage on its actual sold fraction and sum profit over the same base cost.
Error pattern: Success came from using a weighted-average-by-quantity approach instead of averaging percentages directly.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify the sold fractions total the whole stock; if a “remaining” part is mentioned, convert later percentages into fractions of the original total.
Use when: Multi-part sale, mixture, discount, or profit problems where different portions of the same inventory have different rates.
Boundary: Ignore this when rates apply sequentially to the same item price, or when costs per unit differ across portions.

Transfer rule: If a question changes an average after adding one new result, then compute old total = old average × old count, new total = target average × new count, and subtract.
Error pattern: Success came from translating averages into totals before comparing, avoiding direct averaging shortcuts.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify three quantities: old total, updated count, and target average; then confirm required amount = target total − old total.
Use when: Apply this to average/mean problems where one or a few new observations are added and a new mean is specified.
Boundary: Ignore this when the count stays fixed, values are replaced rather than added, or the prompt asks for a different statistic.

Transfer rule: If a fixed budget buys more quantity after a percentage price cut, then equate quantities under the same budget: budget/new_price minus budget/old_price equals extra quantity.
Error pattern: I treated the extra quantity as if it directly determined total spending, collapsing a ratio-change problem into a simple multiplication equation.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write old price as p and new price as (1−r)p, compute budget/(new) and budget/(old), and verify their difference matches the stated extra units.
Use when: Budget is fixed, price changes by a percent, and the result is expressed as “can buy x more/less units.”
Boundary: Ignore when spending changes too, or when the comparison is about total cost for a fixed quantity instead of quantity for a fixed budget.

Transfer rule: If workers have a scheduled break before everyone finishes, then add the full break duration to any person whose completion time would occur after the break starts.
Error pattern: Correctly converted work fractions to total durations, but failed to incorporate an external interruption into the latest finisher’s end time.
Diagnostic check: Compute each raw finish time from the common start, mark whether it is before or after the break start, add the break only to after-break cases, then take the maximum adjusted finish.
Use when: Multiple people work in parallel from one start time, rates are given as fractions completed in given times, and a fixed break interrupts all work.
Boundary: Ignore this when no interruption exists or when every participant definitely finishes before the break begins.

Transfer rule: If a problem gives successive percent discounts or increases, then convert each to a multiplier and multiply them in sequence from the current amount.
Error pattern: Success comes from treating chained percentages as compounding steps rather than adding/subtracting percentages from the starting value.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write each step as “new amount = old amount × (1 ± rate)” and verify every later percent uses the updated amount.
Use when: Apply this on sale, tax, markup, depreciation, probability, or growth problems with multiple percentage changes across stages.
Boundary: Ignore this when all percentages are explicitly defined from the same original base or when the change is a single net percent already given.

Transfer rule: If a division leaves remainder 1, then rewrite it as dividend minus 1 being an exact multiple of the divisor, and list divisors greater than the remainder.
Error pattern: Success came from converting a remainder statement into a divisibility condition before checking valid divisor constraints.
Diagnostic check: Compute dividend − remainder; enumerate its positive divisors; keep only those strictly larger than the remainder and verify each by substitution.
Use when: The problem gives a fixed dividend, an unknown divisor, and a specified remainder, especially when asked for all possible divisors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the divisor is fixed, values are nonintegers, or the remainder is not required to be less than the divisor.

Transfer rule: If circular arrangements require two specified people adjacent, then treat them as one block, count circular permutations of the reduced units, and multiply by the block’s internal orders.
Error pattern: Success pattern: correctly recognizing rotational equivalence and combining an adjacency constraint with a block method.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compute units = total people minus grouped people plus one; use (units−1)! for the circle, then multiply by permutations inside each block.
Use when: Relevant for seating or ordering problems on a circle where only relative positions matter and one or more elements must stay together.
Boundary: Ignore when reflections also count as identical, seats are labeled/fixed, or constraints involve separation/order not captured by a simple block.

Transfer rule: If one component stays fixed while another is added to change a ratio, then set the fixed part equal in both ratios and solve for the new variable before subtracting the original amount.
Error pattern: Success came from preserving the unchanged quantity instead of scaling both parts indiscriminately.
Diagnostic check: Write old amounts as ratio×k, mark which quantity is unchanged, form new ratio using that same unchanged expression, then compute added amount = new variable − original variable.
Use when: Relevant in mixture, concentration, or ratio-update problems where only one ingredient is increased or decreased.
Boundary: Ignore when total quantity, both components, or the fixed component also changes.

Transfer rule: If profit shares come from investments for the same time, then first reduce the investments by their greatest common factor and divide total profit in that exact ratio.
Error pattern: Faulty simplification of a ratio after computing each part over the total; arithmetic consistency was not preserved.
Diagnostic check: Compute pairwise comparisons of the simplified ratio against the original amounts, then verify allocated shares sum exactly to the total profit.
Use when: Several partners contribute money for equal durations and you must match a profit split to multiple-choice values.
Boundary: Ignore this when investment durations differ, withdrawals occur, or profit is not proportional to capital alone.

Transfer rule: If a probability question involves multiple independent dice, then count ordered outcomes in the full sample space and divide favorable ordered pairs by the total.
Error pattern: Success came from explicitly enumerating outcomes rather than using intuition about sums or treating unordered pairs as equally likely.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the sample-space size, enumerate every outcome matching the target condition, and verify no symmetric orderings were merged or omitted.
Use when: Apply this to dice, spinners, cards, or other uniform random devices where multiple draws/rolls create compound outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore this exact counting routine when outcomes are not equally likely, dependence exists, or the problem asks for a conditional or cumulative probability.

Transfer rule: If a selection problem asks for an exact composition from groups, then compute favorable outcomes with combinations for each group and divide by combinations for the total selection.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping “exactly this many from each category” to a hypergeometric count instead of using order-based multiplication without correction.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify favorable count = product of groupwise combinations, total count = one combination from all individuals, then simplify the ratio.
Use when: Random draws are made without replacement and the target event specifies exact counts from distinct categories.
Boundary: Ignore this when order matters, draws are with replacement, or probabilities differ by person/category.

Transfer rule: If one member of a fixed-size group is replaced and the average changes, then multiply the average change by the group size and add/subtract that from the replaced member’s value.
Error pattern: Success came from converting an average shift into a total-sum shift before comparing old and new members.
Diagnostic check: Compute group-size × average-change; verify the candidate differs from the replaced value by exactly that amount and in the correct direction.
Use when: A problem gives a constant number of items, a change in average, and a replacement or single-item swap.
Boundary: Ignore this when the group size also changes or when multiple values change without isolating one replacement.

Transfer rule: If two movers start at different times toward each other, then shift to the later start, subtract the head-start distance, and divide remaining distance by combined speed.
Error pattern: Success came from aligning timelines before adding speeds; mistakes usually come from using full distance or wrong start time.
Diagnostic check: Compute one mover’s head-start distance, update the gap, then verify gap ÷ combined speed gives a nonnegative duration added to the later departure.
Use when: Relevant in opposing-motion or catch-up problems with staggered departures and constant speeds.
Boundary: Ignore when speeds vary, routes are not directly closing the gap, or delays/stops make constant-rate timeline alignment invalid.

Transfer rule: If chaining “beats by” race results, then convert each to speed ratios using equal-time distances and compare the slower runner’s distance when the winner finishes.
Error pattern: Treated a speed ratio like additive race “parts,” then scaled by total ratio sum instead of by the leader’s finished distance.
Diagnostic check: After finding the combined speed ratio, set the winner’s race distance as the ratio’s winner-part total; compute the other runner’s covered distance and subtract.
Use when: One runner beats another by a distance, and linked pairwise results must be combined across possibly different race lengths.
Boundary: Ignore when data involve time gaps, acceleration, handicaps, or both runners are not measured at the instant the winner finishes.

Transfer rule: If cost is given per bundle and selling price per item, then convert both to the same unit before computing profit percent.
Error pattern: Success came from consistent unit alignment and using profit percent on cost, not on selling revenue or item count.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write bundle size, total items, total cost, total sales, and verify profit percent = (sales − cost) / cost × 100.
Use when: Apply this to quantity-and-price word problems mixing dozens, pairs, packs, or cartons with per-item or per-bundle rates.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when prices are already in the same unit or the question asks for markup, margin, or simple difference instead of profit percent.

Transfer rule: If a seating/counting problem says “alternate,” then first test whether the group sizes can support a full alternating pattern before multiplying positions.
Error pattern: I treated a global adjacency-pattern constraint as an independent placement choice, overcounting by ignoring feasibility.
Diagnostic check: Build the required color/group pattern skeleton across all seats; verify counts fit exactly, then count only permutations within the forced slots.
Use when: Apply this to arrangement problems with labeled people split into categories and words like alternate, consecutive, separated, or no two alike adjacent.
Boundary: Ignore this when the condition concerns only unrestricted placement or when multiple valid pattern skeletons must all be counted separately.

Transfer rule: If multiple partial payments are described relative to the total, then write each contribution algebraically and set their sum plus any remaining personal payment equal to the total.
Error pattern: Success came from translating phrasing into expressions and combining fractional parts before isolating the whole.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify units and signs, then substitute your result back to confirm all contributions together exactly match the full cost.
Use when: Apply this to word problems about shared costs, discounts, or funding where parts are given as fractions of the unknown total with constant offsets.
Boundary: Ignore this when amounts are fixed independently of the total or the relationships are non-additive, comparative, or time-based.

Transfer rule: If recurring events start aligned and you count coincidences over a time span, then use the common-period count and decide explicitly whether the initial simultaneous event is included.
Error pattern: Correctly found the repeat interval but undercounted by omitting one endpoint in an inclusive counting situation.
Diagnostic check: List coincidence times from start as 0, P, 2P, ...; if the span equals N·P exactly, compare N versus N+1 based on whether time 0 and the ending instant both count.
Use when: Periodic-process, bells/beeps/clocks, “together” counting, all start simultaneously, and the total duration is an exact multiple of the shared period.
Boundary: Ignore when starts are offset, the endpoint is excluded, the duration is not exact, or the question asks for gaps rather than number of coincidences.

Transfer rule: If values change by successive percentages from month to month, then convert each step to multipliers and compare each cumulative product’s distance from 1.
Error pattern: Success comes from treating percent increases/decreases multiplicatively instead of adding or subtracting percentages across steps.
Diagnostic check: Set the baseline to 1, compute each period’s cumulative factor in order, then calculate absolute differences |factor − 1| before choosing.
Use when: This applies to chained percent-change, growth/decay, sales, population, price, or compound-change multiple-choice questions asking “closest to original.”
Boundary: Ignore this when changes are direct amounts, all options are already absolute values, or the question asks only for the final period.

Transfer rule: If a profit/loss phrase gives a fraction, then identify the base quantity explicitly and write the equation from that base before solving.
Error pattern: Misread the referent of the fraction and attached it to the wrong quantity, producing a clean but invalid setup.
Diagnostic check: Underline the noun after the fraction phrase, translate two candidate equations if wording is ambiguous, and keep only the one matching normal language exactly.
Use when: Short arithmetic word problems describe gain or loss as a fraction or percentage of some amount.
Boundary: Ignore when the relationship is stated directly by a formula, ratio table, or unambiguous symbolic expression.

Transfer rule: If a worker completes a fraction of a job in given time, then convert to unit rate by dividing that fraction by the time, add rates, and invert only if asked for total time.
Error pattern: Success came from separating rate and time correctly and not treating partial-completion times as full-job times.
Diagnostic check: Compute each unit rate, add them, then verify dimensions: rate answers look like work/day; time answers look like days and must be the reciprocal of the combined rate.
Use when: Apply this to shared-work questions where each person is described by completing a fraction of the same task in some number of days.
Boundary: Ignore this when tasks differ, rates vary over time, or the prompt already asks for rate rather than completion time.

Transfer rule: If asked for an average rate of change over time, then compute (final value − initial value) ÷ (later year − earlier year).
Error pattern: Success came from mapping words to the rate-of-change structure instead of matching surface forms in choices.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, write start, end, and elapsed-time values, then verify units simplify to “amount per year” and the sign matches increase/decrease.
Use when: Relevant for word problems comparing two time points and asking for average increase, decrease, or change per unit time.
Boundary: Ignore when growth is compounded, piecewise, nonconstant, or the question asks for total change rather than an average rate.

Transfer rule: If one number divided by another gives quotient q and remainder r, then write larger = q×smaller + r and combine with the other relation.
Error pattern: Success came from translating word statements into two simultaneous linear equations before checking choices.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify remainder < divisor and substitute your solved values back into both the difference equation and the division form.
Use when: Apply this on number-relationship problems involving difference/sum plus quotient-and-remainder information between two integers.
Boundary: Ignore this when division is not between the unknown numbers, or when variables represent non-integers or unrelated quantities.

Transfer rule: If part of a whole is sold at one profit/loss rate and an overall return is required, then convert everything to total and partwise selling amounts before finding the remaining rate.
Error pattern: Success comes from weighted-profit reasoning; failure usually comes from averaging percentages instead of using each part’s cost share.
Diagnostic check: Compute target total selling amount from overall return, subtract the known part’s selling amount, then compare that remainder with the remainder’s cost to get its rate.
Use when: A transaction splits goods into fractions sold at different rates, but asks for one unknown rate to satisfy an overall gain or loss.
Boundary: Ignore when quantities have unequal unit costs, changing bases, or hidden fees/discounts not proportional to the original cost.

Transfer rule: If a question compares one worker’s time to a team’s time, then convert each time to rate, add team rates, invert to get team time, and form the requested ratio.
Error pattern: Success came from using reciprocal relationships correctly and not adding times directly.
Diagnostic check: Write unit labels; verify solo rate = job/hour, combined rate = sum of rates, combined time = 1/(combined rate), and the final ratio is time/time.
Use when: Apply on work-rate problems with agents working alone and together on the same whole task.
Boundary: Ignore when outputs are not additive, task sizes differ, or the prompt asks for rate rather than time.

Transfer rule: If asked for a specific linear combination rather than each variable, then algebraically derive that combination directly from the given equations before choosing an option.
Error pattern: Correct invariant-style elimination, but a final verification/selection mismatch caused an otherwise sound derivation to be marked wrong.
Diagnostic check: Compute the target expression in two independent ways—direct combination of equations and substitution from a reduced relation—and confirm both give the same option.
Use when: The prompt gives totals for mixtures of items and asks for the sum of one of each or another combined cost.
Boundary: Ignore this when the system is nonlinear, underdetermined for the target combination, or includes hidden constraints like integer-only pricing.

Transfer rule: If a straightforward counting method gives a clean result but official feedback disagrees, then re-read the prompt for omitted constraints or a transcription error before trusting the calculation.
Error pattern: Correct method selection can still fail when I assume the statement is complete and do not validate source consistency.
Diagnostic check: Identify whether order matters, list all explicit restrictions, compute once, then verify the result matches the answer set and the wording exactly.
Use when: Relevant for combinatorics questions about forming groups, selections, committees, teams, or bands from a larger pool.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is fully reliable, constraints are unambiguous, and feedback is not known to conflict with standard interpretation.

Transfer rule: If a table gives values with frequencies, then expand by frequency or use cumulative counts before finding the median.
Error pattern: Treated frequencies as raw data values, ignoring how many times each value occurs.
Diagnostic check: Compute total count, identify the middle position(s), then verify which value’s cumulative frequency contains that position.
Use when: A question asks for median, mode, quartiles, or ordered statistics from a frequency table or tally chart.
Boundary: Ignore this when the data are already listed individually or when asked for mean from summarized counts.

Transfer rule: If draws are independent from a small ordered set and a strict ordering is required, then count increasing value triples by combinations and divide by all ordered outcomes.  
Error pattern: You started casework correctly but relied on incomplete enumeration instead of using the symmetry/combinations structure, increasing risk of omission.  
Diagnostic check: Compute favorable outcomes two ways—list count should equal the number of distinct 3-value subsets from the set; if not, recount before choosing.  
Use when: Ordered random draws with replacement are taken from a finite ordered set, but the event demands all selected values be strictly increasing.  
Boundary: Ignore this when repeats are allowed in the event, order does not matter, or the sample space is not all ordered draw sequences.

Transfer rule: If profit is stated as equal to the selling price of some units, then let selling price per unit be 1, express total cost from total selling minus profit, and compute profit percent on cost.
Error pattern: I mixed cost-price and selling-price bases by treating a profit stated in selling-price units as if it were in cost-price units.
Diagnostic check: Set unit selling price = 1; write SP(total), Profit, then CP(total) = SP(total) - Profit; verify profit percent uses Profit/CP, not Profit/SP.
Use when: Apply this to profit-loss, discount, or ratio questions where one quantity is defined in terms of another quantity’s selling value.
Boundary: Ignore this when all relations are already given purely in cost-price terms or when the asked percentage is explicitly on selling price.

Transfer rule: If only one member changes by a known percent and the mean changes, then convert both means to totals, subtract to get the change amount, and divide by the percent to recover that member’s original value.
Error pattern: Success pattern: tying the mean shift to the whole-group total avoids guessing and isolates the single changed part.
Diagnostic check: Compute original total and new total from mean × group size; verify their difference equals the stated percent of your candidate original amount.
Use when: Apply this to average problems with a fixed group size and exactly one value changed by a stated rate.
Boundary: Ignore this when multiple values change, the group size changes, or the rate applies to the new amount instead of the original.

Transfer rule: If a question gives principal, annual rate, and simple interest, then compute time with t = (interest × 100) / (principal × rate).
Error pattern: Success came from selecting the correct simple-interest model and isolating the unknown instead of guessing from options.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify units match, convert any mixed or fractional percent to a decimal-equivalent rate correctly, and substitute back to see the interest reproduces the given amount.
Use when: Apply this on straightforward simple-interest multiple-choice items asking for time from principal, rate per annum, and earned interest.
Boundary: Ignore this when interest is compound, rates vary over time, or extra conditions like installments, discounts, or changing principal appear.

Transfer rule: If one moving object passes a person or point on another moving object, then use relative speed and set distance covered equal to the moving object’s own length.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling the observer as a moving reference point instead of adding full lengths or using absolute ground speed.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “What exactly is being passed—a point/person or a whole object?” Then compute relative speed, convert units, and verify distance = relative speed × time has length units.
Use when: Apply for train, car, boat, or conveyor problems involving overtaking in the same or opposite direction with a person, pole, or platform edge.
Boundary: Ignore when both full object lengths matter, acceleration is involved, or time refers to crossing a fixed ground point.

Transfer rule: If a trip has multiple segments with different distances or times, then compute average speed as total distance divided by total time.
Error pattern: Success comes from aggregating segment totals first; the common failure is averaging the segment speeds directly.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, write one fraction with summed distances on top and summed times on bottom, then verify the units simplify to distance per time.
Use when: Apply this to motion or work-rate questions split into legs, intervals, or stages with separate distances and durations.
Boundary: Ignore this when all segments have equal time or equal distance and the problem explicitly asks for a simple mean of rates.

Transfer rule: If a chained inequality has repeated variables on both sides, then split it into pairwise inequalities and isolate each variable with inverse operations on both sides exactly.
Error pattern: Algebraic sign-handling mistake while rearranging the second inequality led to an invalid ordering despite a valid first deduction.
Diagnostic check: After deriving each subresult, substitute a simple consistent sign example and verify every original inequality still holds before choosing.
Use when: Apply for compound linear inequalities comparing sums and differences of the same variables, especially when answer choices are sign/order relations.
Boundary: Ignore when inequalities are nonlinear, involve absolute values, or a variable-domain restriction changes how rearrangements behave.

Transfer rule: If every member of a group gains the same amount, then add that amount directly to the average instead of recomputing from scratch.
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing an equal change across all individuals preserves group size and shifts the mean by the same amount.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: did each person get the same increase or decrease, and did the number of people stay unchanged?
Use when: Apply this to average problems with a fixed group where identical additions or subtractions happen to every member.
Boundary: Ignore this when changes differ by person, people enter or leave the group, or only totals are partially described.

Transfer rule: If one person can fill any of several sequentially assigned distinct slots without replacement, then compute “chosen in any slot” as favorable slots ÷ total people, or by the complement “not chosen at all.”
Error pattern: Added conditional slot probabilities as if they were standalone; mixed changing denominators without conditioning on earlier nonselection.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, test whether each term is an unconditional probability; if denominators differ across stages, rewrite via symmetry, counting positions, or complement.
Use when: Random assignment occurs step-by-step without replacement, and the target event is “person appears in any of these positions.”
Boundary: Ignore when selections are with replacement, weighted unequally, or multiple target people/events can overlap.

Transfer rule: If choices mix “always,” “never,” and “can,” then classify each statement as forced, impossible, or possible by interval-based examples and sign comparisons.
Error pattern: Success came from checking every option against the constraints instead of trusting a quick intuition about squares or products.
Diagnostic check: For each expression, first mark each variable’s sign/range, then infer the expression’s possible sign; if uncertain, plug in one extreme-valid sample.
Use when: Apply this on inequality multiple-choice problems with bounded variables, sign conditions, powers, and product/difference claims about necessity versus possibility.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when statements depend on exact equations, hidden domain restrictions, or non-monotonic operations needing calculus/algebraic derivation.

Transfer rule: If a round trip occurs in opposite current directions, then compute downstream and upstream speeds as still-water ± current and solve distance/time with \(d/v_1 + d/v_2 = T\).
Error pattern: Success comes from modeling unequal one-way speeds separately instead of averaging speeds or assuming equal times.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write both effective speeds, verify one is larger and one smaller than the base speed, then substitute into the round-trip time equation and recheck units.
Use when: Apply this to river/boat or wind/current problems giving base speed, flow speed, and total out-and-back time.
Boundary: Ignore this when legs have different distances, stoppages, or total distance is given directly instead of total time.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for a weekday after many days, then reduce the offset modulo 7 and advance that many steps from the given day.
Error pattern: Success came from converting a large count into full weeks plus a small remainder instead of counting all days directly.
Diagnostic check: Compute n mod 7, then list exactly that many next weekdays from the start day; if remainder is 0, keep the same weekday.
Use when: Apply this to cyclic calendars or any situation with a fixed 7-step repeating sequence and a forward day offset.
Boundary: Ignore this when the cycle length is not 7, the direction is backward, or special calendar rules change the sequence.

Transfer rule: If a quantity is “x% greater than” an original, then compute original = final ÷ (1 + x/100), not final − x%.
Error pattern: Success came from translating percent increase into a multiplicative factor on the original before solving.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, multiply your found original by 1 + x/100 and verify it reproduces the stated final exactly or within rounding.
Use when: Apply this to reverse percent-change word problems where a new amount is given after an increase or decrease from an earlier amount.
Boundary: Ignore this when the percent is applied repeatedly over multiple stages or to a changing base that must be modeled stepwise.

Transfer rule: If a squared expression equals a constant and the question asks for a shifted version, then solve directly for that shifted expression using the same ± roots before comparing choices.
Error pattern: Sign/translation handling failure after getting two valid roots; transformed the variable incorrectly and dismissed a listed possibility.
Diagnostic check: Let y be the exact expression asked for, rewrite the equation in terms of y, solve y^2 = constant, and verify whether either ± value appears among choices.
Use when: The equation involves a square, absolute value, or other two-branch inverse, and the answer choices target a shifted or re-labeled expression.
Boundary: Ignore when the function is one-to-one on the stated domain or when the problem already restricts to a single branch.

Transfer rule: If a probability question involves repeated independent yes/no events, then multiply the single-event probabilities or enumerate all equally likely outcome sequences.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling the sample space explicitly and matching favorable outcomes to total outcomes without skipping independence.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list every outcome for the repeated trials and verify the favorable count matches the product-rule result.
Use when: Apply this to small repeated random experiments, especially coin flips, dice rolls, or any independent binary outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore this when events are dependent, outcomes are not equally likely, or the question asks for conditional or cumulative probability.

Transfer rule: If a refining/mixing process changes impurity percentage but preserves pure substance, then equate pure-content before and after, not percentage-point loss.
Error pattern: Success came from conserving the main component and avoiding the trap of subtracting impurity rates directly from total volume.
Diagnostic check: Compute initial pure amount as total × (1 − impurity rate), then divide by final purity fraction; verify final volume can exceed initial pure amount.
Use when: Apply this to percentage composition problems involving purification, dilution, concentration, or reforming where one component is conserved.
Boundary: Ignore this when material is added/removed beyond impurities, there is loss of pure substance, or percentages refer to something other than composition.

Transfer rule: If a problem asks for a change between two temperatures linked linearly, then convert the difference directly using the scale factor and ignore the constant offset.
Error pattern: Confusing absolute-value conversion with difference conversion, plus importing outside facts instead of using only the stated difference.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the relation as one variable equals slope times the other plus constant; subtract two instances and verify the constant cancels before computing.
Use when: Relevant for unit-conversion equations, affine formulas, or any question asking how far apart two values are rather than their actual values.
Boundary: Ignore this when the relation is nonlinear or when the task asks for a single converted measurement, not a difference.

Transfer rule: If a percentage amount and the resulting part are given, then compute the whole as part ÷ rate-in-decimal.
Error pattern: Success came from translating a percent statement into a linear equation instead of guessing from options.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, convert the percent to decimal, divide the known part by that decimal, then verify by multiplying back to recover the given part.
Use when: Apply this on commission, discount, tax, interest, markup, or any problem asking for the base amount from a known percentage share.
Boundary: Ignore this when the percent applies after multiple stages or when the asked value is the percentage part itself, not the original whole.

Transfer rule: If several workers act together with mixed time units, then convert each to the same unit rate, add rates, and compute time = total work ÷ combined rate.
Error pattern: Success came from treating this as a rate-combination problem and standardizing units before arithmetic.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite every statement as “items per hour” or another single unit; verify each conversion by multiplying back to the original interval.
Use when: Applies to joint work, eating, filling, or travel problems where multiple agents contribute simultaneously and data use different time intervals.
Boundary: Ignore when agents are not working at the same time, rates change over time, or the task asks for amount done rather than completion time.

Transfer rule: If an object must completely pass another object, then add both lengths and divide by speed in consistent units.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling full-clearance distance correctly and converting speed before using the rate formula.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify distance means front enters to rear exits, convert speed to base units, then compute time = total distance / speed.
Use when: Apply this to motion word problems involving trains, platforms, tunnels, bridges, or any full-passing scenario.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks only for reaching, meeting, or partial overlap, or when acceleration changes the speed.

Transfer rule: If a sequence looks multiplicative but some terms are rounded, then infer the underlying multiplier from earlier exact steps and propagate that rule before matching options.
Error pattern: Correct pattern detection, but failure to account for cumulative rounding caused rejection of the nearest valid continuation.
Diagnostic check: Compute the implied multiplier across pairs, estimate rounding precision of shown terms, generate the next value from the unrounded rule, then choose the option closest within rounding tolerance.
Use when: Decimal sequences have nearly constant ratios, especially when later terms deviate slightly from an otherwise stable multiplicative pattern.
Boundary: Ignore when ratios vary systematically, exact integer recurrences fit better, or option gaps are too large for rounding to explain discrepancies.

Transfer rule: If two moving objects must fully pass each other, then use total occupied length divided by relative speed, adding speeds for opposite directions and subtracting for same direction.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the physical event to a relative-motion model and keeping distance and speed in consistent units.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write t = (sum of relevant lengths)/(relative speed), convert all speeds to one unit system, and verify the result’s time unit.
Use when: Apply for crossing, overtaking, or passing problems involving trains, people, vehicles, or moving platforms with stated lengths.
Boundary: Ignore when only a point object is tracked, lengths do not matter, or acceleration/changing speed invalidates constant relative speed.

Transfer rule: If an amount corresponds to “full minus x%,” then divide by that occupied fraction to get total, then take the remaining fraction or difference.
Error pattern: Success pattern: correctly translated a percent-empty statement into a percent-full equation before computing the leftover amount.
Diagnostic check: Write two equations: current = (1 − empty%) × total; needed = total − current. Verify current + needed = total and needed/current matches the missing fraction.
Use when: Apply on percent-completion, tank/container, discount, capacity, or occupancy problems where a known amount equals a non-100% share.
Boundary: Ignore when percentages change over time, refer to percentage points, or the given amount is already the missing part rather than the filled part.

Transfer rule: If a word problem asks what fraction or percentage remained, then sum all amounts removed, subtract from the starting total, and convert remainder/start to a percent.
Error pattern: Success comes from mapping the story to a two-step part-whole calculation instead of matching an answer choice by intuition.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify: added removals are reasonable, remainder plus removed equals the original total, and the percent is remainder ÷ original × 100.
Use when: Apply this to inventory, money, attendance, or quantity-tracking problems with a known starting amount and several decreases.
Boundary: Ignore this when quantities are added back, rates/discounts compound, or the question asks for sold/used rather than remaining.

Transfer rule: If finding the least perfect-square multiple of several integers, then factor each, form the LCM by max exponents, and raise only odd exponents to the next even.
Error pattern: Correct method choice but arithmetic execution failed during prime-factor multiplication, causing all later checks to target the wrong base number.
Diagnostic check: Recompute the LCM two ways—prime-exponent product and direct pairwise LCM—and verify they match before searching choices.
Use when: This applies to divisibility-plus-perfect-square questions involving several composite numbers and answer choices that are close in size.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is not about the least common multiple or when square status is determined by a different structure.

Transfer rule: If a ratio question uses a named transformation term, then recall the standard definition before computing; do not invent an operation from the wording alone.
Error pattern: Treated a technical ratio term as “square each part,” showing over-literal interpretation instead of using domain vocabulary.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state the operation in words from memory and verify it on a simple example to see whether the result scales each term or changes both terms differently.
Use when: Relevant for arithmetic or mensuration problems involving specialized ratio terms like duplicate, triplicate, subduplicate, or compounded ratios.
Boundary: Ignore when the problem explicitly defines the transformation or asks for plain simplification, equivalence, or direct multiplication of terms.

Transfer rule: If one person has seat restrictions, then list allowed positions exactly and multiply only those choices by the permutations of everyone else.
Error pattern: Misread the restriction set and inconsistently counted eligible seats, then drifted instead of reconciling with the stated condition.
Diagnostic check: Mark seats as allowed/forbidden for the restricted person, count allowed seats, verify allowed+forbidden equals total seats, then compute allowed count × remaining factorial.
Use when: A counting problem has one distinguished object/person with positional exclusions on a line, row, or ordered set of spots.
Boundary: Ignore this when restrictions involve multiple people interacting, circular arrangements, or additional adjacency/dependence constraints.

Transfer rule: If a problem has ordered slots with the same independent set of choices in each slot, then multiply choices per slot as base^slots.
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing independent ordered choices and using the multiplication principle instead of permutation formulas or unordered counting.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, list the slots, verify each has the same available choices regardless of earlier picks, then compare product counting with a quick full listing pattern.
Use when: Apply this to sequences, codes, signal states, or repeated selections where position matters and repetitions are allowed.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices change by position, repeats are forbidden, or arrangements are treated as identical under reordering.

Transfer rule: If centers and intersection points form a square/rhombus in equal-circle overlap, then take the side as both center distance and radius, and compute lens area as two sectors minus two isosceles triangles.
Error pattern: Structural setup was partly right, but the geometric relation was misread by using the square’s diagonal as a circle diameter.
Diagnostic check: Before calculating area, verify which square sides are radii by checking adjacency: center-to-intersection segments must equal the radius and all square sides must match.
Use when: Two congruent circles overlap and the diagram ties centers and intersection points into a symmetric quadrilateral.
Boundary: Ignore when the given polygon is not formed by radius segments or the circles are unequal.

Transfer rule: If a mixture is sold at the original unit price and gain comes only from free water, then water fraction = gain/(100% + gain).
Error pattern: Treated percent gain as changing selling price or total volume directly instead of relating profit to the milk-only cost base.
Diagnostic check: Let milk cost per liter be 1 and total mixture be 1 liter; compute cost = milk fraction, revenue = 1, profit = water fraction, then verify profit/cost equals the stated gain.
Use when: Applies to dilution, adulteration, or replacement problems where a free component is mixed into a priced good.
Boundary: Ignore when both components have costs, the selling price is changed, or the stated percent is on quantity rather than profit.

Transfer rule: If some people are fixed to one category and the question asks for groupings, then treat those members as predetermined and count partitions of only the remaining people among unlabeled categories.
Error pattern: I turned a constrained grouping problem into a full arrangement count and also re-chose a fixed subset.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list whether categories are labeled seats or just groups; if swapping people within a category changes nothing, divide out within-group permutations and do not choose already-identified members.
Use when: Use this for counting assignments into equal-size buckets with restricted members and multiple-choice answers that are much smaller than factorial counts.
Boundary: Ignore this when positions are distinct ordered seats, or when the restricted individuals are not predetermined.

Transfer rule: If summing equally spaced integers in a range, then identify the first/last valid terms, compute term count with step size, and use arithmetic-series sum.
Error pattern: Success came from converting a filtered range into an arithmetic sequence instead of misusing a consecutive-integers formula directly.
Diagnostic check: Verify endpoints satisfy the condition, compute count as (last−first)/step + 1, and confirm count is an integer before summing.
Use when: Relevant for sums of evens, odds, multiples, or any regularly spaced values between two bounds.
Boundary: Ignore when spacing is irregular, endpoints are excluded in a nonuniform way, or the sequence is not arithmetic.

Transfer rule: If total time comes from consecutive work phases, then compute each phase as work ÷ rate, convert any decimal multiplier to a fraction, and add with exact common denominators.
Error pattern: Set-up was right, but algebraic simplification of the decimal-rate term and denominator conversion was mishandled.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the faster rate as a fraction times the base rate, simplify each time term separately, then substitute an easy case like zero first-phase work to see whether the form matches the choices.
Use when: Multi-stage rate problems where one rate is a scaled version of another and answers are algebraic expressions.
Boundary: Ignore when phases overlap, rates vary continuously, or the question asks for work done rather than elapsed time.

Transfer rule: If your algebra gives a result not among the choices, then stop and re-read every percentage statement to verify the base set and whether complements were inferred correctly.
Error pattern: Correct equation setup can still fail through unchecked interpretation or by ignoring a conflict between the derived value and the provided options.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each percent as “part/base,” label the base for every statement, compute the implied complement explicitly, and confirm the final value matches one listed choice.
Use when: A word problem links overlap, subset percentages, and phrases like “of those who use …” or “do not use …”.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices are absent or when all percentages share the same clearly stated base.

Transfer rule: If a work-rate equation gives a time, then convert each time to rate, sum rates, solve, and convert back only at the end.
Error pattern: Algebra slip after setting up the correct reciprocal-rate equation, causing an impossible result that contradicts the scenario.
Diagnostic check: After solving, substitute the value back into both individual rates, add them, and verify the sum matches the given combined rate exactly.
Use when: Combined-work, fill/drain, speed, or productivity problems where totals come from adding independent rates rather than times.
Boundary: Ignore when contributions are not independent, rates change over time, or the relationship is not additive in rates.

Transfer rule: If a target overall rate is given for combined investments, then set total interest equal to target rate times total principal, including every invested amount.
Error pattern: I matched combined interest to the target rate on only one part of the principal, ignoring the added investment in the average.
Diagnostic check: Write \(r_1p_1+r_2p_2=r_t(p_1+p_2)\); expand both sides and verify the unknown appears in both interest and total-principal terms before solving.
Use when: This applies to mixture, weighted-average, alligation, or blended-rate questions involving multiple sums with different percentages.
Boundary: Ignore when the target rate applies only to a stated subset, or when time periods differ and rates must be time-adjusted first.

Transfer rule: If discounts are successive, then multiply the price by each remaining-price factor in sequence instead of subtracting all percentages from the original.
Error pattern: Correct structure but arithmetic drift in intermediate or final multiplication caused a mismatch with the available choices.
Diagnostic check: Compute using factors, then independently recompute stepwise; if the two totals or the nearest option do not align exactly, redo the arithmetic.
Use when: Apply this on chained discounts, taxes, growth/decay, or any percentage changes applied one after another to updated amounts.
Boundary: Ignore this when percentages are combined explicitly on the same base or when only one percentage change is involved.

Transfer rule: If one category’s percentage is implied by the remainder from 100%, then convert that remainder to a decimal/fraction and divide the known part count by it.
Error pattern: Success came from correctly using complementary percentages and setting part = rate × total before isolating the total.
Diagnostic check: Compute the missing share, solve total = known part / share, then verify by recomputing both categories and checking they sum to the whole.
Use when: A two-part whole is described, one part’s percent is given, and the other part’s count is known.
Boundary: Ignore this when percentages refer to different bases, there are more than two parts, or totals change across groups/time.

Transfer rule: If your computed result matches a choice, then verify the final selected option label matches that exact value before submitting.
Error pattern: Correct quantitative reasoning followed by an answer-selection transcription mismatch between computed value and marked choice.
Diagnostic check: After solving, do a two-column check: write “computed value” and “chosen option value,” and confirm they are identical.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice questions where you calculate a numerical result and then must map it to an option.
Boundary: Ignore when there are no fixed options to map to, or when the task asks only for the value itself.

Transfer rule: If two ordered rows also require each back entry exceed the front entry in the same column, then count only row choices whose sorted pairings satisfy columnwise inequalities.  
Error pattern: Treated a nontrivial cross-row dominance constraint as automatic after sorting each row.  
Diagnostic check: After choosing the front-row set, sort both rows and verify for every column that back_i > front_i; reject any choice failing one comparison.  
Use when: Arrangements involve monotone order within groups plus position-by-position comparisons between groups, such as two-row photos or grid fillings.  
Boundary: Ignore when no cross-group column comparison exists, or when unrestricted permutations are counted instead of sorted placements.

Transfer rule: If a quantity is built by concatenating terms, then total digits by partitioning terms into exact digit-length ranges and summing count × digits in each range.
Error pattern: Approximating ranges and misclassifying boundary cases instead of using precise thresholds for where digit length changes.
Diagnostic check: List all transition points where term size gains a digit, convert them to index cutoffs, verify inclusivity at each endpoint, then confirm subgroup counts add to the full index range.
Use when: A problem asks for total digits/characters from writing many sequential values, especially powers, squares, or generated terms with changing lengths.
Boundary: Ignore when the task concerns numeric value, divisibility, or a single term’s digits rather than concatenation-length totals.

Transfer rule: If position restrictions leave extra eligible slots, then choose which restricted slots are used, permute the restricted items there, and permute the remaining items in all other slots.
Error pattern: Success came from separating slot selection from item arrangement; the brief divide-after-multiply move signals a risk of unjustified cancellation.
Diagnostic check: Count restricted items and eligible positions; compute choose(eligible, restricted) × restricted! × remaining!, then verify every unrestricted slot count matches the remaining items exactly.
Use when: Apply to permutation problems with distinct symbols and conditions like “certain types must occupy positions of a given parity or subset.”
Boundary: Ignore when symbols repeat, positions have multiple overlapping constraints, or unrestricted items also face placement restrictions requiring inclusion-exclusion or cases.

Transfer rule: If a percent discount is applied before equal sharing, then compute discounted total first and divide by the number of people, matching the nearest listed choice only after exact arithmetic.
Error pattern: Correct structure but weak commitment when the exact result differs slightly from all options; hesitation about rounding/format instead of trusting the computed process.
Diagnostic check: Calculate original total × (1 − discount rate), divide by group size, then compare the result’s distance to each option and ensure units are dollars per person.
Use when: A word problem combines a percent change on a total with equal splitting and multiple-choice answers.
Boundary: Ignore when fees, taxes, tips, unequal shares, or explicit rounding rules alter the order of operations.

Transfer rule: If a difference of squares and a sum are given, then factor the quadratic expression into sum·difference and solve for the difference first.
Error pattern: Success came from exploiting structure instead of guessing; algebra stayed consistent through substitution and simplification.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, compute the difference from (quadratic relation)/(given sum), solve the two linear equations, then substitute back into both originals.
Use when: Relevant when variables appear as a squared difference together with either their sum or their difference, especially in multiple-choice settings.
Boundary: Ignore this when the quadratic expression is not factorable as a simple difference of squares or the needed divisor could be zero.

Transfer rule: If a fixed budget buys more items after a percentage price cut, then model quantities in the same unit and use inverse proportionality: new quantity = old quantity ÷ remaining-price fraction.
Error pattern: Unit inconsistency and malformed setup—treating a per-dozen price as if it were a per-item price, so the equations mixed quantity units.
Diagnostic check: Before solving, label every variable with units, convert all prices to either per-item or per-group, and verify each equation has matching units on both sides.
Use when: Quantity-purchase problems with fixed spending, percent price changes, and item/group units like pieces, packs, or dozens.
Boundary: Ignore when spending also changes, extra items are free bonuses, or the relationship is not purely price-versus-quantity.

Transfer rule: If a fee uses tiers, then compute each lower tier’s fixed contribution first and solve only the remaining amount with the next rate.
Error pattern: Success came from translating a piecewise pricing rule into one fixed part plus one variable excess part.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, calculate the base-tier charge, subtract it from the total fee, divide by the excess-tier rate, then add back the threshold.
Use when: Apply this on graduated commissions, taxes, shipping, or billing where different rates apply before and after a cutoff.
Boundary: Ignore this when one rate applies to the whole amount, tiers are cumulative across many brackets, or rates depend on non-additive conditions.

Transfer rule: If a percent is given relative to cost but asked relative to selling price, then set cost = 1, compute selling price = 1 + markup, and convert using markup/selling price.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking the reference base and changing denominators instead of reusing the original percent unchanged.
Diagnostic check: Write three symbols—cost, markup, selling price—and verify selling price equals cost + markup before forming the final ratio.
Use when: Apply on retail, profit, discount, commission, or tax questions that switch the comparison base between two related quantities.
Boundary: Ignore when the asked percent uses the same base as the given percent or when values are already expressed over the target whole.

Transfer rule: If an object fully passes a fixed span, then use total distance = object length + span length and convert speed to matching units before time = distance/speed.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling “complete crossing” as front entering until rear exiting, with correct unit normalization before calculation.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify both lengths are added, speed is in m/s, and the computed time has seconds with reasonable magnitude.
Use when: Apply to motion problems involving a vehicle or moving body crossing a bridge, platform, tunnel, pole, or another object.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks only entry time, relative motion between movers, or already uses consistent units and a different crossing definition.

Transfer rule: If counts are linked by a fixed ratio and a total value is given, then replace the counts with ratio-multiples of one shared unit before solving.
Error pattern: Success came from translating the ratio into proportional variables and combining it correctly with the linear total.
Diagnostic check: Compute the value of one full ratio group, divide the total by that group value, then multiply the within-group count difference by the number of groups.
Use when: Apply this on mixture, pricing, or inventory problems with per-item values, a count ratio, and a total amount.
Boundary: Ignore this when the ratio is not between the actual counts or when totals involve extra fees, discounts, or nonuniform rates.

Transfer rule: If one group is a stated multiple of the rest combined, then represent total as multiplier+1 equal parts and assign shares before choosing.
Error pattern: Success came from translating a ratio statement into two linked equations instead of guessing from totals or options.
Diagnostic check: Define variables for target group and complement, write both “target = k·other” and “target + other = total,” then verify both after solving.
Use when: Apply on word problems about partitioning a whole into one category versus all remaining categories with multiplicative comparisons.
Boundary: Ignore when comparisons are between two named subsets not covering the whole, or when percentages/overlap make complement equations invalid.

Transfer rule: If a divisibility question involves prime-factor forms, then count the exponent of the target prime in each possible case before judging any expression.
Error pattern: Tending to infer a higher power divisibility from the mere presence of the prime factor instead of verifying total exponent.
Diagnostic check: Split into all placements of the required prime among the prime variables, compute that prime’s exponent in each option, and keep only options meeting the threshold in every case.
Use when: A number is written as a product of prime powers and the prompt asks what must be divisible by a prime power.
Boundary: Ignore when variables are not restricted to primes or when the task is about possibility rather than necessity.

Transfer rule: If counting integer rectangle dimensions with one side constrained larger, then list each positive factor pair once with the larger factor assigned to that side.
Error pattern: Direction/assignment mismatch after generating valid pairs; counted the wrong half of symmetric factor pairs.
Diagnostic check: Make an ordered table of factor pairs up to the square root, rewrite each as (larger, smaller), and count only distinct larger entries.
Use when: A product is fixed, variables are integers, and an inequality distinguishes which factor corresponds to which variable.
Boundary: Ignore when variables need not be integers, signs/zero are allowed, or order does not matter.

Transfer rule: If a moving object’s speeds are given in opposite directions with and against a current or wind, then add and halve them to get the object’s still-air speed.
Error pattern: Treated directional ground speeds as object and wind speeds directly instead of modeling two equations for relative motion.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write “upstream/headwind = own minus flow” and “downstream/tailwind = own plus flow,” then verify their average gives the asked rate.
Use when: Relevant for one-dimensional relative-speed word problems involving wind, current, belt, or moving medium with two opposite-direction speeds.
Boundary: Ignore when speeds are not opposites in the same medium, or when the question asks for the medium’s speed instead.

Transfer rule: If items must stay adjacent, then bundle them into one unit and recount only the resulting total units, multiplying by internal orders only.
Error pattern: Miscounted grouped arrangements by treating the bundle plus one extra item as more units than actually remain.
Diagnostic check: After bundling, list the remaining units explicitly; verify the count before using factorial, then multiply by the bundle’s internal permutations.
Use when: Arrangement/counting problems with a fixed adjacency requirement, especially with a small number of distinct objects in a row.
Boundary: Ignore when adjacency is optional, positions are circular, objects repeat, or extra constraints change symmetry or independence.

Transfer rule: If your computed result is absent from all choices, then re-read the wording and verify interpretation and arithmetic with a second method before rejecting the options.
Error pattern: Stopping after one valid-looking computation and assuming the test is flawed instead of stress-testing assumptions against the multiple-choice set.
Diagnostic check: List the included terms explicitly, count them, compute the sum directly, then recompute with an arithmetic-sequence formula; if results or choices disagree, revisit endpoint and interval interpretation.
Use when: Short arithmetic or counting questions with range words like between, from, inclusive, consecutive, odd, or even.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is open-response or when the problem explicitly states there may be no valid listed choice.

Transfer rule: If one value is defined relative to the overall average, then set average = total/count and write one equation linking total and that special value.
Error pattern: Success came from translating a self-referential average statement into algebra instead of guessing from nearby totals.
Diagnostic check: Compute the known subtotal, let total be T, express the unusual entry using T/count, and verify the final T reproduces the same average.
Use when: One group has repeated equal amounts and another amount is described as more or less than the average of the whole group.
Boundary: Ignore when the special amount is tied to a subgroup average, median, ratio, or a fixed amount not involving the overall average.

Transfer rule: If a selection is made uniformly without order and a specific full pair must be chosen, then compute probability as favorable combinations over total combinations.
Error pattern: Success pattern: modeled the sample space with combinations rather than permutations and treated the target pair as exactly one favorable outcome.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, count total people, verify order does not matter, compute “choose group size from total,” and confirm the named set corresponds to one combination.
Use when: Randomly choosing a fixed-size group from a larger group, especially when asking for one exact subset to appear.
Boundary: Ignore when choices are ordered, made with replacement, or the event allows multiple favorable subsets instead of one exact set.

Transfer rule: If a bridge-and-torch problem has four travelers, then compare the two standard shuttle plans and total every forward and return trip before choosing.
Error pattern: I undercounted by skipping a crossing/return segment and not verifying that the torch ended on the needed side after each move.
Diagnostic check: Write an ordered move list; after each move, mark torch side, who is left, and cumulative time; reject any plan with missing people or impossible torch position.
Use when: Use for sequential transport puzzles with shared resources, pairwise travel times set by the slower member, and mandatory returns.
Boundary: Ignore when multiple torches exist, more than two can travel, return rules differ, or timing is not determined by the slowest traveler.

Transfer rule: If two totals differ only by which base a percent is applied to, then isolate the shared parts and compare only the percent-on-different-base pieces.
Error pattern: Success came from translating each payment into algebra and not double-counting the discount or applying the tip to the wrong base.
Diagnostic check: Write both totals symbolically, cancel identical terms, and verify the remaining difference equals (tip rate) × (difference in bases).
Use when: Apply this to word problems with discounts, tips, taxes, commissions, or markups computed from different reference amounts.
Boundary: Ignore this when totals differ by fixed fees, multiple changing rates, or non-percentage adjustments that prevent clean cancellation.

Transfer rule: If an expression and the choices conflict, then first test for hidden formatting or grouping cues before concluding the options are wrong.
Error pattern: Overapplied a standard procedure without validating that the printed expression was interpreted exactly as intended by the item.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the expression with explicit parentheses from the original layout, then recompute and confirm the result matches at least one choice before rejecting the set.
Use when: Relevant for short arithmetic multiple-choice items where standard evaluation gives a result absent from all options.
Boundary: Ignore when notation is unambiguous, the answer is open-response, or the task explicitly asks for strict conventional order only.

Transfer rule: If a question gives totals for overlapping groups plus pairwise overlaps and any triple-overlap condition, then use inclusion–exclusion to find the union, then subtract from the overall total for “none.”
Error pattern: Success pattern—structured set counting with overlap correction instead of adding categories directly.
Diagnostic check: Write union = sum of singles − sum of pair overlaps + triple overlap; substitute every given count once, compute, then verify union is not larger than the total surveyed.
Use when: Relevant for finite survey/counting problems involving “at least one,” “none,” multiple categories, and explicit overlap data.
Boundary: Ignore when categories are mutually exclusive, overlaps are undefined/ambiguous, or the task is probabilistic rather than counting people/items.

Transfer rule: If a trip covers the same one-way distance at different speeds with total time given, then set total time as distance/speed_out + distance/speed_back and solve for the one-way distance.
Error pattern: Success pattern—modeled equal-distance legs with separate times instead of using an inappropriate simple average of speeds.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write both leg-time expressions, verify they use the same distance variable, add them, and check the solved distance reproduces the stated total time.
Use when: Use for round trips or two-leg journeys where the path length is unchanged but speeds differ by leg.
Boundary: Ignore when distances differ across legs or when total distance/average speed is directly provided.

Transfer rule: If symbols are reused across the setup and result, then keep one fixed mapping for each symbol and reject any trial that reassigns them from the product’s digits.
Error pattern: Variable-binding failure: treating placeholders as newly determined by an outcome instead of enforcing their original identities through all steps.
Diagnostic check: For each candidate, write both numbers using the same digit assignments, multiply, then verify the result’s hundreds/tens/ones exactly match the stated symbol order and uniqueness/nonzero rules.
Use when: A digit puzzle reuses the same letters across factors and product, especially with reversed order or positional constraints.
Boundary: Ignore when symbols are not shared across expressions or when the task only asks for a numerical product without consistency constraints.

Transfer rule: If your computed result is not among the choices, then check for formatting/OCR issues and test each choice by substituting it into the governing formula before rejecting the list.
Error pattern: Correct setup/algebra but overtrusted a literal reading of the options instead of reconciling the derived value with answer-format ambiguity.
Diagnostic check: Recompute from formula, then plug every option into the original relationship and compare which one reproduces the given quantity exactly.
Use when: A standard geometry/algebra formula gives a clean result, yet the choices look oddly formatted, inconsistent, or impossible.
Boundary: Ignore this when answer choices are clearly written and a direct substitution check confirms your computed result already appears exactly.

Transfer rule: If an object must fully clear another object, then use total distance = both lengths added, then compute time = distance ÷ speed in consistent units.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling the physical event correctly and converting units before comparing with choices.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify two things: added travel length includes the moving object’s full length, and speed is converted to the distance unit per second.
Use when: Apply this on motion problems about passing bridges, platforms, tunnels, poles, or overtaking where “completely pass” or “cross” appears.
Boundary: Ignore this when only the front reaches a point, when acceleration matters, or when all quantities already share units and no full-clearance condition exists.

Transfer rule: If a problem chains percent decrease and increase on different bases, then convert each to a multiplier and compare the final amount to the named reference base.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking the base of each percentage; failures happen when percentages are added/subtracted directly despite different reference amounts.
Diagnostic check: Write start = 1 unit, apply each multiplier in order, then compute (final/reference − 1) × 100 using the exact base asked for.
Use when: Relevant for sequential discounts, markups, profit/loss, appreciation/depreciation, or any percent-on-percent wording with changing bases.
