Boundary: Ignore when all percentages are explicitly on the same unchanged base or when the question asks only for the final amount.

Transfer rule: If every symbol from two groups is used once and no same-group adjacency is allowed, then first force an alternating group pattern and count internal permutations separately.
Error pattern: Success came from translating adjacency restrictions into a structural arrangement before multiplying counts.
Diagnostic check: Verify that any valid string must alternate group types at every position; then count possible starting group patterns and multiply by permutations within each group.
Use when: This applies to permutation problems with two equal-sized categories, all distinct items, and a ban on adjacent items from the same category.
Boundary: Ignore when group sizes differ, repetitions are allowed, or adjacency depends on specific item values rather than category membership.

Transfer rule: If two linear equations ask for a per-item difference, then subtract the equations first to isolate that difference before solving individual values.
Error pattern: Success came from structured elimination; the reliable pattern is converting word totals into aligned equations and targeting the asked quantity directly.
Diagnostic check: Define variables, write both equations, compute one equation minus the other, and verify the resulting coefficient/sign matches the requested “more than” direction.
Use when: Apply this to two-item mixture or purchase problems with two totals and a question about relative cost, count, or difference.
Boundary: Ignore this when relationships are nonlinear, involve percentages/ratios only, or there are more unknowns than independent equations.

Transfer rule: If arrangements are on a circle and only relative positions matter, then fix one item as an anchor and permute the rest.
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing rotational symmetry and converting a circular count into a linear factorial count.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: would rotating the entire arrangement create a “new” arrangement? If no, divide out rotations by fixing one position.
Use when: Relevant for seating, necklaces, round tables, or any arrangement where only relative order around a loop matters.
Boundary: Ignore when seats are labeled, orientations matter, reflections are identified too, or extra restrictions change the symmetry.

Transfer rule: If asked for a decreased/final price after a percent decrease, then compute original × (1 − rate), not just the discount amount.
Error pattern: Confusing the amount removed with the remaining amount after the reduction.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label the target as “discount” or “new total,” then verify whether your result is smaller than the original by exactly the stated percent.
Use when: Percent increase/decrease problems ask for final value, sale price, remaining quantity, or new total after a change.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question explicitly asks only for the amount of change, discount, gain, or loss.

Transfer rule: If a statement says “x percent of y less than z,” then parse it as “(x percent of z) minus y,” unless grouping words force otherwise.
Error pattern: Misattached the subtraction to the base of the percent instead of to the resulting commission expression.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the commission in words, then in symbols; test with a sample sale price to see whether the fixed amount is subtracted before or after taking the percent.
Use when: Percentage phrases are mixed with constants, especially wording like “plus,” “less than,” “of,” or “straight commission.”
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when parentheses, tables, or explicit formulas already make the operation order unambiguous.

Transfer rule: If a fixed fraction of inventory is unsellable and profit is on original outlay, then set price = cost × desired revenue factor ÷ sellable fraction.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling spoilage as fewer sellable units; risk remains anchoring to a computed value without verifying the profit base.
Diagnostic check: Assume 1 unit bought; compute total cost, remaining sellable amount, required total revenue, then divide required revenue by sellable amount and compare.
Use when: Relevant in pricing, mixture, yield, shrinkage, or wastage problems where loss changes the denominator before markup is applied.
Boundary: Ignore when percentages are sequential on the same base already specified, or when profit is defined per surviving unit rather than on total purchase cost.

Transfer rule: If a fixed-budget word problem changes unit price and quantity, then equate total spending before and after as quantity × unit price.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling an invariant total instead of comparing choices directly or mixing up item price with total budget.
Diagnostic check: Define variables, write both total-cost expressions, confirm they represent the same unchanged amount, then solve and convert units carefully.
Use when: Apply this to purchase scenarios with one buyer, constant money, and a stated change in per-item cost causing a new item count.
Boundary: Ignore this when the total money also changes, extra fees/discount structures appear, or quantities are not whole-item purchases under one fixed budget.

Transfer rule: If pure solute is added to a mixture, then set up new-solute/new-total = target concentration, adding the amount to both numerator and denominator appropriately.
Error pattern: Success came from conserving component amounts and modeling the changing total, instead of using a simple percent-difference shortcut.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, write initial solute mass, define added amount, form the fraction equation, solve, then verify the result makes the final ratio equal the target.
Use when: Apply this to concentration or mixture problems where a pure component is added and the overall mass changes.
Boundary: Ignore this when material is removed, another mixture is blended in, or the total amount is fixed by the setup.

Transfer rule: If a motion problem has a delayed start and a comparison like “twice as far,” then define one total-time variable, convert each traveler’s active time separately, and translate the comparison literally before simplifying.
Error pattern: Success came from structuring rates-times-distances systematically; risk remains in algebra cleanup or mismatching the derived expression to the listed choice.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, substitute your final expression back into both distance formulas and verify the target ratio holds exactly and all active times are nonnegative.
Use when: Use this for rate-distance questions with staggered starts, opposite directions, and relationships between distances rather than meeting points.
Boundary: Ignore this when the condition is about separation, relative speed, averages, or changing rates over intervals.

Transfer rule: If lengths with mixed units must be exactly measured by one greatest segment, then convert all to one unit and take their GCD/HCF.
Error pattern: Success pattern: normalized units first, then used common-divisor reasoning instead of comparing mixed-format values directly.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite every quantity in the smallest shared unit; verify the chosen segment divides each total with zero remainder.
Use when: Apply on “greatest possible length/unit” problems involving several distances or measures written in different unit combinations.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for approximation, least common multiple, or quantities are not all exact whole counts in a common unit.

Transfer rule: If a total is built from nested averages over groups and items, then multiply all levels and compare the result’s magnitude to the nearest power of ten.
Error pattern: Success came from translating the word problem into a multiplicative structure and using place-value scale to choose the closest order of magnitude.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, estimate each factor in scientific notation, multiply mantissas and add exponents, then verify the final magnitude matches the exact-product rough size.
Use when: Apply this to multi-level counting problems with averages per subgroup and answer choices given as powers of ten or broad magnitudes.
Boundary: Ignore this when averages are incompatible, weighted unevenly in a way that blocks direct multiplication, or the question asks for an exact value rather than scale.

Transfer rule: If chained percent comparisons link three quantities and a difference is given, then convert each statement to multiplicative factors of one base variable before subtracting.
Error pattern: Success pattern—represent relative changes with equations instead of comparing percentages directly or mixing reference quantities.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite “x% more/less than” as multipliers, express both compared amounts in the same base, and verify the stated difference equals the given constant.
Use when: This applies to percent increase/decrease chains, salary/price/age comparisons, and difference-between-two-terms questions.
Boundary: Ignore when percentages refer to the same original base, absolute changes only, or when hidden constraints make multiple solutions possible.

Transfer rule: If forming ordered strings from distinct letters without reuse, then count with permutations: multiply descending choices for each position or use nPr.
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing order matters and all symbols are unique, so permutation logic—not combinations—fits.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark whether repetition is allowed, whether any letters repeat, and whether arrangements with different orders count as different.
Use when: Apply this to word/arrangement counting problems that choose some positions from a set of distinct symbols.
Boundary: Ignore this when repeats are allowed, some symbols are identical, or restrictions make simple nPr incomplete.

Transfer rule: If actions alternate with fixed transforms and a final state is given, then reverse each transform in exact reverse order to recover the start.
Error pattern: Success came from respecting sequence order and using inverse operations rather than guessing from choices or combining rules incorrectly.
Diagnostic check: Write the move list from start to finish, then invert it stepwise from the end, checking each reverse step matches the responsible actor’s rule.
Use when: Relevant in sequential-process, turn-taking, recursive, or function-composition questions with a known endpoint and deterministic updates.
Boundary: Ignore when rules depend on hidden conditions, are non-invertible, or the process order/number of moves is uncertain.

Transfer rule: If a total combines quantities of different items, then multiply each unit price by its quantity and add the subtotals.
Error pattern: Success came from separating categories and using straightforward arithmetic instead of guessing from nearby choices.
Diagnostic check: Write one subtotal per item type, verify decimal placement after each multiplication, then add and estimate mentally to confirm the sum’s size.
Use when: Apply this on multi-item price totals, shopping-word problems, or any question mixing counts with decimal unit costs.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices depend on discounts, tax, missing quantities, or comparisons rather than a direct subtotal-and-sum calculation.

Transfer rule: If a lifespan crosses from B.C. to A.D., then count completed birthdays across the era boundary and explicitly exclude any year zero.
Error pattern: Off-by-one from mixing elapsed calendar labels with age, especially near an era transition.
Diagnostic check: Write the sequence around the boundary, verify adjacent years switch directly, then count anniversaries reached by the death date.
Use when: Dates involve B.C./A.D., inclusive-looking endpoints, or wording asks for age rather than raw span.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic for same-era dates or when the calendar system explicitly includes a year zero.

Transfer rule: If combining subgroup averages, then compute each subgroup’s total as count × average, sum those totals, and divide by the summed counts.
Error pattern: Success pattern—used weighted-average structure instead of averaging averages or mixing counts with measurements in the wrong places.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, verify units: numerator should be a total of the measured quantity, denominator should be total people, and the result should keep the original measurement unit.
Use when: Relevant whenever several groups have different sizes and a common average-like quantity must be merged into one overall average.
Boundary: Ignore when groups overlap, weights are not counts, or the task asks for a simple mean of already equal-weight values.

Transfer rule: If your computed value matches a choice, then verify the selected option label and the value are the same before submitting.
Error pattern: Correct calculation followed by answer-transcription mismatch between worked result and chosen option.
Diagnostic check: After solving, compare three items in order: derived value, option text containing that value, and final marked choice; they must all match.
Use when: Relevant in multiple-choice questions where you compute a numeric or symbolic result and then must map it to a listed option.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is free-response or when no option mapping is required after the derivation.

Transfer rule: If finding a unit digit after subtraction, then subtract the two last digits modulo 10 and wrap negatives by adding 10.
Error pattern: Correctly identified power cycles but failed in modular subtraction by treating a negative difference as the final last digit.
Diagnostic check: Compute each term’s last digit, do the subtraction, then if the result is below 0 replace it with result + 10 before selecting.
Use when: Relevant for unit-digit or modulo-10 questions involving powers and a final subtraction or any operation that can go negative.
Boundary: Ignore when the expression asks for the full value, uses a modulus other than 10, or subtraction is not part of the task.

Transfer rule: If a side-length question asks “how many values,” then first decide whether values are restricted to integers or whole-number side lengths before counting.
Error pattern: Applied a continuous interval correctly but failed to infer the domain needed for a finite count from multiple-choice context.
Diagnostic check: Derive the strict inequality interval, then test whether counting all real numbers gives infinity; if choices expect a finite count, recount only admissible integers inside the interval.
Use when: Geometry or side-length problems ask for the number of possible values of an unknown length rather than just its range.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the prompt explicitly allows any real measurement or directly asks for the interval/range.

Transfer rule: If a moving object passes a person/point, then use relative speed = object length ÷ passing time, adding speeds for opposite directions and subtracting for same direction.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling the event in the observer’s frame and matching passed distance to only the moving object’s length.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify units are consistent, compute relative speed from distance/time, choose sign by direction, then convert back to the requested unit.
Use when: Apply this to train, vehicle, or runner pass-by problems involving one full passing time, known length, and motion direction.
Boundary: Ignore this when both bodies have relevant lengths to include, acceleration occurs, or the event is not a complete pass-by.

Transfer rule: If a distance/rate problem yields a value outside all choices, then verify whether the prompt asks for distance, time, or a ratio before selecting or rejecting options.
Error pattern: Solved the algebra correctly but failed at answer-type validation and assumed the listed choices must match the computed quantity.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, compare the unit of your result with the unit implied by the question stem and each option style; if they mismatch, reinterpret the target.
Use when: Rate-and-time multiple-choice items involve two travelers, a time difference, and unusually small answer choices versus a large computed value.
Boundary: Ignore this when answers are open-response or when options clearly share the same unit and scale as your derived result.

Transfer rule: If category totals and the number of time periods are both fixed, then write both equations and eliminate variables before testing choices.
Error pattern: I started casework and parity checks without first reducing the system, causing inefficient search and a missed valid integer solution.
Diagnostic check: Compute the baseline total using the lowest category for all periods, compare the excess to per-category increments, and verify nonnegative integers satisfy both sum and count constraints.
Use when: This applies to word problems with several outcome types, fixed period count, fixed per-type values, and a total accumulated amount.
Boundary: Ignore this when periods are not fixed, categories can repeat without count limits, or values are probabilistic rather than exact.

Transfer rule: If each person’s amount is given as a fraction of everyone else’s total, then rewrite it as person = [fraction/(1+fraction)] × overall total.
Error pattern: Started a valid system but failed to simplify by converting “of the others” into direct shares of the whole.
Diagnostic check: For each statement x = k(other sum), replace other sum with total − x, solve x = k(total − x), and verify all shares sum to the total.
Use when: Verbal algebra problems describe several contributors, each tied to the sum of the remaining contributors.
Boundary: Ignore when relations compare one person directly to another or include extra constraints beyond a single shared total.

Transfer rule: If a rate is given in the aiding direction and the flow speed is known, then first subtract flow from aided rate to get still-water speed, then subtract flow again for opposing rate.
Error pattern: I used a one-step subtraction and then guessed from choices instead of modeling both directions from the base speed.
Diagnostic check: Write the identities aided = base + flow and opposing = base − flow; solve base, compute opposing, and reject any answer not matching exactly.
Use when: Relative-motion problems involve boats, swimmers, walkers, or cyclists moving with/against wind, stream, or current.
Boundary: Ignore this when the given rate is already the no-flow speed or when the motion is not additive/subtractive.

Transfer rule: If a word range names days inclusively, then count every listed day and tally all already-completed days before solving for the remainder.
Error pattern: Miscounting categories in a sequence and omitting previously fixed contributions, causing the target-total equation to exclude known terms.
Diagnostic check: Write each day in order, mark practiced days, count them, compute known total as count × daily amount, then compare with required total from average × number of days.
Use when: Averages are spread over calendar intervals, repeated daily amounts, or phrases like “through” and “combined” appear.
Boundary: Ignore when the period length or included dates are explicitly enumerated or no day-range interpretation is needed.

Transfer rule: If a trip has multiple speed segments, then compute average speed as total distance divided by total elapsed time, not by averaging speeds.
Error pattern: Success came from aggregating the underlying quantity correctly across segments before forming the final rate.
Diagnostic check: For each segment, calculate time = distance/speed, sum all times and distances, then divide; confirm units reduce to distance per time.
Use when: Apply this on weighted-rate, travel, work-rate, or mixture-style problems where parts have different durations or distances.
Boundary: Ignore this when all segments last equal time or the question explicitly asks for a simple mean of listed rates.

Transfer rule: If two travelers cover the same distance with a speed difference and a time difference, then write time as distance/speed and set the time subtraction equal to the given gap.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling rates with reciprocal relationships instead of comparing speeds or times linearly.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, compute both travel times from your candidate speeds and verify their difference matches the stated time gap exactly.
Use when: Apply this on constant-distance rate problems involving average speeds, one faster participant, and a stated finish-time difference.
Boundary: Ignore this when distances differ, speeds vary over segments, or the relationship is not based on constant rate = distance/time.

Transfer rule: If a profit/price word problem gives fixed cost, per-unit cost, target profit, and sales volume, then compute required price as (fixed costs + unit cost×volume + target profit) ÷ volume.
Error pattern: Success came from translating the story into a revenue equation instead of guessing from choices or mixing total and per-unit quantities.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write units on each term, verify total revenue minus total cost equals target profit, and divide only after summing all total-dollar amounts.
Use when: Apply this to break-even or target-profit questions with fixed costs, variable costs, expected quantity, and an unknown selling price.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when quantity is unknown, costs are nonlinear/tiered, or taxes, discounts, or multiple products change the revenue model.

Transfer rule: If times and a fixed rate difference are given, then convert each time to pages-per-minute, equate the combined rate to the sum, and solve rates before total work.
Error pattern: Mixing total-work expressions with rate-difference information caused an inconsistent equation and missed a simple rate-first setup.
Diagnostic check: Compute the known solo and joint rates, subtract to get the other machine’s rate, then verify that this difference matches the stated extra pages per minute.
Use when: This applies to joint-work or machine problems giving completion times plus a constant speed difference.
Boundary: Ignore when the difference is not an absolute rate gap, or when productivity varies over time or by workload.

Transfer rule: If counting sets that sum to a target, then enumerate all distinct-element subsets systematically, not just single square plus leftover.
Error pattern: Stopped at one-step complement checks and ignored multi-term combinations; failed to perform exhaustive case partitioning.
Diagnostic check: List all allowed square values up to the target, branch from the largest downward, and for each partial sum recursively test remaining smaller squares without repeats.
Use when: The problem asks for the number of sets/subsets of special numbers adding to a fixed total.
Boundary: Ignore this when repetition is allowed, order matters, or the task asks only whether one example exists.

Transfer rule: If a quantity is changed in both cost and selling terms with a new profit rate, then write both revised values from the same original variable and equate them.
Error pattern: Success came from consistent percent-to-multiplier translation and keeping the profit rate tied to the revised cost, not the original one.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify each percentage is applied to its proper base and that the revised selling price expression is defined in two independent ways.
Use when: Apply this on profit-loss word problems where purchase price, selling price, and percentage gain/loss are all altered across hypothetical scenarios.
Boundary: Ignore this when relationships are additive only, or when percentages are not referenced to cost/selling bases.

Transfer rule: If asked for a percent “of all groups that include X” also including Y, then condition the denominator on groups already containing X.
Error pattern: Used the full sample space instead of the restricted sample space; ignored the conditional phrase in the question.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite as “Among groups with X, what fraction also have Y?” Then count denominator = choose remaining spots after fixing X; numerator = choose remaining spots after fixing X and Y.
Use when: Relevant in subset-selection/combinatorics problems with wording like “that include,” “given,” “among those containing,” or nested conditions.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for an unconditional probability/count over all possible groups or arrangements.

Transfer rule: If a percent discount amount is given, then compute original value as discount ÷ (percent/100).
Error pattern: Success pattern: translated a verbal percent reduction into an equation linking part and whole correctly.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, verify by multiplying your found original by the discount rate; it must reproduce the stated reduction exactly.
Use when: The problem gives a percentage of an unknown total as a known amount, especially for discounts, rebates, tax, commission, or interest.
Boundary: Ignore when the percentage applies to a changed base, multiple sequential percentages occur, or the given amount is the final paid amount.

Transfer rule: If partners invest different amounts for different durations, then allocate profit by amount × active time and divide in that ratio.
Error pattern: Success comes from converting each person’s contribution into capital-time units before comparing shares.
Diagnostic check: Compute each participant’s amount-time product, simplify to a ratio, and verify all shares add exactly to the total profit.
Use when: Apply this to partnership, joint investment, or work-sharing questions where entries/exits happen at different times.
Boundary: Ignore this when profit is divided by a fixed agreement, equal split, salary, interest, or another stated rule overriding contribution-time.

Transfer rule: If a number has unknown digit(s) and divisibility conditions, then solve for the missing digit(s) with each rule before comparing choices.
Error pattern: I treated the visible digits as fixed and ignored the placeholder, causing premature elimination and a guess.
Diagnostic check: Write the full digit pattern, assign a variable to each blank, apply every divisibility test, intersect the resulting allowed values, then map surviving values to place positions.
Use when: Relevant for digit puzzles with placeholders, place-value questions, and simultaneous divisibility or modular constraints.
Boundary: Ignore when no digit is unknown or when the task is simple direct computation rather than constraint satisfaction.

Transfer rule: If a fixed-distance speed problem gives time reductions for successive speed increases, then write one equation per change using d/speed and convert all time differences to hours first.
Error pattern: Success comes from translating comparative statements into equations before computing; failures usually mix which two times are being compared or mishandle unit conversion.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify each equation’s left and right sides are times, substitute your candidate back into both relations, and confirm both stated time decreases hold exactly.
Use when: Apply this on constant-distance travel questions with multiple hypothetical speed changes and stated decreases in travel time.
Boundary: Ignore this when distance also changes, acceleration matters, or the prompt asks for ratios/averages without direct time-difference conditions.

Transfer rule: If equally spaced objects include one at each endpoint, then divide the total length by objects minus one to get spacing.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing the number of intervals from the number of placed objects.
Diagnostic check: Sketch endpoints and count gaps for a small sample; verify gaps = objects − 1 before dividing.
Use when: This applies to uniform spacing along a segment, fence, road, row, or yard with endpoint placements specified.
Boundary: Ignore this when spacing is nonuniform, endpoints are excluded, the path is circular, or extra margins/gaps are described separately.

Transfer rule: If asked for the least percent in all of several categories, then use the lower bound max(0, sum of percentages − (number of categories − 1)×100).
Error pattern: I treated one set as if it could sit inside all others and confused “minimum guaranteed overlap” with “possible maximum nesting.”
Diagnostic check: Add the given percentages, subtract 100 once for each extra category beyond the first, and compare that bound with any intuitive arrangement.
Use when: This applies to minimum-guarantee overlap problems with percentages/counts over one whole population and words like “at least,” “minimum,” or “must.”
Boundary: Ignore when categories are not over the same total, when exact overlap structure is given, or when the question asks for a maximum.

Transfer rule: If asked “how much more than” one group is than another, then compute (difference ÷ comparison group) × 100, not difference ÷ total.
Error pattern: Success came from choosing the correct reference base for a relative comparison after finding both subgroup counts.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, say “More than compared to which group?” and verify the denominator is that group’s count.
Use when: Relevant in percent-comparison word problems with two complementary groups or any phrasing like “A is what percent more than B?”
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for percentage points, share of the whole, or just the absolute difference.

Transfer rule: If a work-output problem scales by workers and days, then compute unit rate as total ÷ (workers × days) before rescaling.
Error pattern: Broke proportional reasoning with an arithmetic slip when converting total output into per-worker and per-day output.
Diagnostic check: Recalculate by two paths—unit rate, and scale factor ((new workers/new workers given) × (new days/given days))—and confirm both totals match.
Use when: Quantities are jointly proportional to multiple factors such as people, machines, hours, days, distance, or cost.
Boundary: Ignore when output is not linear or constant-rate, or when constraints, diminishing returns, setup time, or caps change productivity.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for a square’s side from its area, then compute the square root and verify by squaring the candidate choice.
Error pattern: Success came from applying the correct inverse operation, but the reusable habit is to confirm rather than trust an approximate root.
Diagnostic check: Square the shortlisted option exactly; if its product matches the given area digit-for-digit, keep it, otherwise reject it.
Use when: Area-to-side questions for squares appear, especially with decimals and multiple-choice answers that are numerically close.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic for non-square shapes, unit-conversion traps not yet handled, or when the task asks for an estimate only.

Transfer rule: If finding an intercept from two points, then compute the slope, write the line equation, substitute the intercept condition, and solve.
Error pattern: Success came from following a complete algebra chain instead of guessing from the graphless coordinates or choices.
Diagnostic check: Verify the slope sign from coordinate differences, then plug both original points into your equation before setting one variable to zero.
Use when: Use for coordinate-geometry problems giving two points and asking for an axis intercept or line equation.
Boundary: Ignore when the relation is not linear, the intercept is directly given, or a faster exact form is explicitly provided.

Transfer rule: If several shares are defined as fractions of sums of the others, then convert each statement into equations, simplify fractions first, and solve fully before matching choices.
Error pattern: Incomplete algebraic chain; stopping after deriving an intermediate ratio without finishing substitution into the total constraint.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, verify you have explicit values for all variables and that both ratio equations and the total sum hold when substituted back.
Use when: Multi-person distribution or mixture problems where quantities are linked to “as much as” fractions of combined others.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks only for a ratio/proportion and no overall total or absolute amount is required.

Transfer rule: If your computed expression is absent from the choices, then re-read the stem and recompute with a plug-in value before rejecting the options.
Error pattern: Declared an answer-choice error after a first-pass setup instead of stress-testing the interpretation and arithmetic against the provided format.
Diagnostic check: Pick an easy total, compute each per-person amount numerically, subtract, then compare that numeric difference to each option’s value.
Use when: Total cost is fixed, the number of sharers changes, and the task asks for how much more or less each person pays.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is open-response or when answer choices are not expressions that can be checked by substitution.

Transfer rule: If points lie on a rectangle’s diagonal and a segment relation is given, then parameterize positions by fractions of the full diagonal and compute area from coordinate determinants or shared-height ratios.
Error pattern: I stopped at qualitative proportionality and failed to convert the condition into a solvable fraction along the diagonal.
Diagnostic check: Let the diagonal run from 0 to 1, place the two points at parameters s<t, rewrite the relation in s and t, then verify the triangle’s area equals a fixed fraction of the rectangle.
Use when: A figure has points on one diagonal of a parallelogram/rectangle and asks for an interior triangle area from segment constraints.
Boundary: Ignore when points are not collinear on one diagonal or the needed area depends on additional unconstrained lengths.

Transfer rule: If groups share the same base cost per item, then assume a common cost, compute each group’s gain/loss amount, weight by group fraction, and compare net amount to total cost.
Error pattern: Success comes from converting percentages into weighted monetary effects instead of averaging percentages directly.
Diagnostic check: Set total items to 100 and equal cost each; calculate total selling amount and total cost, then verify the net percentage from totals.
Use when: Use for mixed outcomes across portions of items, customers, or transactions with stated proportions and gain/loss rates.
Boundary: Ignore when bases differ across groups or percentages apply to selling price, marked price, revenue, or unequal quantities.

Transfer rule: If a counting prompt includes an independent category choice plus a flavor/item choice, then compute each part separately and multiply them.
Error pattern: I focused on only one visible combination task and ignored an extra independent factor stated in the setup.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, list every noun phrase that could create choices; ask “Does each selected set also require choosing a type/container/version?”
Use when: Apply this on combinatorics questions with selections embedded in a larger scenario containing multiple attributes or stages.
Boundary: Ignore this when added details are descriptive only and do not create distinct outcomes under the problem’s wording.

Transfer rule: If a mixture’s percentage changes because only one component is removed or added, then hold the unchanged component’s mass constant and recompute total mass from the new percentage.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking absolute component amounts instead of subtracting percentages directly from total weight.
Diagnostic check: Calculate the nonchanging part in original units, convert the new composition to its complementary percentage, and verify unchanged-part mass = new total × new fraction.
Use when: Percentage-composition word problems involve mixtures, evaporation, drying, concentration changes, or any scenario where one part stays fixed.
Boundary: Ignore when all components change, extra material is added, or the percentage refers to a different base at each step.

Transfer rule: If a total-count and two-price total are given, then write count and cost equations, substitute, and solve for the requested quantity.
Error pattern: Success pattern: translating a word problem into a linear system and performing consistent substitution/algebra.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, plug the found counts back into both constraints: counts sum correctly, total cost matches exactly, and counts are whole, nonnegative.
Use when: Applies to mixture, ticket, coin, purchase, or pricing problems with two categories, one total quantity, and one total value.
Boundary: Ignore when there are more than two unknown categories or extra constraints make a single substitution check insufficient.

Transfer rule: If compound growth takes a value to a known multiple after N years, then compare factor exponents and use ratio targets (e.g., square vs. fourth power), not “same absolute increase means same time.”
Error pattern: Mistook equal-dollar doubling for equal-time growth without checking the multiplicative factor implied by the first interval.
Diagnostic check: Write target/start as a power of the earlier growth factor; verify whether the later target is one doubling, half the exponent, or some other fraction of the original time.
Use when: Exponential or compound-interest problems give one time-to-multiple fact and ask for time to a different multiple.
Boundary: Ignore for linear/simple-interest settings or when rates change across intervals.

Transfer rule: If a problem asks for profit/loss percent, then compute gain/loss first and divide by the cost price, not the selling price.
Error pattern: Success came from applying the standard percent-change formula in the correct order and with the correct base quantity.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify sign and base: selling below cost means loss, and (difference ÷ cost) × 100 should reconstruct the percent.
Use when: Use this for buying-selling, marked price, discount, profit, or loss questions with two monetary amounts.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for percent of selling price, absolute difference only, or a ratio unrelated to gain/loss.

Transfer rule: If a component is added to a mixture, then write component/total after addition and set it equal to the target fraction.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking both the changed component amount and the changed total instead of adjusting only one quantity.
Diagnostic check: Compute initial component amount from the given percent, define added amount x, form (initial component + x)/(initial total + x), then verify the solved x reproduces the target percent.
Use when: Apply this to mixture, concentration, dilution, or replacement problems where only one ingredient is added and a final percentage is specified.
Boundary: Ignore this when ingredients are removed, multiple components change, or percentages refer to something other than part over whole.

Transfer rule: If a total selling amount and per-unit gain/loss are given, then first compute selling price per unit and adjust by the per-unit gain/loss to get cost price per unit.
Error pattern: Success came from separating total-to-unit conversion before applying the profit/loss relation, avoiding mixing aggregate and per-item quantities.
Diagnostic check: Compute total selling amount ÷ total quantity; then verify cost price per unit − selling price per unit equals the stated loss, or the reverse for profit.
Use when: Relevant in quantity-and-price word problems with total revenue, total units, and a stated per-unit profit or loss.
Boundary: Ignore this when the gain/loss is a percentage, based on totals only, or when quantity units are inconsistent or converted midway.

Transfer rule: If a rate is given per fixed time block, then convert the target time to the same unit, find the number of full blocks, and multiply by output per block.
Error pattern: Success came from matching units before scaling; this avoids mixing minutes with seconds or inverting the rate.
Diagnostic check: Write a unit chain: target time → same unit as rate → number of rate intervals → total output; verify units cancel cleanly.
Use when: Apply for constant-rate production, copying, filling, travel, or work problems with one machine or actor over time.
Boundary: Ignore when the rate changes, there are multiple stages or machines, startup delays, or output is not proportional to time.

Transfer rule: If a counting-probability question gives conflicting totals or labels, then use the actual sample space implied by valid outcomes and count favorable cases within that same set.
Error pattern: Success came from resolving ambiguity by anchoring numerator and denominator to one consistent population instead of mixing stated totals.
Diagnostic check: List all eligible outcomes, verify each favorable case lies in that list, then confirm denominator equals the number of eligible outcomes, not a stray quantity.
Use when: Apply this to discrete probability problems with numbered objects, possible wording inconsistencies, or property-based counts like powers, multiples, or squares.
Boundary: Ignore this when outcomes are weighted, repeated with replacement, or the sample space is explicitly different from the labeled set.

Transfer rule: If an object fully passes a fixed span, then use total distance = object length + span length, and convert speed to matching units before dividing.
Error pattern: Success comes from modeling complete clearance correctly and keeping unit conversions consistent.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write D = moving length + obstacle length, convert speed to m/s, then verify time × speed reproduces D.
Use when: Apply this to trains, ships, or similar moving bodies clearing platforms, bridges, tunnels, or poles.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks only for reaching, overlapping, or partial crossing, or when acceleration/changing speed is involved.

Transfer rule: If combining work rates or fractions, then add with a common denominator, reduce carefully, and take the reciprocal only after simplification.
Error pattern: Arithmetic simplification slip after correct setup; converting a summed fraction to an incorrect equivalent changed the final result.
Diagnostic check: Recompute the combined rate two ways—common-denominator sum and decimal estimate—and verify the reciprocal satisfies rate × time = 1.
Use when: Problems give individual completion times, speeds, or rates and ask for joint time, especially with unlike denominators.
Boundary: Ignore when quantities combine by subtraction, weighted averaging, or direct proportion instead of additive rates.

Transfer rule: If compounding is more frequent than yearly, then convert both rate and time to the compounding period before applying the growth formula and subtract principal only at the end.
Error pattern: Success came from matching units consistently instead of mixing annual values with subannual periods.
Diagnostic check: Compute periodic rate = annual rate ÷ periods per year and total periods = years × periods per year; verify the exponent is an integer/count of compounding intervals.
Use when: Interest or growth questions state a nominal annual rate with monthly, quarterly, or half-yearly compounding over fractional years.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic for simple interest or when an effective rate already matches the stated time unit.

Transfer rule: If multiple fill/empty processes act together, then convert each to a per-time rate, add fillers, subtract drainers, and invert only the final net rate.
Error pattern: Success came from using rate arithmetic instead of averaging times or picking the nearest single tap time.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compute one common-denominator net fraction and verify it is positive and gives a time slightly less than the faster fill-only time when a drain is present.
Use when: Apply this to work-rate, pipes, taps, pumps, or leak problems where several simultaneous processes change one container or task.
Boundary: Ignore this when actions are sequential, rates vary over time, capacities differ, or the question asks for remaining amount after a fixed interval.

Transfer rule: If a counting result does not match any option, then reread the format and constraints and recompute under each plausible assumption before choosing.
Error pattern: I relied on a single interpretation and arithmetic path without reconciling it with the provided answer set.
Diagnostic check: List each position, assign allowed choices per position, mark whether repeats and leading zeroes are allowed, multiply, then verify the total appears among options.
Use when: Apply to ordered arrangement or code-format counting problems with slots, symbols, and explicit repetition rules.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is not slot-based counting or when the answer is open-ended with no alternatives to cross-check.

Transfer rule: If a mixture recipe gives component amounts and asks for one component in a larger total batch, then compute component fraction = component ÷ sum of all recipe parts, then multiply by target total.
Error pattern: Success came from preserving part-to-whole structure instead of scaling from a single ingredient or comparing unlike quantities.
Diagnostic check: First add all recipe amounts with a common denominator; then verify component fraction × original total recreates the original component before scaling.
Use when: Apply to fixed-ratio mixture, recipe, concentration, or blend problems where a total amount of final product is given.
Boundary: Ignore when amounts change independently, extra material is added or lost, or the target is not the total finished mixture.

Transfer rule: If a quantity is reduced by p%, then rewrite it as A × (1 − p/100) before comparing choices.
Error pattern: Success came from converting a verbal percent change into a multiplier instead of doing separate arithmetic on A.
Diagnostic check: Replace A with 100; subtract the stated percent, then verify the matching choice equals the resulting value divided by 100.
Use when: Apply this on percent increase/decrease, discounts, markups, tax, depreciation, or any wording like “subtract/add x% of a quantity.”
Boundary: Ignore this check when the percent is of a different base, when changes occur in sequence, or when the operation is not multiplicative.

Transfer rule: If two specified people must be adjacent in a linear arrangement, then treat them as one block, count arrangements of all units, and multiply by the internal orderings of the block.
Error pattern: Success comes from converting an adjacency constraint into a block-counting factorial problem instead of counting each seat assignment separately.
Diagnostic check: Count total units after bundling adjacent-required people, compute unit permutations, then multiply by each block’s internal permutations; verify no arrangement is double-counted or omitted.
Use when: Apply to row-ordering problems with distinct people/items and one or more “must sit together” constraints.
Boundary: Ignore for circular seating, nonadjacent constraints, identical items, or when extra restrictions break simple block independence.

Transfer rule: If your computed result is not among the choices, then pause and systematically test for interpretation, percentage-base, or counting-scope errors before rejecting the options.
Error pattern: Prematurely trusted an unlisted calculation instead of stress-testing assumptions against the answer set.
Diagnostic check: Recompute with a table of groups, group sizes, price multipliers after discount, and confirm all buyers are assigned exactly once and discounts are applied to price, not revenue totals.
Use when: Multi-stage pricing, discounts, tiered groups, or any word problem where different subsets pay different effective rates.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is open-response or when the answer choices are explicitly stated as potentially flawed.

Transfer rule: If a circle problem gives diameter, then halve it first and compute area with π times radius squared before matching options.
Error pattern: Success came from converting the given measure to the needed one and then choosing the nearest rounded result.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify radius equals diameter divided by two, square that value, multiply by about 3.14, and compare your estimate to choices.
Use when: Apply this for geometry questions about circles where the prompt provides diameter but asks for area and answers differ by rounding.
Boundary: Ignore this when another measure is requested, a non-circle figure appears, or exact symbolic form is required instead of rounded decimals.

Transfer rule: If runners circle a track and must be together again, then set each time as lap length ÷ speed and take the LCM of those lap times.
Error pattern: I matched rates or summed speeds instead of synchronizing full-lap return times to the same point.
Diagnostic check: Compute each person’s one-lap time, reduce units consistently, and verify the chosen time makes every time/single-lap-time ratio an integer.
Use when: This applies to cyclic motion, same starting point and direction, and questions asking when all participants coincide again.
Boundary: Ignore when they need only any meeting point, start at different positions, change direction, or speeds vary over time.

Transfer rule: If two movers start together and meet, then set their travel times equal; with a known distance gap, solve for one distance and add both.
Error pattern: Success pattern: translating “same meeting time” into equal-time equations rather than mixing speed ratios with total distance too early.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify both computed distances give identical times at their respective speeds, and that their difference matches the stated gap.
Use when: Use for opposite-direction motion from different starting points where start times match, meeting occurs, and one traveler’s distance exceeds the other’s by a given amount.
Boundary: Ignore when start times differ, speeds vary over time, or the given difference refers to time, station positions, or remaining distance instead of traveled distance.

Transfer rule: If a ratio describes two groups that exhaust a known total, then reduce the ratio and check whether the sum of its parts divides the total exactly.
Error pattern: Treating a ratio as fixed counts instead of scalable parts causes false elimination of valid options.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, add the two ratio parts; if total ÷ that sum is not a whole number, reject it; otherwise scale both parts and verify nonnegative integers.
Use when: The problem gives a total quantity and a ratio between complementary categories such as broken/unbroken, wins/losses, or boys/girls.
Boundary: Ignore this when categories do not cover the whole set, totals are unknown, or ratios compare unrelated quantities.

Transfer rule: If a problem gives sum, LCM, and sum of reciprocals of two integers, then first compute the product from (sum)/(product) and immediately enforce integer divisibility with product = LCM × HCF.
Error pattern: Algebra was applied mechanically without checking whether the derived product and resulting HCF were valid integers for integer inputs.
Diagnostic check: After finding the product, divide it by the given LCM; if the quotient is not a positive integer, re-examine the reciprocal equation, simplification, or interpretation before choosing.
Use when: Applies to two-integer arithmetic problems combining sum, reciprocal sum, and LCM/HCF relations.
Boundary: Ignore when variables are not restricted to integers or when reciprocal expressions involve additional terms or conditions.

Transfer rule: If workers act for the same duration, then compare their outputs by their rate ratio first and compute the requested percent using the named baseline.
Error pattern: Misread the comparison phrase and used the wrong reference quantity for a percent-difference statement.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, write “percent of what?” and verify the denominator matches the quantity named after “than” or “of.”
Use when: This applies to joint-work, rate, mixture, or production problems where people contribute in the same time interval and one amount is compared to another.
Boundary: Ignore this when times differ across workers, the question asks only for totals, or the comparison is not a relative percent statement.

Transfer rule: If one value exceeds another by a fixed amount and is a stated percent of their sum, then define larger/smaller variables and solve the two equations together.
Error pattern: Success came from translating each sentence directly into algebra instead of guessing from options or mixing up which quantity the percent refers to.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify both conditions numerically on the candidate pair: the difference matches and the specified value equals the given percent of the total.
Use when: Apply this on two-quantity word problems involving a difference plus a fraction or percent of a combined total.
Boundary: Ignore this when the percent is of a separate total, more than two quantities are involved, or the relationship is approximate rather than exact.

Transfer rule: If two parents’ ages are given at births of siblings with a stated age gap, then shift one parent’s age by that sibling gap to the same reference date before comparing.
Error pattern: I compared ages from different years and ignored the need to align both ages to one moment in time.
Diagnostic check: Write the event year for each age statement, mark the sibling age gap, convert both parent ages to the same child’s birth year, then subtract.
Use when: Family-age word problems give ages at different births, especially with “younger/older by” relations between siblings.
Boundary: Ignore this when all ages already refer to the same date or when only one time point is mentioned.

Transfer rule: If quantities are stated to be divisible by a number, then rewrite them as that number times integers and test each expression algebraically.
Error pattern: I mixed valid closure rules with an invalid operation; divisibility is preserved by addition, subtraction, multiplication, and positive integer powers, but not generally by division.
Diagnostic check: Substitute a=kn and b=km, simplify every form, and ask whether divisibility by the base number holds for all integers n,m; try a counterexample for any quotient.
Use when: Apply this on “always divisible/multiple” questions involving several algebraic operations under a shared divisibility condition.
Boundary: Ignore when variables need not be integers, powers are noninteger/negative, or the prompt asks about a specific case rather than all cases.

Transfer rule: If two movers start together on a loop in opposite directions and you need crossings over a time interval, then use relative speed × time for meetings and include endpoint-only meetings if the wording says “before/until” they count.
Error pattern: I treated all meetings as generic and mishandled the distinction between interior crossings and simultaneous returns to the start.
Diagnostic check: Compute total relative laps over the interval, list whether times 0 and the final instant are excluded, and separately check if a meeting occurs exactly at the endpoint.
Use when: Circular-track, repeated-meeting, same-start, opposite/same-direction motion problems with a fixed stopping time.
Boundary: Ignore this when paths are not closed loops or when the question asks for overtakes, laps completed, or positions rather than meetings.

Transfer rule: If two percent changes share the same original baseline and you need the later interval’s change, then convert each to multipliers and divide later by earlier, subtract 1.
Error pattern: Success came from using relative change with the correct reference period instead of subtracting percentages directly.
Diagnostic check: Set the original amount to 1; compute both later amounts, then verify interval increase = (new ÷ old) − 1, not new − old.
Use when: Apply this to chained percentage, growth, decay, markup, or index problems where multiple dates compare back to one base.
Boundary: Ignore this when the asked change is absolute difference, points not percent, or when percentages already use the immediately previous period.

Transfer rule: If quantities are given in a ratio and a total, then assign each as ratio-part × common factor, sum the parts, solve the factor, and compute the requested quantity.
Error pattern: Success came from translating a ratio into algebraic parts instead of guessing from answer choices or mixing up which quantity is requested.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, verify that the computed values preserve the original ratio and that their sum matches the stated total exactly.
Use when: This applies to word problems with two or more linked quantities described by a part-to-part ratio plus an overall sum.
Boundary: Ignore this when the relationship is a difference, product, rate, or direct statement of one value rather than a shared-factor ratio.

Transfer rule: If a mixture question gives two concentrations and a target concentration, then equate total pure substance before and after mixing using concentration × volume.
Error pattern: Success came from conserving the active ingredient and applying the target percent to the combined volume, not averaging percentages directly.
Diagnostic check: Write three quantities explicitly—initial pure amount, added pure amount, and final pure amount—and verify final total volume includes every part added.
Use when: Relevant for blend, solution, alloy, or probability-mix problems with percentages or rates combined across different amounts.
Boundary: Ignore this when no conserved quantity exists, or when percentages apply sequentially to changing bases rather than a single combined mixture.

Transfer rule: If two averages cover equal-sized subject sets sharing all but one item, then cancel the common items and convert the average gap into the difference between the unmatched items by multiplying by the set size.
Error pattern: Treated an average-comparison problem as underdetermined instead of simplifying overlapping groups algebraically.
Diagnostic check: List both groups, mark shared subjects, remove them, then verify only one-vs-one comparison remains and scale the average difference appropriately.
Use when: Two aggregate measures compare mostly identical collections with one replacement and no individual scores are given.
Boundary: Ignore when group sizes differ, multiple unmatched items remain, or extra conditions prevent direct cancellation.

Transfer rule: If a draw asks for “different categories” without order, then count unordered total pairs and multiply category counts for favorable mixed pairs.
Error pattern: Success came from matching sample-space structure to the event and avoiding ordered-count overcounting.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compute total as choose(all, 2), favorable as count(type1)×count(type2), and verify favorable ≤ total and probability is between 0 and 1.
Use when: Apply on two-item draws without replacement from a finite set split into distinct groups, when the event requires one item from each group.
Boundary: Ignore when draws are ordered, with replacement, or involve more than two groups/items unless you generalize the counting carefully.

Transfer rule: If a question asks when one quantity is a fixed amount ahead, then use relative rate: time = target difference ÷ (faster rate − slower rate), with units matched first.
Error pattern: Correct setup but arithmetic/unit-conversion failure after forming the rate-difference equation.
Diagnostic check: Compute the per-minute gap, divide the required gap by it, then convert that time carefully; verify by plugging back both totals at that time.
Use when: Two processes start together, run at constant rates, and the prompt asks for when their counts differ by a stated amount.
Boundary: Ignore when rates change over time, starts are offset, or the relationship is not a simple difference.

Transfer rule: If asked for a prime-factor product, then divide the number repeatedly by the smallest possible prime until only primes remain, and match by multiplicities, not order.
Error pattern: Success came from systematic factor stripping instead of guessing from option appearance.
Diagnostic check: Re-multiply the extracted prime list and confirm it equals the original number; also verify every factor is prime and the count of repeated primes matches.
Use when: Apply on multiple-choice items about prime factorization, divisibility breakdowns, or options that may be reordered versions of the same factors.
Boundary: Ignore when factors need not be prime, when the task asks for a different form, or when options are algebraic rather than numeric products.

Transfer rule: If discounts are described as applying to a previously discounted price, then multiply base price by each remaining-rate in sequence before scaling by quantity.
Error pattern: Success came from interpreting stacked percentage discounts multiplicatively rather than adding discount rates or applying the later discount to the original price.
Diagnostic check: Write the cost as unit price × quantity × (1−first discount) × (1−second discount if threshold met); verify each threshold is satisfied exactly as stated.
Use when: Relevant for tiered quantity promotions, chained percent changes, or wording like “additional,” “after,” or “to the promo price.”
Boundary: Ignore when discounts are flat amounts, mutually exclusive tiers, or the problem explicitly says to combine rates or choose only one offer.

Transfer rule: If a solid’s volume depends on a 2D base, then compute the base area from the given side relations first, then multiply by the prism’s length/height.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the geometry to the standard volume formula and simplifying any radicals before arithmetic.
Diagnostic check: Sketch or label the base, mark which edges form a perpendicular pair, compute area with the triangle formula, then verify units become cubic after multiplying by the prism dimension.
Use when: Apply this to prisms or cylinders built on triangles or other planar bases, especially when equal sides or radical lengths are given.
Boundary: Ignore this when the figure is not a prism-like solid or when the named height belongs to the base triangle rather than the solid.

Transfer rule: If a speed–time question mixes km/hr and seconds, then convert speeds exactly to m/s and keep fractional values until the final comparison.
Error pattern: Loss of accuracy from premature decimal rounding in multi-step relative-speed calculations led to selecting the wrong option.
Diagnostic check: Compute each distance with exact fractions, avoid rounding intermediate lengths, and verify that train length from relative motion plus remaining distance matches the total passing distance.
Use when: Apply this to passing/overtaking problems involving trains, platforms, people, or vehicles with relative speed and multiple timed events.
Boundary: Ignore this when all values are already exact in one unit system or when the task is conceptual rather than numerical estimation.

Transfer rule: If a quantity is given “per one unit” and a total number of units is asked, then multiply the rate by the number of units and keep the units.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping a rate-times-quantity word problem directly to the correct operation instead of adding, dividing, or matching superficially.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, write rate × count, estimate the product’s size, then compute exactly and verify the result’s unit is the requested total amount.
Use when: Apply this to word problems involving hourly pay, unit price, speed, or any “per” relationship asking for a total over several units.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for the rate itself, a remaining amount, a comparison, or includes changing rates across units.

Transfer rule: If equal-sized groups are swapped in a fixed-size average problem, then update the average by adding the difference between incoming and outgoing group averages weighted by their fraction of the whole.
Error pattern: Success came from conserving the total, adjusting only the replaced subset, and keeping the overall count unchanged.
Diagnostic check: Verify count after the change; compute net total change as group size × (incoming average − outgoing value/average); divide by unchanged total size and compare direction with the sign.
Use when: Relevant for average/mean questions with replacements, arrivals and departures, or removing one subset and adding another.
Boundary: Ignore when totals or counts are not preserved, or when subgroup data are not comparable averages/values.

Transfer rule: If age ratios are given at different times, then shift both ages by the full time gap from the same reference point before forming the equation.
Error pattern: Misaligned time translation between people or dates caused an inconsistent algebraic setup despite a correct ratio framework.
Diagnostic check: Define variables at one chosen time, convert every statement to that time, and verify each person gets the same net year adjustment.
Use when: Problems compare ages using phrases like “years ago,” “hence,” “now,” and give ratios at two different times.
Boundary: Ignore when all quantities already refer to one time point or when absolute age differences alone determine the answer.

Transfer rule: If a circle graph sector represents p percent of a whole, then compute its angle as (p/100) × 360.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping a percentage directly to the same fraction of a full circle, not comparing choices loosely.
Diagnostic check: Convert the percent to a decimal or fraction, multiply by 360, and verify the result is between 0 and 360.
Use when: Apply this on pie-chart, sector, or “part of a full circle” questions where area is proportional to a stated share.
Boundary: Ignore this when the graphic is not a full circle, sectors are not proportional, or the given value is already an angle.

Transfer rule: If a straightforward computation gives a result absent from the choices, then re-read the expression exactly as printed and test for formatting, transcription, or symbol-interpretation issues before choosing a fallback option.
Error pattern: Prematurely trusted the first parse and arithmetic, without auditing whether the problem statement or options implied a different reading.
Diagnostic check: Recopy the expression, evaluate left-to-right once, then compare digit structure and operation signs against the original and the answer set for any mismatch.
Use when: Short arithmetic multiple-choice items, especially when one computed result is simple but no option matches.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt explicitly allows free-response or states that none-of-the-above should be chosen whenever your computed value is absent.

Transfer rule: If a problem gives group ratios and within-group fractions, then compute the overall fraction with a weighted average using ratio parts, not rounded headcounts.
Error pattern: Success comes from simplifying the group ratio first and aggregating exact fractional contributions across groups.
Diagnostic check: Replace each group by the least common multiple-sized counts that make all stated fractions whole, then total the target members and divide by total participants.
Use when: Relevant for mixture, population-share, survey, or demographic questions with subgroup proportions and an overall proportion.
Boundary: Ignore when groups overlap, ratios are not of totals, or extra constraints change counts after the proportions are stated.

Transfer rule: If counting periodic events over a time interval, then convert endpoints to one unit, compute elapsed time, take the floor of elapsed/period, and add one only if the starting instant is itself an event included in the interval.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling as repeated intervals rather than estimating from answer choices; the main risk is mishandling inclusive endpoints.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, mark whether each endpoint is included and whether an event occurs exactly at the start or end; then verify your count formula matches that inclusion choice.
Use when: Apply this to clocks, flashes, beeps, departures, or any evenly repeating process between two timestamps.
Boundary: Ignore this when spacing changes, there is setup delay, skipped cycles, or the question asks for intervals rather than event count.

Transfer rule: If a sequence shows repeated doubling among known adjacent terms, then test whether the missing term preserves one constant ratio before trying difference patterns.
Error pattern: I chased inconsistent additive gaps and ignored the simpler multiplicative structure visible in most of the sequence.
Diagnostic check: Compute consecutive ratios across the known terms; if the same factor appears on both sides of the blank, insert the value that makes both neighboring ratios match.
Use when: Apply this to ordered-number series, especially decimals, where terms may scale rather than increase by fixed amounts.
Boundary: Ignore this when ratios are undefined, sign changes disrupt scaling, or another verified rule fits all terms more cleanly.

Transfer rule: If two quantities are each bounded and no distribution is stated, then model them as uniformly chosen over all allowed integer values and count all ordered pairs.  
Error pattern: Incomplete sample-space enumeration and stopping before defining both the total outcomes and favorable outcomes.  
Diagnostic check: List every allowed value for each variable, verify the grid size equals (count of first values) × (count of second values), then count only sums inside the strict interval.  
Use when: A probability question gives small integer bounds for two independent counts and asks about their sum meeting inequality conditions.  
Boundary: Ignore this when outcomes are nonuniform, dependent, continuous, or when “less than” refers to labels rather than possible integer holdings.

Transfer rule: If converting speed to m/s, then convert hours to seconds with ×3600 only and compute distance ÷ time before checking choices.
Error pattern: Unit-conversion arithmetic failure; an extra factor was inserted, creating an implausible speed and then guessing from options.
Diagnostic check: Recompute time using dimensional analysis (h→min→s), verify cancellation, then compare with the shortcut km/h ÷ 3.6; both must agree.
Use when: Distance and time use mixed units, especially travel-rate questions requiring conversion among kilometers, meters, hours, and seconds.
Boundary: Ignore when all quantities already share compatible units or when the task is conceptual rather than numerical conversion.

Transfer rule: If moves can add or remove only fixed amounts a and b, then reachable net amounts are integer linear combinations ma + nb, checked against nonnegative intermediate states.
Error pattern: Treated a target as obtainable by vague combining and even equated unequal fractions; ignored subtraction and the algebraic structure of allowable moves.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write every candidate as x·a + y·b with integers; verify exact equality and sketch a legal sequence that never requires unavailable quantities.
Use when: The task involves exact measurement/transfer with fixed-size tools, reversible pours, and asks which totals are possible rather than approximate.
Boundary: Ignore this when tools are continuous, tolerance-based, capacity-limited in a constraining way, or when operations other than fixed add/remove are allowed.

Transfer rule: If a modular-expression answer seems constant, then test it with the smallest allowed input before choosing an option.
Error pattern: I relied on symbolic parity simplification alone and skipped a direct numeric verification against the answer set.
Diagnostic check: Substitute the minimum valid value, compute the expression mod the divisor explicitly, and confirm it matches the derived pattern.
Use when: The problem involves exponents modulo a small base, parity arguments, or converting a base to a simpler congruent form.
Boundary: Ignore this when no valid sample input exists or when the expression depends on unknown conditions not fixed by the prompt.

Transfer rule: If variables satisfy nested divisibility and represent distinct positive ages, then rewrite them as multiples of one base and test each candidate for both integrality and distinctness.
Error pattern: I checked only whether expressions could be integers, ignoring uniqueness constraints and simplifying one quotient incorrectly.
Diagnostic check: Substitute x=uy and z=vx with integers u,v>1; simplify each expression fully, then verify it is an integer and not equal to any existing age.
Use when: Apply this on algebraic word problems with divisibility chains, shared birthdays, and a “cannot be” choice among expressions.
Boundary: Ignore this when quantities need not be integers/distinct, or when divisibility is approximate, modular, or not between the listed variables.

Transfer rule: If a multiple-choice item asks for a single fraction above or below a benchmark, then verify whether exactly one option satisfies the condition before choosing.
Error pattern: I computed several comparisons correctly but failed the selection step by not reconciling results with the single-answer format.
Diagnostic check: After evaluating options, make a tally of which choices pass the condition; if the count is not one, re-read the prompt and recheck every comparison.
Use when: This applies to comparison problems with several candidate fractions, decimals, percents, or ratios against one reference value.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question explicitly allows multiple answers or asks for the largest/smallest rather than mere threshold membership.

Transfer rule: If areas must be found from circumferences, then convert with A = C²/(4π) or compare by squared circumferences before evaluating choices.
Error pattern: Success came from correct formula chaining and preserving exact algebra until the final approximation.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify units become area, square each circumference once, subtract, divide by about 12.57, and compare magnitude to options.
Use when: Apply this on circle questions giving perimeter-like measures and asking for area or area differences.
Boundary: Ignore this when radii, diameters, sectors, or noncircular figures are involved, or when an exact symbolic form is required instead of a numerical choice.

Transfer rule: If a verbal sequence says “divide by a, then multiply by b,” then write it as (x/a)×b=result before simplifying.
Error pattern: Success came from translating the operation order directly into an equation instead of guessing from the choices.
Diagnostic check: Build the expression from left to right, simplify the operation factor, solve, then substitute your value back to verify the stated result.
Use when: Apply this on one-variable arithmetic word problems describing sequential operations like divide/multiply/add/subtract to reach a target value.
Boundary: Ignore this when wording implies grouping, reversed order, hidden units, or comparison relationships rather than a direct operation chain.

Transfer rule: If a subgroup is given as a percent of all owners and the overlap count is known, then convert to the complementary overlap share and divide overlap by that share to get the whole group.
Error pattern: Success came from translating a conditional percentage into an equation about part-to-whole, not mixing base populations.
Diagnostic check: Define the target total as 100%; convert “non-overlap among owners” into “overlap among owners”; verify overlap share × total owners reproduces the stated population share.
Use when: One statement gives an intersection as a population percent and another gives a conditional split within one category.
Boundary: Ignore when percentages refer to different bases, multiple overlapping groups, or counts require inclusion-exclusion beyond one overlap.

Transfer rule: If items bought at different unit rates are mixed, then compute the weighted average: total cost divided by total quantity in the same unit.
Error pattern: Success comes from aggregating costs and quantities before averaging, not taking a simple mean of the listed prices.
Diagnostic check: Multiply each rate by its quantity, sum those costs, sum the quantities, and verify the final unit matches the question before choosing.
Use when: Apply this to mixture, blending, combined purchase, or inventory problems with unequal amounts at different per-unit costs.
Boundary: Ignore this when quantities are equal, or when the question asks for total cost, selling price, profit, or ratio instead of combined unit cost.

Transfer rule: If circular seating has adjacency constraints, then compress the forced adjacent people into a block, count circular arrangements of units with \((n-1)!\), then multiply by only the valid internal orders.
Error pattern: Mixed linear and circular counting, used the wrong number of remaining units, and handled rotational symmetry inconsistently.
Diagnostic check: List the final units after blocking, count those units, apply circular count once, then separately enumerate every constrained internal ordering and verify no person is counted twice.
Use when: People sit around a circle, rotations are equivalent, and some specific people must be consecutive or flank others.
Boundary: Ignore this when seats are labeled, reflections are also identified, or constraints are not representable as fixed adjacent blocks.

Transfer rule: If a word problem links birth year, death age, and age in some later year, then model all three events with separate equations before matching any target year.
Error pattern: I collapsed two different ages into one and treated age in the reference year as equal to age at death.
Diagnostic check: Define birth year b, death year d, death age a; verify both a = d − b and the asked age = reference year − b, and confirm these are not assumed equal unless stated.
Use when: Apply this to chronology, calendar-year, and age-ratio questions with multiple time points.
Boundary: Ignore when only one time point is involved or the problem directly states the same age quantity twice.

Transfer rule: If solving an absolute-value equation gives two solutions, then compute the requested combined quantity carefully, tracking sign through the final operation.
Error pattern: Arithmetic/sign-check failure after correct case splitting; the setup succeeds, but the last combination step is vulnerable.
Diagnostic check: List both solutions, mark each sign, perform the requested operation explicitly, and compare that result with substitution-verified solutions before choosing.
Use when: The problem has absolute value, two algebraic branches, and asks for a sum, product, or other combination of the resulting values.
Boundary: Ignore this when there is only one valid solution branch or when the question asks for a single solution rather than a combined quantity.

Transfer rule: If pricing says “x less” than a prior price, then compute the new unit price as prior price minus that exact amount, keeping units consistent.
