Transfer rule: If multiple annual percentage changes affect the same population in the same year, then combine them into one yearly growth factor and compound across years.
Error pattern: Success came from treating concurrent percentage increases as additive within each year, then applying multi-year compounding instead of multiplying time by rate.
Diagnostic check: Convert each yearly change to factors, multiply factors within one year, raise to the number of years, then subtract 1 and compare with any simple-interest result.
Use when: Percent growth repeats over several periods and more than one source contributes to change on the same base quantity.
Boundary: Ignore this when changes are one-time absolute additions, different bases, or explicitly non-compounding linear adjustments.

Transfer rule: If dividend percent is on face value but return/yield percent is on investment, then equate cash dividend = yield × purchase price.
Error pattern: Success came from separating bases correctly; the only failure was doubting the result because it looked inconsistent with expectations or choices.
Diagnostic check: Compute dividend cash from face value first, then divide by yield rate; finally verify by substituting back that dividend/investment equals the stated return.
Use when: Relevant in stock/share questions mixing face value, dividend rate, market price, investment return, premium, or discount.
Boundary: Ignore when all percentages are on the same base, or when the question asks total income, number of shares, or capital gain instead of purchase price.

Transfer rule: If race margins are given at the same finish time, then convert each result into a speed ratio using finished distance/opponent distance, and chain the ratios.
Error pattern: Treating leftover distances as fixed abilities instead of simultaneous-time comparisons causes invalid direct ranking.
Diagnostic check: Write each matchup as speed = full course : opponent’s covered distance, multiply the linked ratios, then convert the final ratio back into a margin on the full course.
Use when: Head-to-head races share one course length and margins are stated as “wins by x m” or “loses by x m.”
Boundary: Ignore when times are given directly, course lengths differ without normalization, or conditions change between races.

Transfer rule: If an equation invites logs or division, then first restrict to values where those operations are valid and separately check excluded sign/zero cases.
Error pattern: I used a valid transformation on only part of the integer domain, then inferred a count without exhaustive case analysis.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, partition integers into positive, zero, and negative; verify exponent meaning in each bucket; then test whether any transformed equation preserves equivalence on all buckets.
Use when: Integer exponential equations, especially with distinct variables, where logs, roots, or monotonicity are tempting shortcuts.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the domain is explicitly positive reals or when exponent definitions and transformations are already guaranteed valid.

Transfer rule: If a work-rate answer you derive is rational, then rewrite it into the exact choice format by clearing factors, checking parentheses, and comparing equivalent forms.
Error pattern: Valid setup but weak answer-matching; I stopped at one algebraic form and treated nonmatching choices as impossible instead of testing equivalence or notation ambiguity.
Diagnostic check: Substitute easy parameter values that satisfy “together is faster than either alone,” then compute your result and each choice exactly to see which forms agree and stay positive.
Use when: Multiple-choice rate/work problems use symbols, same total work in each statement, and answer choices are algebraically messy fractions.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is free-response or when the issue is clearly a typo/printing error rather than symbolic manipulation.

Transfer rule: If counts are given in a ratio but total is a value, then set quantities as ratio×k, convert all denominations to one unit, and build one value equation.
Error pattern: Success came from separating coin-count ratio from coin-value totals and not treating the ratio as value shares.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, compute value per ratio block, divide the total value by that block value to get k, then multiply by the target ratio part.
Use when: Relevant in mixture/count problems with several denominations or weighted items, a total amount, and a ratio of quantities.
Boundary: Ignore when the ratio describes values, weights, or probabilities directly rather than numbers of items.

Transfer rule: If output depends on workers and days, then compute unit rate as total ÷ (workers × days) and scale by the new workers × days.
Error pattern: Treated a proportional-rate setup inconsistently, deriving a unit rate but mapping it to the wrong total or option.
Diagnostic check: Let one worker-day be the unit; verify baseline total equals unit rate × original worker-days, then apply the same unit rate to the new worker-days.
Use when: Problems describe identical agents producing identical items over time and ask for a new production total under the same rate.
Boundary: Ignore when rates change, workers interfere, setup time matters, or production is not linear in worker-days.

Transfer rule: If distinct items are assigned independently to distinct containers with no restrictions, then count as (number of containers)^(number of items).
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing an independent-choice assignment model and mapping base to choices per item, exponent to item count.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “For one item, how many legal destinations exist, and does that same count repeat independently for every item?”
Use when: Apply this to placements, functions, or assignments where labeled objects each choose one labeled destination and empty destinations are allowed.
Boundary: Ignore this when objects are identical, destinations must all be used, capacities/restrictions apply, or order/sequence matters.

Transfer rule: If asked for percent increase or decrease, then compute change ÷ original amount × 100 before matching choices.
Error pattern: Success came from using the base value correctly instead of dividing by the final value or raw difference only.
Diagnostic check: Write old, new, and change; verify change = new − old, then confirm denominator is the starting amount.
Use when: Apply this on percentage-change questions involving prices, counts, measurements, rates, or any before-and-after quantities.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the problem asks for percent of a total, percentage points, or uses a different stated reference base.

Transfer rule: If converting a position from the front to the back in a complete ordered group, then compute total − front position + 1.
Error pattern: Success came from accounting for the person being counted in both directions instead of using a plain subtraction.
Diagnostic check: Test with an edge case: front position 1 should map to last position = total, and front position = total should map to 1.
Use when: Use this for rank/position reversal questions in a single line, list, queue, or class with no missing members.
Boundary: Ignore this when there are ties, skipped positions, multiple groups, or the count excludes some members.

Transfer rule: If total spending must stay constant while unit price changes by p%, then multiply quantity by 1/(1+p) and compute reduction as p/(1+p).
Error pattern: Success came from treating the situation as an inverse proportion instead of subtracting the price increase directly from quantity.
Diagnostic check: Set old expense to 1, scale the new price factor, solve new quantity = 1/(price factor), then compare old and new quantity as a percent decrease.
Use when: Relevant in fixed-expenditure, fixed-work, or constant-product percentage problems where one factor rises or falls and the other must compensate.
Boundary: Ignore when the total is not constant, multiple factors change together, or the question asks for the new quantity rather than the percent reduction.

Transfer rule: If a path is defined by fixed width around the inside of a rectangle, then require the rectangle’s side lengths before computing path area or cost.
Error pattern: Correct pattern: recognizing when given total area alone underdetermines a geometry-dependent quantity.
Diagnostic check: Test two different rectangles with the same area; if they yield different path areas, conclude the data are insufficient.
Use when: Area, perimeter strips, borders, frames, margins, or inner/outer pathways depend on both shape dimensions and a fixed width.
Boundary: Ignore this when enough dimensions, perimeter, or an equivalent relation uniquely determines the needed area.

Transfer rule: If a solid’s total surface area is asked and a radius is given, then write the standard formula first, substitute carefully, and round only at the end.
Error pattern: Success came from applying the correct geometry formula and delaying approximation until after exact simplification.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify units are squared, compute the squared radius explicitly, multiply by the fixed coefficient, then estimate with a common constant approximation to see which option is closest.
Use when: This fits direct mensuration multiple-choice questions for standard shapes where one dimension determines area or volume.
Boundary: Ignore this when dimensions are incomplete, curved and lateral areas are distinguished, or exact symbolic form is requested instead of a rounded value.

Transfer rule: If your computed result is absent from all choices, then pause and audit units, wording, and hidden assumptions before selecting any option.
Error pattern: Prematurely trusted a straightforward cut-count model and then guessed from choices instead of reconciling the mismatch.
Diagnostic check: Count pieces and cuts separately, convert every unit once, then verify your result appears among the options; if not, re-read for alternate meanings or misprints.
Use when: Length-cutting, partitioning, or rate questions where pieces, cuts, and unit conversions can differ.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt explicitly states there is no typo/ambiguity or when a direct formula already matches a listed choice.

Transfer rule: If distinct items go into identical containers, then count set partitions by occupancy pattern and divide out container relabelings; do not use labeled-container formulas directly.
Error pattern: Treated indistinguishable containers as if only size partitions mattered, ignoring which distinct items can realize each size pattern.
Diagnostic check: List each allowable occupancy multiset, count assignments for that multiset with combinations, divide by repeated equal-size blocks, and sum all cases.
Use when: Distribution problems have different objects, identical groups/boxes, and unrestricted empty groups or a cap on the number of groups.
Boundary: Ignore when containers are labeled, items are identical, or constraints couple specific items to specific containers.

Transfer rule: If two objects under the same lighting form similar triangles, then keep the same height-to-shadow ratio and solve with one proportion.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the situation to proportional similarity instead of guessing or comparing differences.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, write both known pairs, set one ratio orientation, solve, then verify the result scales by the same factor as the heights.
Use when: Apply this for shadow, mirror, ladder, or sight-line word problems with constant angle conditions and corresponding lengths.
Boundary: Ignore this when angles differ, conditions change between cases, or the relationship is not linear similarity.

Transfer rule: If a quantity changes by a fixed multiplicative factor per interval, then move backward by dividing by that factor and compare fractions exactly.
Error pattern: Treated fractional targets as equal time steps under exponential change, instead of checking the actual factor difference between states.
Diagnostic check: Compute target/current; if that ratio is less than one interval’s multiplier, the time gap must be less than one interval.
Use when: Growth or decay is exponential, states are given as fractions or percentages, and the question asks for an earlier or later time.
Boundary: Ignore when change is linear/additive, rates vary by interval, or intermediate states depend on extra constraints.

Transfer rule: If a bridge-crossing puzzle has two-person trips and return trips, then compare the two standard ways to move the two slowest and choose the smaller total.
Error pattern: I fixated on one plausible sequence and failed to enumerate the competing shuttle strategies systematically.
Diagnostic check: Sort times; compute cost of sending the two slowest using fastest-shuttle vs second-fastest-shuttle formulas, then add the remaining base crossings and verify every return carrier.
Use when: Apply this to torch/bridge problems with crossing times, pair limits, and a need to minimize total elapsed time.
Boundary: Ignore this when capacities differ, return is unnecessary, crossing times interact non-additively, or optimization is not the task.

Transfer rule: If a question asks about numbers of the form n!+k with 2≤k≤n, then test divisibility by k first.  
Error pattern: Success came from using factorial divisibility to eliminate all candidates instead of checking primality laboriously.  
Diagnostic check: For each candidate n!+k in the interval, verify n! is divisible by k, then note n!+k = k(m+1), so it is composite.  
Use when: Apply this to consecutive integers added to a factorial, especially when the added values are within the factorial’s factor range.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the offset is outside 2 through n, or when the expression is not a factorial plus a nearby integer.

Transfer rule: If a total budget is split evenly over time, then compute the expected amount by the checkpoint and compare actual minus expected to decide under/over.
Error pattern: Success came from converting a yearly total to a per-period rate and scaling it before comparing, instead of comparing actual to the full total.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write expected-to-date = total ÷ number of periods × periods elapsed; then check the sign of actual − expected.
Use when: Apply this to word problems with equal allocations, a stated elapsed number of periods, and a request for under budget or over budget.
Boundary: Ignore this when allocations are unequal, spending categories interact, or the question asks for a remaining balance rather than a variance.

Transfer rule: If a word problem yields a valid pair but the choices are single values, then reread the ask and map each option to the specific requested component before answering.
Error pattern: Correct computation but failure to align the computed results with the answer format or what the options are actually encoding.
Diagnostic check: After calculating, underline the exact unknowns, count how many values the answer should contain, and verify whether each option represents one value, a pair, or a derived quantity.
Use when: Relevant in rate, ratio, or formula problems where you compute multiple related quantities but the choices look shorter or differently formatted.
Boundary: Ignore when the response format explicitly asks for all computed values and the options clearly present full matching pairs.

Transfer rule: If two group totals and the count in exactly one group are given, then set only-total = (group1 − overlap) + (group2 − overlap) and solve for overlap.
Error pattern: Success came from translating “only one” into the sum of the exclusive parts instead of using the union directly.
Diagnostic check: Define x as overlap; write the two exclusive counts, add them, and verify the result matches the stated “exactly one” count.
Use when: This applies to two-set counting problems involving overlap, exclusive membership, or “both” versus “only one.”
Boundary: Ignore this when there are more than two sets, weighted counts, or the condition refers to total attendees rather than exclusive membership.

Transfer rule: If a 3D shape’s face areas are expressed via edge lengths, then rewrite each area in edge variables and multiply before matching to volume.
Error pattern: I matched dimensions by intuition and skipped algebra, missing repeated edge factors created by multiplying multiple face areas.
Diagnostic check: Let adjacent edges be x, y, z; compute the three face areas, multiply them, simplify powers, and compare with xyz and its powers.
Use when: The problem relates products of face areas, edge lengths, surface measures, and volume in boxes or other orthogonal solids.
Boundary: Ignore this when quantities are added, not multiplied, or when faces are not determined directly by perpendicular edge pairs.

Transfer rule: If an integer equation compares a polynomial term with an exponential term, then test all sign/domain cases first and prove a cutoff after which the exponential permanently dominates.
Error pattern: Partial casework plus an unfinished growth argument led to assuming the count without excluding remaining integers.
Diagnostic check: Split into negative, zero, and positive integers; verify sign compatibility; check a few small positive values; then show the ratio between consecutive positive terms passes a one-way threshold.
Use when: Integer-solution questions involve powers on both sides, especially polynomial-versus-exponential growth and a request for how many solutions exist.
Boundary: Ignore when variables are not restricted to integers or when monotonicity/ratio arguments fail because signs, bases, or exponents vary with the input.

Transfer rule: If a product equation is solved by matching prime exponents, then first factor every given total completely and verify by multiplying back.
Error pattern: Arithmetic setup was sound, but a single prime-factorization mistake corrupted all later exponent comparisons.
Diagnostic check: Recompute the target number’s prime powers independently, then confirm they rebuild the original number before equating exponents.
Use when: Apply this on multiplicative counting problems with repeated-value items, equal-count conditions, or expressions rewritten into prime bases.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is not driven by prime-factor matching, or when quantities are additive rather than multiplicative.

Transfer rule: If combining groups with different sizes, then compute each group’s total and divide the summed totals by the summed counts.
Error pattern: Success came from using a weighted average instead of averaging the listed averages directly.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compare your result to the smallest and largest group averages; it must lie between them and be closer to the larger group’s average if that group is bigger.
Use when: Relevant for any merged-average question involving multiple groups with unequal counts, frequencies, or weights.
Boundary: Ignore this when groups have equal size or when the prompt asks for a simple mean of the group averages themselves.

Transfer rule: If one new score changes an average after n prior cases by d, then set prior total as n×a and new total as (n+1)×(a+d).
Error pattern: Success pattern—translate “average increases by” into a total-sum equation instead of guessing from options or mixing old and new averages.
Diagnostic check: Compute added score minus the increase times new count; the result must equal the previous average, and substituting back should reproduce the stated increase.
Use when: Relevant in running-average word problems where one latest observation changes the mean by a stated amount.
Boundary: Ignore when multiple new observations are added, weights differ, or the change is not in the arithmetic mean.

Transfer rule: If a percentage word problem yields a value absent from the choices, then re-check what quantity the options encode before finalizing.
Error pattern: Correct algebra, but mismatch between the computed measure and the answer format/baseline expected by the test.
Diagnostic check: Define CP = 100, compute discounted SP from the given profit, then compute both profit% and SP-as-%-of-CP; compare which one matches the choice style.
Use when: Relevant in retail markup/discount/profit questions where one percentage is applied to price and another percentage describes gain.
Boundary: Ignore when the question explicitly fixes the denominator and the choices are direct profit percentages with no ambiguous formatting.

Transfer rule: If speed is constant in two passing scenarios, then set distance ratios equal to time ratios and subtract the train-only distance from the combined distance.
Error pattern: Success comes from modeling “pass object” as total covered length, not from comparing times without mapping them to distances.
Diagnostic check: Compute speed as train length divided by the shorter passing time; multiply by the longer time, then remove the train length once.
Use when: Apply to moving-object passage problems where the same object crosses a point, pole, person, tunnel, bridge, or platform at unchanged speed.
Boundary: Ignore when speed changes, acceleration matters, or both objects move so relative speed must replace the object’s own speed.

Transfer rule: If pay consists of cash plus an item for a full term, then prorate the entire package, not the cash alone.  
Error pattern: I treated the noncash item as outside the contract’s proportional value, causing a partial-compensation equation to be set up incorrectly.  
Diagnostic check: Let the item’s value be x; write full-term value = cash + x, partial-term value = fraction(cash + x), set it equal to received cash + substitute item, then solve.  
Use when: Employment, wage, rent, or contract problems mix money with goods and ask for a missing item’s value after part of the term.  
Boundary: Ignore when the item is a bonus, penalty, or non-prorated condition, or when the problem explicitly says only cash accrues proportionally.

Transfer rule: If an inequality is multiplied by a variable constrained only to be nonnegative, then split cases: zero gives equality; positive preserves the inequality.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized how squaring ordered integers behaves and ignored sign-sensitive operations and edge cases.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, test extreme legal values, including zero for any nonnegative multiplier and opposite-sign examples for powers or absolute values.
Use when: Apply this on must-be-true algebra questions with integers, inequalities, exponents, or multiplication by a constrained parameter.
Boundary: Ignore this when all quantities are explicitly positive or when the operation is known to be order-preserving on the stated domain.

Transfer rule: If combining groups with different averages, then convert each average to a total, add totals, and divide by the combined count.
Error pattern: Success came from using weighted-average reasoning instead of averaging the averages directly.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write “total1 = avg1×count1, total2 = avg2×count2, combined avg = (total1+total2)/(count1+count2)” and verify units stay consistent.
Use when: This applies to average-over-groups problems where separate sample sizes and group averages are given and an overall average is asked.
Boundary: Ignore this when all groups have equal sizes, or when the question asks for change in average rather than a combined average.

Transfer rule: If a set has a fixed mean and asks what an ordered subset sum could be, then derive hard lower/upper bounds from total sum and ordering before judging choices.
Error pattern: Treated “less than the total” as sufficient and guessed by plausibility instead of enforcing subset-order constraints.
Diagnostic check: Let total be n·mean; for the largest k values, verify candidate S satisfies S < total and S > k·(total/n), then build or imagine a matching ordered example.
Use when: Averages, positive quantities, and phrases like “greatest,” “smallest,” or “could be” appear in discrete-number problems.
Boundary: Ignore when extra structure fixes exact values or when quantities may be nonpositive, changing the ordering bounds.

Transfer rule: If asked for percent increase/decrease, then compute change ÷ original amount and convert to a percent before matching choices.
Error pattern: Success comes from using the original value as the base; common failure is dividing by the new value or using a raw difference.
Diagnostic check: Subtract old from new, divide by the starting amount, then estimate with benchmark fractions/decimals to see which option is closest.
Use when: This applies to before-vs-after comparisons, year-over-year sales, prices, populations, or any quantity-change percentage question.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for percent of a whole, percentage points, or uses a different reference base explicitly.

Transfer rule: If a fixed-job problem changes only team size and days at equal per-person rate, then keep workers × days constant and solve for total workers before converting to additional workers.
Error pattern: Success came from separating total required workers from extra workers and using inverse proportionality correctly.
Diagnostic check: Compute baseline person-days and verify new workers × new days matches it; then subtract the original team size only at the end.
Use when: Relevant for constant-rate joint-work questions asking how many more or fewer people are needed to meet a new deadline.
Boundary: Ignore when rates differ across workers, productivity changes over time, or the task size is not fixed.

Transfer rule: If a set’s average is no greater than every subset’s average, then test singleton subsets; infer the whole-set average must equal each element, so all entries are identical.
Error pattern: I checked only sufficiency and missed deriving necessary consequences from the strongest subsets, then failed to propagate that consequence to related statistics.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compare the full-set mean to each one-element subset’s mean; if any element differs, one singleton violates the condition.
Use when: Apply this to quantifiers like “any/every subset,” especially with means and claims about equality, size, or median.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when subsets are restricted, empty subsets are allowed differently, or the condition is about some subset rather than all subsets.

Transfer rule: If a score “fails by” some marks below a pass percentage, then add the shortfall to the score to get passing marks, set that equal to the stated percent of total, and solve.
Error pattern: Success pattern—translating verbal deficit statements into an equation before checking options.
Diagnostic check: Compute required-pass = obtained + shortfall; divide by the pass-rate as a decimal; verify the resulting total gives back the same passing score when multiplied by the percent.
Use when: Relevant in percentage pass/fail, cutoff, deficit, or surplus problems where an obtained score and distance from the threshold are given.
Boundary: Ignore when the percentage applies to something other than total marks, or when shortfall/excess is relative rather than absolute.

Transfer rule: If selecting people with a “no spouses together” constraint, then first choose the required number of households and then choose one eligible person from each household.
Error pattern: Correct structure, but failed to reconcile the count with the answer set and missed a final arithmetic/feasibility verification.
Diagnostic check: Compute by two methods—households-then-people and total combinations minus invalid selections—and confirm they match before choosing.
Use when: Counting selections from grouped entities where at most one member can be chosen from any group.
Boundary: Ignore when groups can contribute multiple members, restrictions depend on more than group membership, or order matters.

Transfer rule: If two quantities are given by a ratio and both are changed equally before a new ratio is stated, then represent them as common-factor multiples and form one proportion after the change.
Error pattern: Success came from translating ratio language into algebra consistently instead of guessing values from choices.
Diagnostic check: Define terms as a·k and b·k, apply the stated change to both, cross-multiply carefully, solve for k, then verify both original and updated ratios.
Use when: This fits ratio problems where the same amount is added to or subtracted from each quantity and a second ratio is provided.
Boundary: Ignore this when changes are unequal, involve products/percentages, or extra constraints make simple common-factor modeling invalid.

Transfer rule: If a group average is given at an earlier time, then convert it to that time’s total and shift every existing member equally to the present before adding newcomers.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking totals across time changes instead of mixing a past average with a present headcount.
Diagnostic check: Compute the old total, add the uniform time increase times the original group size, then subtract this current total from the new group total implied by the new average.
Use when: Relevant in age or quantity-average problems with time shifts, changing group size, and a request for one added member’s current value.
Boundary: Ignore when no time shift occurs or when members are replaced/changed non-uniformly rather than all aging equally.

Transfer rule: If asked for the probability of special powers in 1 to N, then count valid k with k^p ≤ N and divide by the total count.
Error pattern: Success came from boundary-based enumeration rather than scanning all values or guessing from nearby powers.
Diagnostic check: Compute the largest integer root floor(N^(1/p)); list its powers and verify the next power exceeds N before forming the fraction.
Use when: The set is a consecutive integer range and the target property is “perfect square/cube/power” or another form generated by exponentiation.
Boundary: Ignore this when outcomes are not equally likely, the range is not consecutive, or the property is not determined by an integer-root cutoff.

Transfer rule: If a ratio term gets its own percent change, then multiply each original part by its own factor and clear decimals before simplifying.
Error pattern: Success came from treating ratios as scalable quantities and applying percentage increases to each term separately, not to the whole ratio.
Diagnostic check: Write base parts as variables, compute updated terms, convert factors to integers with a common multiplier, then divide by the overall gcd.
Use when: This applies to ratio problems where different members receive different percentage increases or decreases and the result asks for a new ratio.
Boundary: Ignore this when all members share the same percent change, since the original ratio then remains unchanged.

Transfer rule: If speed and time use different units, then convert speed to distance-per-second before applying distance = speed × time.
Error pattern: Success came from disciplined unit conversion and direct use of the basic motion formula.
Diagnostic check: Write units at each step; verify time is in seconds, speed is per second, and resulting distance unit is consistent.
Use when: This applies to uniform-motion questions giving speed in hourly units and time in seconds or minutes.
Boundary: Ignore this when motion is non-uniform, extra rates or stops are involved, or the task asks for average speed instead.

Transfer rule: If a total is built from nested averages across groups and items, then multiply all levels and compare only the resulting order of magnitude.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: translating a verbal aggregate into a product instead of averaging again or matching a single factor to a power of ten.
Diagnostic check: Estimate each factor to one significant digit, multiply, and count digits; then verify the exact product stays in the same power-of-ten range.
Use when: A word problem gives counts of groups, average members per group, and average amount per member, asking for an overall total or nearest magnitude.
Boundary: Ignore when averages are weighted inconsistently, units do not compose multiplicatively, or the question asks for a per-group/per-item rate rather than a total.

Transfer rule: If a word problem describes sequential operations ending in a known result, then translate them into an equation and undo operations in reverse order.
Error pattern: Success came from preserving operation order and using inverse operations instead of guessing from the choices.
Diagnostic check: Define a variable, write each action symbolically in order, solve, then substitute the value back to verify it reproduces the stated final result.
Use when: Apply this to one-variable arithmetic stories involving multiply/add/subtract/divide steps and a final outcome.
Boundary: Ignore this when the situation requires counting cases, comparing ratios, or interpreting geometry/data rather than reversing linear operations.

Transfer rule: If a word problem gives changing ratio conditions after people/items leave, then write separate state equations for each stage and map the final value back to the asked initial quantity.
Error pattern: Solved the algebra correctly but failed at answer mapping, selecting the wrong choice despite obtaining the right computed value.
Diagnostic check: Before submitting, compare your derived quantity to the prompt target, then verify the chosen option matches that exact value and stage.
Use when: Counts change across steps, ratios are stated in words, and the question asks for an earlier amount rather than the last state.
Boundary: Ignore this when no multiple-choice mapping is required or when the task asks only for the final state directly.

Transfer rule: If one quantity is a stated percent of another and their total is known, then write the larger as a decimal multiple of the smaller and solve the total equation.
Error pattern: Success pattern: translating verbal percent relations into algebraic ratios before comparing options.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, verify the percent phrase means “of the other amount,” convert percent to multiplier, and substitute back to confirm the two parts add to the stated total.
Use when: Apply this on word problems with two related payments, prices, or counts linked by a percent and a combined sum.
Boundary: Ignore this when the percent describes a change from an original value or when more than two dependent quantities are involved.

Transfer rule: If two “after transfer” comparisons are given, then define original amounts, write one equation per scenario using post-transfer amounts, and solve simultaneously.
Error pattern: Success came from translating relational wording directly into algebra instead of guessing from choices or comparing original amounts.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, substitute the solved amounts back into both transfer scenarios and verify each target ratio holds exactly.
Use when: This applies to word problems about two quantities changing by fixed transfers and then being compared by multiples.
Boundary: Ignore this when comparisons involve percentages, unknown transfer amounts, or changing totals beyond simple one-time exchanges.

Transfer rule: If a quadrilateral has equal sides and perpendicular bisecting diagonals, then find the missing diagonal from half-diagonals with the side as hypotenuse, then use the diagonal-area formula.
Error pattern: Success pattern: decomposing the figure into a right triangle and chaining geometry formulas correctly.
Diagnostic check: Halve the known diagonal, solve \((\text{side})^2-(\text{half diagonal})^2\), double that result for the other diagonal, then compute area and verify units are squared.
Use when: A shape gives a side length plus one diagonal, and its diagonals are known to bisect at right angles.
Boundary: Ignore when diagonal relations differ, the figure is not this equal-sided kite type, or another direct area formula is provided.

Transfer rule: If a cube’s surface area is given, then divide by 6 to get one face’s area, take the square root for edge length, then cube it for volume.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the quantity to the correct cube formulas and preserving the operation order from area to length to volume.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify units and chain: total area → face area → edge; then recalculate by checking 6(edge²) matches the given area.
Use when: Apply this on 3D geometry questions about cubes where one measure is surface area and another requested measure depends on edge length.
Boundary: Ignore this when the solid is not a cube or when the given quantity is lateral area, perimeter, diagonal, or involves unit inconsistencies.

Transfer rule: If an age statement compares different times, then define present age as a variable and translate each time shift into an equation before choosing.
Error pattern: Success came from correctly mapping “future” to addition and “past” to subtraction, then solving the linear relation without shortcut guessing.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, list each phrase as “present ± years,” verify signs, solve, then substitute the result back into both time-shifted expressions to confirm the stated multiplier.
Use when: Apply this to single-person age word problems involving relative times, multipliers, and a unique present-age value.
Boundary: Ignore this when the problem involves multiple people, ratios between people, or non-linear constraints requiring more than one variable.

Transfer rule: If ages are given in a past ratio and a present total, then set past ages as common multiples of the ratio and add back the time shift before summing.
Error pattern: Converted a ratio into separate pairwise equations incorrectly/inconsistently, creating algebra that loses the shared scale factor.
Diagnostic check: Let past ages be k·a, k·b, k·c; convert each to present ages by adding the same years, sum them, and verify the resulting present ages recreate the stated past ratio.
Use when: A problem gives several people’s ages, a total at one time, and a ratio at another time after an equal shift for all.
Boundary: Ignore when the quantities are not all shifted by the same amount or the ratio is not for the same reference time.

Transfer rule: If a selling price is payable after time on credit, then discount that future amount to present cash value using the given interest rate before comparing with cost.
Error pattern: Treated the credit amount as principal earning extra interest, instead of recognizing it already includes the time value of money.
Diagnostic check: Compute present value = future amount ÷ (1 + rate × time) for simple interest; then subtract cost price and verify the sign and magnitude.
Use when: Relevant in profit-loss questions involving deferred payment, credit sales, bills due later, or any stated annual rate with a time delay.
Boundary: Ignore when the amount is explicitly cash today, no financing period exists, or compound-interest treatment is clearly required.

Transfer rule: If two people start equal and later one has a stated multiple of the other, then assign one variable to both starts and write the post-spending equation directly from the comparison.
Error pattern: Success came from translating the verbal relationship into a single linear equation instead of guessing from choices.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, verify both leftover expressions use the same start value, the multiplier is attached to the correct person’s remainder, and substitution reproduces the stated multiple.
Use when: Apply this on equal-start money, age, distance, or quantity problems with different changes and a later multiplicative comparison.
Boundary: Ignore this when starts are not equal, the relationship is additive/difference-based, or the amounts changed are percentages or rates.

Transfer rule: If a price is defined by a markup that is a percent of the selling price, then write an equation with selling price on both sides before applying any discount.
Error pattern: I collapsed separate stages and treated the discounted price as if it directly defined the original selling-price equation.
Diagnostic check: Define variables for cost, listed price, and sale price; verify markup = listed − cost, discount = listed − sale, and profit = sale − cost.
Use when: This applies to multi-step percent word problems involving markup, discount, and profit based on different reference amounts.
Boundary: Ignore this when all percentages share one explicit base or when only a single percent change is involved.

Transfer rule: If an overall average lies outside the range of all segment speeds, then first test feasibility before doing algebra.
Error pattern: Skipped a range/consistency check and kept manipulating equations after the setup already implied an impossible average.
Diagnostic check: Compute the minimum and maximum possible overall average from the segment rates; if the stated overall average is outside that interval, flag contradiction or reread for a missed condition.
Use when: A problem gives multiple segment rates or weighted averages and asks for a total time, distance, or mixture amount.
Boundary: Ignore when rates can be negative, units differ, or there are stops, reversals, or hidden segments affecting the overall average.

Transfer rule: If a selling price includes a stated profit on cost, then compute cost as selling price ÷ (1 + profit rate).
Error pattern: Success pattern: translated a percentage-over-base statement into the correct multiplier relationship instead of subtracting the percent directly.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write “selling = cost × multiplier,” identify the base of the percent, convert the percent to a decimal, and verify by recomputing the stated profit from your result.
Use when: Relevant in markup, discount, profit, loss, tax, or interest questions that ask for the original amount from a final amount.
Boundary: Ignore when the percentage is not applied to the unknown base or when multiple sequential percentage changes are involved.

Transfer rule: If a word problem says two operation sequences give the same result, then write each sequence as an algebraic expression in the stated order and set them equal.
Error pattern: Success comes from translating sequential language correctly, especially preserving parentheses when an operation applies to a modified starting value.
Diagnostic check: Before solving, paraphrase each sequence aloud as symbols, expand only after checking grouping, then substitute your result back into both original sequences.
Use when: Apply this to compare “first do this, then do that” descriptions, especially linear operations with multiplication after addition or subtraction.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is not about equal outcomes from two sequences or when non-algebraic estimation is explicitly required.

Transfer rule: If asked for a winner’s share, then first identify the largest count, sum all counts, divide winner by total, and convert to a percent before matching choices.
Error pattern: Success came from using a full ratio-to-total calculation instead of guessing from the biggest number alone.
Diagnostic check: Verify two things: the selected share is less than 100% and winner count plus others exactly equals the denominator used.
Use when: Apply this on multiple-count comparison problems asking what fraction or percentage one category contributes to the whole.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices ask for margin, difference, rank, or a percentage change rather than part-of-total share.

Transfer rule: If a rate must be expressed in new time or distance units, then convert units stepwise with conversion factors and cancel units explicitly.
Error pattern: Success came from structured dimensional analysis instead of guessing from nearby-looking choices.
Diagnostic check: Write the rate as a fraction, multiply by distance conversion, divide by time conversion, and verify the final unit is the requested one.
Use when: This applies to speed, density, price-per-unit, work rates, or any multiple-choice problem requiring unit changes.
Boundary: Ignore this when units already match the question or when the task depends on a nonconversion relationship.

Transfer rule: If a data-sufficiency age problem asks whether information is enough, then test each statement alone and each pair for unique solvability before computing any final value.
Error pattern: Solved the full system instead of judging sufficiency; treated consistency of all statements as answering the question.
Diagnostic check: For every single statement or pair, write the implied equations, count independent constraints versus unknowns, and verify whether they determine one unique age.
Use when: Multiple statements describe ratios or time-shifted ages, and the task is to decide sufficiency rather than directly find values.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt explicitly asks for the value using all given information, not which statements are sufficient.

Transfer rule: If two present quantities are in ratio a:b and a later ratio is given, then set them as ak and bk, convert the time shift to the same unit, and form one proportion after adding/subtracting that shift.
Error pattern: Success came from translating a ratio word problem into algebra instead of guessing from options.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, verify the time conversion, apply the shift to both quantities, solve for k, and substitute back to see the future ratio matches exactly.
Use when: This fits age or quantity ratio problems with a common unknown scale factor and a stated change after some elapsed time.
Boundary: Ignore this when changes are unequal, multiplicative, conditional, or involve more than one independent time/event constraint.

Transfer rule: If a variable is in the denominator of a division equation, then isolate it by multiplying both sides by that variable and dividing by the other side.
Error pattern: Success came from correctly inverting the division relationship instead of treating the divisor like a factor on the original side.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, substitute your candidate back into the original division statement and verify the quotient matches exactly.
Use when: Apply this for one-step equations where an unknown appears as the divisor or denominator in a simple ratio.
Boundary: Ignore this when the unknown is not in the denominator or when additional operations require multi-step rearrangement first.

Transfer rule: If prices change by a constant step across ordered levels, then define the variable for the specifically asked level and build the arithmetic sequence from that anchor.
Error pattern: Misanchoring the unknown to the wrong endpoint of an ordered sequence, causing a valid series setup to answer a different quantity.
Diagnostic check: Before solving, write the first and last terms explicitly and ask, “Does my variable name the requested endpoint?” Then verify sequence direction matches the wording.
Use when: Ordered tiers, increasing/decreasing schedules, arithmetic sequences, totals over all levels, or endpoint values are involved.
Boundary: Ignore when the asked quantity is not an endpoint/term value or the pattern is not constant-step arithmetic.

Transfer rule: If a sale gives total selling amount, quantity, and profit per unit, then compute selling price per unit first and subtract profit per unit to get cost per unit.
Error pattern: Success pattern—translated a per-unit profit statement into a linear per-unit equation instead of mixing total profit and unit price.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify that (total selling amount ÷ quantity) − profit per unit gives a sensible positive unit cost.
Use when: Relevant in quantity-and-price word problems with total revenue and a stated profit or loss for each item, metre, or piece.
Boundary: Ignore when profit/loss is given as a percentage, on total cost only, or when units have unequal prices.

Transfer rule: If a pairing/counting question asks whether two from one group can share the same partner “and vice versa,” then first decide whether the situation is one-to-one matching or unrestricted pair formation.
Error pattern: Success came from identifying the hidden matching constraint instead of multiplying all possible cross-group pairs.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the scenario as a bipartite matching test: can any person have degree greater than 1 under the stated activity at one time?
Use when: Apply this to dance, seating, marriage, assignment, or partner questions with equal groups and ambiguous wording about sharing partners.
Boundary: Ignore this when repeated interactions, sequential rounds, or many-to-many relationships are explicitly allowed.

Transfer rule: If asked which command makes a reusable saved device configuration, then choose the command that copies the active configuration into persistent startup storage.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping task intent to configuration state and storage target, not from picking a familiar abbreviation.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, ask: does this command explicitly reference both the current config source and nonvolatile startup destination, and is its syntax complete?
Use when: Relevant for CLI administration questions about saving, backing up, writing memory, or preserving settings across reboot.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is about exporting configs externally, vendor-specific aliases, file servers, or temporary session-only changes.

Transfer rule: If one number divided by another gives a quotient and remainder plus a stated difference, then write larger = quotient×smaller + remainder and also larger − smaller = difference, then solve simultaneously.
Error pattern: Success came from translating word statements directly into two linear equations instead of guessing from choices.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify the candidate satisfies both tests: division reconstructs quotient/remainder and subtraction matches the given difference.
Use when: Apply this to integer word problems involving quotient-remainder relations, comparisons between two values, and multiple-choice traps.
Boundary: Ignore this when the relation is not exact division with remainder or when quantities are non-integer/approximate.

Transfer rule: If converting minutes to hours, then divide the total minutes by 60 and compare the quotient to the choices.
Error pattern: Success came from using the unit relationship directly instead of guessing from answer size or superficial matching.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, compute quotient × 60 to verify it recreates the original minutes with no remainder error.
Use when: Apply this on single-step time-unit conversion questions involving minutes and hours in multiple-choice form.
Boundary: Ignore this when units are not minutes-to-hours, when mixed units are requested, or when extra rates/contexts change the operation.

Transfer rule: If several expressions are all set equal to one shared value, then solve each variable from that common value before substituting into the target expression.
Error pattern: Success came from correctly unpacking a chained equality into separate simple equations and avoiding unnecessary shortcuts.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the statement as multiple equations to the same constant, isolate each variable, then substitute and verify the result reproduces the original equalities.
Use when: A problem gives linked equal expressions and asks for a product or combination of the variables.
Boundary: Ignore this when the statement is not a true shared equality chain or when variables are related by different independent conditions.

Transfer rule: If motion occurs on a moving surface, then compute speeds in a single reference frame and add/subtract only for relative gap-closing or ground speed as appropriate.
Error pattern: Mixed reference frames—treating gap-closing speed as if it were absolute travel speed, causing inconsistent time calculations.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each stated speed “relative to surface,” “relative to ground,” or “between people,” then verify every distance uses a matching speed.
Use when: Objects move on belts, trains, boats, or currents, especially when someone walks first and then stops while the platform keeps moving.
Boundary: Ignore when all speeds are already given in the same frame or when only one object moves with no relative-position comparison.

Transfer rule: If a word problem mixes percents and averages, then convert each percent to a decimal/fraction, apply the averaging operation to the whole stated pair, and combine like terms carefully.
Error pattern: Arithmetic simplification failure after correct setup, especially mis-converting a decimal coefficient to a fraction/percent.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, rewrite the final coefficient in at least two equivalent forms and verify they match exactly; e.g., decimal ↔ fraction ↔ percent.
Use when: Relevant for algebraic translation problems with verbal operations such as “average,” “add,” and percent-of-a-variable terms.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is conceptual, geometric, or does not require symbolic simplification of numerical coefficients.

Transfer rule: If a total must be split equally among n recipients after removing some items, then keep exactly the remainder when dividing the total by n.
Error pattern: Success came from translating a word problem into a divisibility/remainder check instead of testing options or guessing.
Diagnostic check: Compute total mod group size; verify that total minus that remainder is a whole-number multiple of the group size.
Use when: The problem asks how many to remove, keep, or set aside so the rest can be shared equally among identical groups or people.
Boundary: Ignore this when leftovers are allowed, shares need not be equal integers, or extra constraints change the split.

Transfer rule: If an expression has grouped sums multiplied by factors, then simplify each group first and multiply all resulting factors once.
Error pattern: Success came from applying operation order correctly and not skipping any factor in a multistep product.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each parenthesized part as a single value, list every remaining multiplication factor explicitly, and tick off each factor as used.
Use when: Relevant for arithmetic expressions mixing addition inside grouping symbols with several chained multiplications.
Boundary: Ignore when operations include variables, hidden conventions, or nonstandard notation needing algebraic interpretation rather than straightforward evaluation.

Transfer rule: If counting structured sequences from fixed endpoints, then convert endpoints into a divisibility condition and separately apply every wording constraint to each candidate.
Error pattern: Correct algebra, but weak interpretation/edge-case filtering after generating candidates.
Diagnostic check: List all candidate parameter values, then mark each against a checklist: endpoint condition, minimum length, positivity, distinctness, and whether “starts/ends with” is interpreted correctly.
Use when: Relevant for counting arithmetic or geometric sequences in a finite set where endpoints and a minimum number of terms are specified.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks only for existence, a single construction, or when terms need not be integer members of the given set.

Transfer rule: If asked for perfect-square divisors of an integer, then prime-factor it and allow only even exponents up to each prime’s exponent.
Error pattern: Success came from applying exponent parity correctly instead of listing divisors unsystematically or checking only obvious squares.
Diagnostic check: Write the factorization, generate allowed exponent sets {0,2,4,...} for each prime, form all products, then verify each product divides the original number.
Use when: This applies to divisor-classification questions involving perfect squares, cubes, kth powers, or sums/counts of restricted divisors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is not about divisors of one number or when the restriction is not based on exponent patterns.

Transfer rule: If a selection requires “at least one” from a subgroup, then count all valid-sized groups and subtract groups made entirely from the complementary subgroup.
Error pattern: Success pattern: using complementary counting avoids missing mixed cases or double-counting separate case splits.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, compute both methods—complement and direct partition by subgroup counts—and verify they match.
Use when: Relevant for unordered group-selection problems with categories and a condition like “at least one,” “not all,” or “includes someone from.”
Boundary: Ignore when order matters, members can repeat, or the restriction is not naturally expressed as excluding an easy complementary set.

Transfer rule: If two slowdown scenarios differ only in where reduced speed begins, then equate the change in delay to the extra affected distance times the per-km time penalty.
Error pattern: Success came from comparing scenarios instead of solving for the full trip; isolate only the segment whose speed changed.
Diagnostic check: Compute penalty rate as (1/new speed − 1/original speed), multiply by the shift in accident point, and verify it matches the delay difference in consistent time units.
Use when: Relative-speed word problems give two cases with the same route, same normal speed, and different lengths traveled under disruption.
Boundary: Ignore when more than one factor changes between cases, or when delays include fixed stoppages, variable speeds, or schedule changes.

Transfer rule: If a total-with-subgroup percentages problem gives an overall count and one subgroup’s rate, then convert all percentages to counts and use overall literate count minus known subgroup literate count.
Error pattern: Success came from structuring the data into totals, subgroup sizes, and subgroup-qualified counts before subtracting.
Diagnostic check: Compute subgroup sizes from the whole, compute the overall qualified count, compute the known subgroup qualified count, then verify known qualified count does not exceed its subgroup or the overall total.
Use when: Apply this to population partition problems with one whole split into complementary groups and a property rate given overall plus for one group.
Boundary: Ignore when groups overlap, percentages use different bases, or rates are conditional on another hidden category.

Transfer rule: If a security quotes dividend/interest on face value but sells at a market price, then compute yield as annual payout ÷ purchase price × 100.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing nominal rate from actual return on amount invested.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write two quantities with units—cash payout per standard holding and cash paid to buy it—then divide payout by cost and convert to percent.
Use when: Relevant for bond/stock-at-premium-or-discount questions giving a stated rate plus a quoted buying price.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks only for the stated coupon/dividend rate or when taxes, brokerage, redemption, or time adjustments are included.

Transfer rule: If a problem asks for an approximate value from near-integers/near-round numbers, then estimate each term by nearby easy values and compare the total to the closest option before finalizing.
Error pattern: Exact arithmetic was mostly fine, but the final mapping from computed value to answer choice used inconsistent approximation/rounding logic.
Diagnostic check: Compute a quick rounded version of every term, add them, then verify your detailed result is nearer the selected option than any neighboring option.
Use when: Apply this on numerical multiple-choice items with decimals close to whole numbers, exponents, and several operations where choices differ by modest gaps.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt requires an exact value, choices are extremely far apart, or approximation could change operation-sensitive results.

Transfer rule: If a solid’s formula includes a constant like π but choices are plain numbers, then compare answer formats before approximating.  
Error pattern: Correct setup, but format-check weakness: treating an expression with π as if it were already comparable to integer-only options.  
Diagnostic check: Compute symbolically first, then ask: “Do the options expect an exact form or the coefficient/factor before the constant?”  
Use when: Geometry or measurement questions use formulas with constants, radicals, or unit conversions and the answers are multiple-choice.  
Boundary: Ignore this when choices explicitly include the constant/symbolic form or the prompt clearly demands a decimal approximation.

Transfer rule: If a speed ratio is built from “length per step” and “steps in the same time,” then compute speed = step length × step rate and multiply the two ratios in a common orientation.
Error pattern: Mixing equal-distance and equal-time statements without converting both into a single speed expression causes ratio inversion or incomplete simplification.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, write two factors explicitly—(first entity’s step length)/(second’s) and (first’s step count in same time)/(second’s)—then multiply and verify units reduce to distance/time.
Use when: Relevant in race, wheel, work, or motion problems that compare stride size, rotations, strokes, or counts over equal time.
Boundary: Ignore when all quantities are already direct speeds or when the comparison is not over equal times.

Transfer rule: If a ratio gives one group’s parts and its actual count, then find the unit per part by dividing and scale the other group’s parts.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping ratio parts to quantities instead of adding parts and treating the total as the requested group.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write “known group = ___ parts = ___ items,” compute items per part, then multiply by the target group’s parts.
Use when: Apply this on part-to-part ratio problems involving categories, mixtures, teams, or populations where one category’s count is given.
Boundary: Ignore this when the ratio is not category-to-category, totals are given directly, or the relationship is additive, percentage-based, or inverse.

Transfer rule: If a word problem gives total savings and a relationship between discount rates, then write both variables as decimals/percents consistently and solve the full two-equation system to the end.
Error pattern: Set-up was correct, but execution failed by not finishing the algebra and likely not checking the result against the choices.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, isolate one rate, substitute, solve numerically, then plug both rates back into the total-savings equation and the rate-sum condition.
Use when: Apply this on purchase/discount problems with multiple item types, different prices or quantities, and one aggregate savings constraint.
Boundary: Ignore this when there is only one unknown rate or when discounts are sequential rather than separate linear contributions.

Transfer rule: If two sellers’ total gross profits are compared, then compute profit per unit as price minus cost and set (required units × that profit) ≥ competitor’s total profit.
Error pattern: Success came from translating the word problem into a per-unit margin comparison before using any answer choices.
Diagnostic check: Write both unit margins, multiply the known seller’s margin by its units, divide by the other margin, then verify the result is not less than the needed minimum.
Use when: Relevant for business-word problems involving price, cost, profit, sales volume, and “at least as much.”
Boundary: Ignore when the comparison uses revenue, percentage profit, fixed costs, or changing margins instead of constant per-unit gross profit.

Transfer rule: If a figure has one pair of parallel sides and a perpendicular gap, then compute area as half the sum of the parallel sides times the gap.
Error pattern: Success came from identifying the right shape formula and simplifying in the correct order without mixing perimeter or averaging errors.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify units are squared, add only the parallel sides, divide that sum by two once, then multiply by the height.
Use when: Apply this for trapezium/trapezoid area questions that give two bases and the perpendicular distance between them.
Boundary: Ignore this when the given measure is a slanted side, when sides are not parallel, or when the task is perimeter rather than area.

Transfer rule: If a quantity is converted from linear units to cubic units, then cube the scale factor before applying it to volume.
Error pattern: Success came from respecting dimensionality instead of using the same conversion factor for length, area, and volume.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, write both methods—convert each dimension first and multiply, then compute volume first and apply the cubic factor—and confirm they match.
Use when: This applies to rectangular-prism volume problems or any unit conversion involving powers of length.
Boundary: Ignore this when units are already identical or the quantity is not geometric measure with dimensional exponents.

Transfer rule: If a pricing problem has a fixed fee per item and a usage-based fee, then compute both per item, add them, and only then scale by quantity.
Error pattern: I dropped one cost component by focusing only on the variable rate and ignored the stated per-unit service charge.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list every priced term in the prompt, mark each as fixed or variable, and verify each appears in the final expression.
Use when: Apply this to word problems with repeated units, setup fees, service charges, taxes, or any mixed-cost structure.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt truly has only one pricing component or already provides an all-inclusive per-item total.

Transfer rule: If two independent uniform picks come from the same finite range, then compute P(second > first) by counting ordered pairs or using symmetry, and handle ties separately.
Error pattern: Treated the number of larger values as constant and ignored that it depends on the first draw; failed to average over all first outcomes.
Diagnostic check: List favorable counts for a few first-draw values (lowest, middle, highest); if they vary, sum or average them, then verify P(>) = P(<) and remaining probability is ties.
Use when: Comparing two random draws from the same bounded discrete set, especially with possible equal outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore when draws are from different distributions/ranges or when the question conditions on a specific first value.

Transfer rule: If a price changes from a known gain rate to a target loss rate, then first recover cost by dividing by (1 + gain rate) and then multiply by (1 − loss rate).
Error pattern: Confusing the loss amount with the selling price, then selecting a nearby option instead of enforcing exact percent relationships.
Diagnostic check: Write both equations symbolically—known selling price = cost × (1 + rate), target selling price = cost × (1 − rate)—and verify the second is below cost.
Use when: A percent profit or loss is given and you must convert from one markup/markdown state to another.
Boundary: Ignore when percentages are on different bases or the problem asks only for approximate estimation.

Transfer rule: If a question asks how much is saved from a discount, then compute original price minus sale price.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping “save” to the difference between two prices, not adding or comparing loosely.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label the larger amount “original” and the smaller “sale,” then verify subtraction gives a positive savings.
Use when: Apply this to word problems involving discounts, markdowns, sale prices, or money saved relative to a usual cost.
Boundary: Ignore this when asked for final cost, percent discount, unit price, or when extra coupons, taxes, or quantities change the comparison.

Transfer rule: If a problem gives a polynomial form with an unknown constant for a known sequence sum, then rewrite the standard formula in matching powers and equate coefficients before substituting values.
Error pattern: Success comes from structural matching of equivalent formulas rather than jumping straight into arithmetic.
Diagnostic check: Expand the standard expression fully, sort by powers, compare each coefficient term-by-term, then evaluate only after the constant is fixed.
Use when: Relevant for algebra word problems that hide a familiar closed-form formula inside a partially specified polynomial.
Boundary: Ignore when no standard identity is known or when expressions are not intended to be algebraically equivalent for all inputs.

Transfer rule: If an operation is defined by a formula, then substitute the current input exactly and reapply the same definition step by step for repeated operations.
Error pattern: Success came from treating the symbol as a unary function and evaluating compositions directly instead of guessing from familiar notation.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write the intermediate image of the first input, then apply the definition again to that result and compare both stages.
Use when: This fits problems with custom operators, starred notation, recursive-looking symbols, or repeated function application on a given value.
Boundary: Ignore this when the symbol denotes a standard arithmetic operation or when extra constraints redefine outputs beyond direct substitution.

Transfer rule: If equal amounts of two concentration mixtures are combined, then average the target concentration and subtract from the whole if asked for the complement.
Error pattern: Success comes from recognizing a weighted-average setup and answering the requested non-target part, not stopping at the averaged target concentration.
Diagnostic check: Assume one unit of each mixture; compute target amount in each, total target over total volume, then verify complement + target = 1.
Use when: This applies to mixture, concentration, percent composition, alloy, or solution questions with stated combining ratios.
Boundary: Ignore this when amounts are unequal, percentages use different bases, or the question asks for absolute amount instead of resulting fraction.

Transfer rule: If a count-and-total problem has two ticket/item prices, then define quantities, write one count equation and one cost equation, substitute, and solve.
Error pattern: Success pattern—translated words into a two-equation system and used elimination/substitution without skipping variable definitions.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, plug the found counts back into both constraints and verify they are whole numbers, nonnegative, and sum/cost match exactly.
Use when: Apply this to two-category mixture, purchase, or ticket problems with a fixed total number and fixed total amount.
Boundary: Ignore this when there are more than two unknown categories or when totals are probabilistic, approximate, or missing.

Transfer rule: If a figure is formed by two families of parallel lines, then count each parallelogram by choosing any 2 lines from one family and any 2 from the other, then multiply.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping each shape to an unordered pair of boundaries in each direction rather than counting regions or intersections.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify a one-to-one match: every chosen 2-and-2 set creates exactly one shape, and every such shape corresponds to exactly one 2-and-2 set.
Use when: Apply this to gridlike line-arrangement problems with exactly two directions of parallels creating quadrilateral cells.
Boundary: Ignore this when lines are not in two parallel families, extra directions exist, or the question asks for bounded regions other than those shapes.

Transfer rule: If a geometry question asks for a shaded fraction, then first reconstruct the exact shaded region from the diagram and express target/whole as separate areas before using formulas.
Error pattern: Solved from text-only assumptions, inventing equal lengths and treating the whole figure as shaded instead of extracting relationships actually shown.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, list every segment or region used and mark each as given, derived, or assumed; if any area step depends on an assumed diagram fact, stop.
Use when: Relevant in diagram-based geometry with shading, parallel lines, composite figures, or area ratios where unlabeled visual structure matters.
Boundary: Ignore when the full region definitions and measurements are explicitly stated algebraically with no missing diagram information.

Transfer rule: If straightforward evaluation yields no listed option, then re-read every symbol and operation from the original prompt before concluding the choices are wrong.
Error pattern: Prematurely trusted an initial parse and escalated to “bad options” instead of checking for a transcription or operator-reading mistake.
Diagnostic check: Recopy the expression, name each operator in order, then compute once more from that exact recopy before comparing with choices.
Use when: Short arithmetic multiple-choice items where one misread symbol, sign, or grouping would drastically change the result and create an apparent mismatch.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is unambiguous after recopying and independent recomputation still confirms the same result.

Transfer rule: If a condition asks for possible final digits under primality, then test each allowed prime-ending digit by modular divisibility of the transformed expression, not by whether the resulting last digit itself looks prime.
Error pattern: Treated a one-digit ending as evidence of primality instead of checking whether the whole transformed number is forced composite.
Diagnostic check: List allowable prime endings, compute the transformed ending for each, and reject any case where the transform is always divisible by 2, 5, or 3 for numbers with that ending.
Use when: Problems ask for possible units digits of primes under another arithmetic condition like linear transforms.
Boundary: Ignore when the property depends on full magnitude or non-modular structure, so last-digit tests are insufficient.

Transfer rule: If an overall average comes from one known subgroup and the rest, then write a weighted-average equation or use alligation to solve for the missing group size.
Error pattern: Success came from translating averages into total amounts before combining, avoiding guesswork from answer choices.
Diagnostic check: Compute subgroup totals as average × count, form total = subgroup total + remainder total, then verify the solved count reproduces the stated overall average.
Use when: A problem gives an overall mean, one subgroup’s mean and size, and another subgroup or remainder mean, with an unknown total size.
Boundary: Ignore this when averages are not combined linearly, counts are not fixed whole items, or hidden weighting/percent changes replace simple grouping.

Transfer rule: If a process repeatedly removes “half the current amount plus a fixed extra,” then work backward with inverse step: previous = 2 × (next + fixed extra).
Error pattern: Treated the fixed extra as if it vanished in reversal, causing simple doubling instead of undoing both operations in order.
Diagnostic check: Start from the ending amount; for each repetition, add back the fixed extra first, then double; finally simulate one forward step to verify every stage stays whole.
Use when: Repeated-transfer puzzles say “half and some more,” “half plus one,” or similar wording over multiple rounds.
Boundary: Ignore when the amount removed is not based on the current total, or when the rule changes between rounds.

Transfer rule: If multiple workers’ solo times are given and one is stated x% faster, then convert each to daily rates, scale the faster rate by 1+x, sum rates, and divide total work by the combined rate.
Error pattern: Success came from using rate addition and proportional scaling instead of averaging times or scaling days directly.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify units: each person’s rate is work/day, combined rate is their sum, and estimated time decreases when more workers are added.
Use when: Relevant for work-rate problems with parallel workers, percentage speed comparisons, and a different total workload than the base workload.
Boundary: Ignore for sequential tasks, changing rates over time, dependencies between workers, or when “faster” refers to time reduction rather than rate.

Transfer rule: If a mixture problem gives two component prices, a total amount, and a target average price, then write total-quantity and total-value equations and solve for the requested component.
Error pattern: Success came from translating the word problem into a consistent two-equation system instead of guessing from answer choices.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, verify the found amounts add to the stated total and that their weighted average equals the target unit price.
Use when: Apply this to blend, mixture, or average-cost questions with exactly two components and one overall total.
Boundary: Ignore this when prices are nonlinear, there are more than two unknown components, or the target is not a weighted average.

Transfer rule: If two travel speeds cause late/early arrivals, then equate distance using a common scheduled-time variable and convert all minute offsets to hours first.
Error pattern: Set-up was promising, but execution failed by not finishing the algebra and checking the result against both timing conditions.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify that slower-time minus faster-time equals the total offset gap, and that each computed time gives the same distance.
Use when: Apply to word problems with one fixed route, different constant speeds, and arrival deviations relative to the same target time.
Boundary: Ignore when distance changes, speeds vary during the trip, or offsets are not measured from one common scheduled arrival.

Transfer rule: If source shares don’t form a valid partition or exceed 100% together, then compute defect probability as total expected defects divided by total combined output, not by a weighted average on the stated percentages alone.
Error pattern: Success came from sanity-checking inconsistent production shares and reverting to a concrete count-based aggregation.
Diagnostic check: Assume a convenient common total, convert each source’s share and defect rate into expected defect counts, sum outputs and defects, then divide; also verify the final probability lies between the individual defect rates.
Use when: Multiple groups contribute output with separate defect/error rates and the participation percentages look awkward or inconsistent.
Boundary: Ignore this when group shares are explicitly conditional, mutually exclusive and exhaustive, or the problem already gives normalized selection probabilities.

Transfer rule: If a full container undergoes repeated remove-and-refill with equal volumes, then multiply the target substance by (1 − removed/total) for each replacement.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking concentration proportionally after each refill instead of subtracting the same raw amount twice.
