Error pattern: Success pattern—used first differences instead of forcing unrelated formulas, and verified the increment between differences stayed constant.
Diagnostic check: Compute all adjacent differences, then compute differences of those differences; confirm the second-level values are constant before predicting the next term.
Use when: Apply to ordered number sequences where terms grow smoothly and several consecutive gaps suggest a regular increase or decrease.
Boundary: Ignore when second-level values are not stable, or when another clear structure dominates, such as alternating subsequences, geometric growth, or digit-based rules.

Transfer rule: If one known quantity is described as different multiples of two earlier quantities, then solve each earlier quantity separately by dividing the known quantity by each stated multiplier.
Error pattern: Misread chained comparisons by assigning both multipliers to one base variable instead of linking the known value independently to each referenced part.
Diagnostic check: Write three labeled parts; convert every phrase into equations anchored to the known part; verify each multiplier points to the correct hour/item before summing.
Use when: Relevant for word problems with sequential categories and phrases like “x times as many as” comparing one known amount to multiple others.
Boundary: Ignore when relationships are additive, cumulative, rate-based, or when all multipliers clearly share the same single base quantity.

Transfer rule: If a problem gives a difference and a division result with quotient and remainder, then write larger = quotient×smaller + remainder and combine with the difference equation.
Error pattern: Success came from translating words into two consistent linear equations before checking choices.
Diagnostic check: Verify the remainder is smaller than the divisor, solve for the smaller value, reconstruct the larger value, then recheck both original conditions.
Use when: Apply this on number puzzles involving two integers linked by a stated difference and a quotient–remainder relation.
Boundary: Ignore this when there is no remainder-based division statement or when variables are not related by exact integer division.

Transfer rule: If maximizing an subgroup left unmarried, then first place required married people into the opposite group up to that group’s size; any remainder must come from the target subgroup.
Error pattern: Ignored capacity limits in the non-target group and assumed all required members with a property could be assigned there.
Diagnostic check: Compute totals for target group, other group, and required-property group; if required-property total exceeds other-group size, subtract the excess from the target-group maximum.
Use when: Grouping problems give whole-population counts or fractions and ask for a maximum or minimum overlap between categories.
Boundary: Ignore when categories are not exhaustive/disjoint, pairings impose extra constraints, or the question asks for an average/probability instead of an extremal count.

Transfer rule: If sector angles form an arithmetic sequence around a full circle and one extreme term is given, then use sequence-sum plus extreme-term equations, then convert the target angle to area by dividing by the full-circle angle.
Error pattern: Correct algebra setup but failed to carry the process through to the requested quantity and final unitless fraction.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, compute all sequence terms, identify the requested rank, and verify its area fraction equals its central-angle fraction of the whole circle.
Use when: A circle is partitioned into sectors whose central angles follow a uniform step pattern, and the question asks for a sector’s area share.
Boundary: Ignore when sectors are not in arithmetic progression or when area depends on varying radii, not just central angles.

Transfer rule: If maximizing members of one set outside two others, then first minimize the union of those two using inclusion–exclusion, then place as much of the target set as possible in the complement.
Error pattern: I subtracted an overlap from the target set directly instead of reasoning with the smallest possible coverage of the blocking sets.
Diagnostic check: Compute union = size(first) + size(second) − overlap; compute outside = total − union; the maximum target-only count is the smaller of target size and outside.
Use when: Relevant in set-counting, Venn diagram, percentage-to-count, or “largest/smallest possible” overlap problems with partial intersection data.
Boundary: Ignore when extra constraints tie the target set to the other sets, or when asking for an exact count rather than an extremum.

Transfer rule: If counting integers with a parity or step restriction on an inclusive interval, then use count = ((last − first)/step) + 1 after confirming both endpoints qualify.
Error pattern: Correct series sum, but endpoint-inclusive counting failed by listing terms and not matching the count formula.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, compute the restricted-count two ways: formula and explicit endpoint sequence; ensure first, last, and total count agree.
Use when: A problem combines an arithmetic-series total with the number of terms meeting a regular pattern such as even, odd, or every kth integer.
Boundary: Ignore this when endpoints are excluded, bounds are not integers, or the set is not an evenly spaced sequence.

Transfer rule: If one angle is described as a fixed amount greater than another, then write an equation for the two unknown angle measures before substituting any value.
Error pattern: Replaced a relational statement with a direct assignment, treating a difference condition as though one angle’s measure was given outright.
Diagnostic check: Define interior = exterior + stated difference, combine with interior + exterior = straight angle, solve both, then verify the exterior also gives a whole-number side count from a full turn.
Use when: Angle problems involve regular polygons and wording like greater than, less than, exceeds, or differs by.
Boundary: Ignore when an angle measure is explicitly provided directly, not comparatively.

Transfer rule: If asked what percent a part is of a whole, then compute part ÷ total × 100 before comparing choices.
Error pattern: Success came from using the part-to-whole ratio directly instead of adding unrelated categories or using the wrong denominator.
Diagnostic check: Pause and verify the numerator is the requested subset, the denominator is the full set, and the resulting percent is between 0 and 100.
Use when: Apply this on category-share, survey, inventory, or population questions that ask what fraction or percentage one group represents.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices ask for a raw count, a difference, a ratio between two parts only, or when categories overlap ambiguously.

Transfer rule: If a money problem gives two bill types, a total value, and the count used, then write count and value equations before choosing.
Error pattern: Success came from translating all quantities consistently and using the change in item count rather than the starting count alone.
Diagnostic check: Compute bills used as start minus remaining, set variables for each type, solve the 2×2 system, then verify both total count and total value.
Use when: Apply this on mixture/count problems with two denominations or item types and both a total amount and a total number used.
Boundary: Ignore this when denominations are not fixed, more than two types are involved, or the count after the transaction does not determine used items.

Transfer rule: If one worker makes a known fraction of the total in a given time, then convert that to a per-total hourly rate before forming the joint-work equation.
Error pattern: Success came from choosing the whole job as 1 and translating sequential production into additive rates on remaining fractions.
Diagnostic check: Define total work as 1, compute each stated phase as rate × time, and verify the first phase plus the second phase sums exactly to 1.
Use when: Apply this on constant-rate work problems with fractions of a whole, multiple phases, and one phase done jointly after another done solo.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when rates change over time or when quantities are not all parts of the same fixed total.

Transfer rule: If a selection problem says “at least/at most” from a subgroup, then split into exact subgroup counts and sum combinations for each case.
Error pattern: Success comes from exhaustive, non-overlapping casework that matches the quota; failure is skipping a feasible count or double-counting overlapping cases.
Diagnostic check: List every allowable subgroup count, compute “chosen from subgroup” and “chosen from complement” for each, then verify each pair totals the required overall selections.
Use when: Apply this to constrained-combination questions with a fixed total chosen and a minimum or maximum drawn from an identified subset.
Boundary: Ignore this when order matters, repetitions are allowed, or the restriction links choices in a non-count-based way.

Transfer rule: If two movers start together on a loop in opposite directions, then first-meeting time = loop length ÷ sum of their speeds, after converting all units consistently.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling “meet” as relative motion around one full loop and handling unit conversion before arithmetic.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify speeds share the same distance-time units, add them only for opposite directions, then divide track length by that relative speed and confirm the result’s time unit.
Use when: Use for circular-track, repeated-path, or loop problems asking first meeting, catch-up, or encounter time.
Boundary: Ignore when the path is not closed, start points differ, there are stops/turns, or the question asks laps, distance covered, or a later meeting.

Transfer rule: If distance stays constant, then compute it once as speed × time and divide by the new time to get the required speed.
Error pattern: Success came from using the direct proportionality between speed and time for a fixed distance instead of guessing from options.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write D = S×T, verify units cancel correctly, then substitute the new time and confirm the product with that time returns the same distance.
Use when: Apply this on motion problems that explicitly keep distance unchanged while changing travel time or speed.
Boundary: Ignore this when distance also changes, there are multiple trip segments, or rates are not constant.

Transfer rule: If a shuttle moves at constant speed between two objects approaching each other, then find collision time from relative speed and multiply by the shuttle’s speed.
Error pattern: Success comes from replacing many back-and-forth legs with one total-time calculation instead of tracking each segment.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, compute approach time = initial separation ÷ sum of approach speeds; then total shuttle distance = shuttle speed × that time.
Use when: Use for repeated-turnaround motion with constant speeds, fixed initial gap, and a stopping event when movers meet.
Boundary: Ignore when speeds change, turnarounds take time, directions are not straight toward each other, or the endpoint condition is not the meeting time.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for every possible ordering and gives time per move/rearrangement, then compute the number of orderings first and multiply by that time only if one move corresponds to producing one ordering.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping “every possible combination” to permutations of distinct items, then converting count to total time.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write n!, then verify the wording means arrangements/orderings rather than subsets, and confirm the time unit applies per generated arrangement.
Use when: Small-count arrangement problems mix counting language with a fixed time per step or per result.
Boundary: Ignore this when items repeat, order does not matter, or time depends on swaps/paths instead of completed arrangements.

Transfer rule: If a square root contains a decimal times a power of ten, then rewrite it as √(coefficient)·10^(half the exponent) and estimate the coefficient separately.
Error pattern: Success came from decomposing the radical instead of guessing from nearby choices.
Diagnostic check: Compute the order of magnitude first: halve the exponent, then multiply by an estimate of √(coefficient), and verify the result lies between adjacent benchmark roots.
Use when: Relevant for radicals of scientific notation, especially estimation or “closest value” multiple-choice questions.
Boundary: Ignore when exact simplification is straightforward from perfect-square factors or when no estimation/comparison is needed.

Transfer rule: If a standard counting formula gives a result outside all choices, then re-read the wording and test whether the question is actually asking for per-person count, not total pair count.
Error pattern: Applied the familiar handshake-pairs formula automatically and ignored a mismatch with the answer set.
Diagnostic check: Compute both quantities: unique pair total n(n−1)/2 and single-person interactions n−1; choose only after matching the exact noun in the question and the options.
Use when: Short combinatorics word problems about greetings, links, matches, or connections among everyone in a group.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt explicitly says “altogether,” “total number of pairs,” or otherwise clearly requests the global count.

Transfer rule: If a rotating hand’s angle is given, then convert angle to elapsed time using that hand’s fixed degrees-per-hour rate and add the elapsed time to the starting time.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping circular motion to a constant rate instead of guessing from nearby hour marks.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compute degrees per hour for the named hand, divide the stated angle by that rate, and verify the result matches whole or fractional hours.
Use when: Apply this to analog-clock questions involving hand rotation, elapsed time, and a clearly specified starting time.
Boundary: Ignore this when the hand is unspecified, the clock is inaccurate, or the question depends on hand overlap/relative motion rather than one hand’s own rotation.

Transfer rule: If a fixed-work problem changes workers and time, then keep workers × time constant and solve the missing factor by division.
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing inverse proportion and converting the situation into a constant-work equation.
Diagnostic check: Compute total work units from the first scenario, substitute into the second, and verify the new workers × new time equals the same total.
Use when: Apply this to rate problems where identical workers or machines complete the same unchanged job under different time limits.
Boundary: Ignore this when productivity differs across workers, work amount changes, or setup/overhead makes output nonconstant.

Transfer rule: If multiple workers combine on one job, then convert each time to a unit rate, add the rates, and invert only once at the end.
Error pattern: Success came from treating time and rate separately instead of averaging times or adding raw hours.
Diagnostic check: Compute each worker’s job-per-time rate, sum them, then verify the combined time is less than the fastest individual time.
Use when: Apply for shared-work, fill/drain, travel-rate, or any “working together” problem with the same total task.
Boundary: Ignore when people split different tasks, efficiencies change over time, or rates are not constant or independent.

Transfer rule: If prices pass through successive profit stages, then work backward by dividing by each multiplier in reverse order.
Error pattern: Success came from correctly reversing chained percentage changes instead of adding percentages or subtracting profits directly.
Diagnostic check: Write each stage as current price = previous price × (1 + profit rate), then invert all stages and estimate the result before matching choices.
Use when: Apply this to multi-step buying/selling, markup, discount, tax, commission, or growth sequences with a known final amount.
Boundary: Ignore this when percentages share the same original base, or when the problem asks for net change from a common starting value.

Transfer rule: If evaluating a greatest-integer expression, then replace each term with the largest integer not exceeding it, handling negatives by moving to the next more negative integer.
Error pattern: Success came from applying the definition term-by-term instead of truncating decimals toward zero.
Diagnostic check: For every negative non-integer, verify your result is smaller than the original value and differs from the integer part by exactly one step downward.
Use when: This applies to floor/greatest-integer notation, especially sums mixing positive and negative decimals.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic for nearest-integer, ceiling, truncation, or when all terms are already integers.

Transfer rule: If a divisibility question depends on a digit sum, then compute the full digit sum twice independently before testing any choices.  
Error pattern: Arithmetic slip in the setup produced a valid method applied to a wrong intermediate total.  
Diagnostic check: Add digits left-to-right, then regroup them differently; both totals must match before using a divisibility rule or comparing options.  
Use when: The problem asks for a missing digit or choice based on divisibility by 3 or 9, especially in a multi-digit number.  
Boundary: Ignore this when divisibility is determined by other features, like last digit(s), factors, parity, or modular conditions unrelated to digit sums.

Transfer rule: If an object passes a stationary point/person, then use only its own length as distance and convert speed to m/s before dividing.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the crossing scenario to the correct distance model and performing unit conversion before calculation.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “What exactly must fully clear what?” then verify distance equals full object length and speed units are meters per second.
Use when: Apply this to motion problems where a moving body passes a fixed observer, pole, signpost, or any zero-length reference point.
Boundary: Ignore this when both bodies move, the obstacle has nonzero length, or the question asks for meeting/overtaking rather than complete passing.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for average percent increase per year over several years without saying compounded, then compute total percent change from the initial value and divide by the number of years.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the wording to a simple average-rate model instead of forcing compound growth.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does the problem mention annual compounding, fixed yearly growth factor, or CAGR?” If no, use arithmetic averaging.
Use when: Applies to population, sales, marks, or totals changing over a stated time span with a request for average yearly percent increase.
Boundary: Ignore this when growth is explicitly compounded, exponential, or asks for equivalent annual rate.

Transfer rule: If a grouping problem imposes exact category counts within each group, then first convert totals into category buckets and count valid selections by multiplying combinations from only the required buckets.
Error pattern: Success comes from classifying people by intersecting attributes before counting, rather than choosing from the whole set and filtering later.
Diagnostic check: List each bucket size, verify only the needed buckets matter, compute each required choose-value, and confirm the product matches one complete group composition.
Use when: Apply this to partition or selection problems with fixed quotas by sex/age/type and independent category requirements per group.
Boundary: Ignore this when members can repeat, groups are ordered, buckets overlap ambiguously, or constraints link choices across groups.

Transfer rule: If a fence-cost question gives a square’s area and rate per unit length, then compute side = √area, perimeter = 4×side, then cost = perimeter×rate.
Error pattern: Success pattern: translated area into side length first, then used perimeter rather than confusing area-based and boundary-based pricing.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify units form a chain: square units → linear units → currency; write the three-step formula and check each step’s unit.
Use when: Apply this on geometry word problems involving enclosing a square or rectangular region with a per-foot or per-meter charge.
Boundary: Ignore this when pricing depends on area covered, non-square shapes, partial fencing, or extra fixed/material costs.

Transfer rule: If two groups contribute different amounts of two items and totals are given, then define variables, write one equation per item, solve, and sum the group counts only at the end.
Error pattern: Success came from translating each verbal contribution rate into aligned linear equations without mixing categories or totals.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, plug the solved counts back into both item-total equations and separately verify the requested output is the combined people count, not one variable.
Use when: Apply this to word problems with exactly two participant types, two resource totals, and per-person contribution rates.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when totals are nonlinear, rates vary by person, or the question asks for something other than the combined count.

Transfer rule: If multiple workers complete the same whole job in different times, then convert all times to one unit, add rates as job/time, and invert once to get total time.
Error pattern: Success came from rate-based reasoning and consistent unit conversion before combining contributions.
Diagnostic check: Set total work = 1; compute each rate as 1/time in the same units; add them; final time should be less than the fastest single time.
Use when: Use for shared-work, pipes, pumps, machines, or any simultaneous completion problem with differing time units.
Boundary: Ignore when workers interfere, capacities change over time, or outputs are not additive on the same fixed job.

Transfer rule: If workers start together but must all finish and a fixed break interrupts unfinished work, then compute each total duration, identify who is still working at break time, and add the full break only to those affected before taking the maximum finish time.
Error pattern: Converted fractional-work rates inconsistently and ignored the interruption in the final completion time.
Diagnostic check: For each person, derive total time by dividing elapsed time by completed fraction, convert units carefully, mark whether completion is before or after the break start, then recompute finish times including any pause.
Use when: Time-and-work problems give partial completion data, mixed units, common start times, and scheduled interruptions.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when no shared finish condition or no break/interrupting event is present.

Transfer rule: If a question asks whether one specific item appears in any of the first k positions of a random ordering, then use favorable positions/total positions, not combinations of groups.
Error pattern: Mixing unordered selection counts with ordered-position events; success comes from matching the counting method to whether order matters.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, list the event as explicit positions; verify your numerator counts those positions once each and your denominator uses the same sample space.
Use when: Relevant for random arrangements, schedules, lineups, draws without replacement, or “first/final few spots” wording about a named item.
Boundary: Ignore this when multiple target items are involved, positions are weighted/nonuniform, or the event depends only on an unordered subset.

Transfer rule: If one percent of a quantity is given and another percent is asked, then scale by the ratio of the percents or find the whole first with decimal form.
Error pattern: Success came from correctly translating percent statements into equations and applying proportional scaling without mixing the base quantity and the part.
Diagnostic check: Convert percents to decimals, verify “given percent × whole = given part,” then confirm target part by multiplying the whole or by ratio; both methods should agree.
Use when: Apply this on single-quantity percent problems where one percentage value of an unknown base determines another percentage value.
Boundary: Ignore this for percent change, discounts, probability, or multi-step setups with different bases or totals.

Transfer rule: If a price includes a markup or discount from a base, then convert the percent to a multiplier on the base and divide the final price by that multiplier to recover the base.
Error pattern: Success comes from treating percentage change multiplicatively, not by subtracting or adding the percent amount directly from the final price.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write “final = base × multiplier,” compute the multiplier from 100% ± change, then verify by multiplying your base back to the stated final.
Use when: This applies to word problems about markups, discounts, tax, commissions, or any percent increase/decrease from an original amount.
Boundary: Ignore this when the percent is defined on the final amount, on profit only, or when multiple sequential changes use different bases.

Transfer rule: If a quadratic is defined by two roots, then write it as k(x−r1)(x−r2), expand, and match coefficients/options.
Error pattern: Success comes from converting roots directly into factors instead of guessing from isolated terms or signs.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify both roots make the candidate polynomial equal zero; if either fails, reject it.
Use when: This applies to multiple-choice quadratics that give roots, factors, intercepts, or ask which equation fits specified zeros.
Boundary: Ignore this when the equation’s scale factor, nonquadratic form, or additional constraints are unknown and options are not equivalent up to multiplication.

Transfer rule: If a quantity is a product of known-factor types, then determine its parity first and use divisor parity before counting divisors.
Error pattern: Success comes from testing a global property early; this avoids unnecessary enumeration and prevents counting impossible divisor categories.
Diagnostic check: Label each factor odd/even, multiply parity symbols, then ask: can a number with that parity have any divisors of the requested opposite parity?
Use when: The prompt gives a number by factorization or constraints on factors and asks for divisors with a parity or divisibility condition.
Boundary: Ignore this when factors are not parity-fixed, addition/subtraction changes parity, or the divisor condition is not about parity/divisibility.

Transfer rule: If one worker’s solo time is given, then define total work from that worker’s rate, not from an unrelated base rate.
Error pattern: Mixed up rate and total-work reference frames, causing the solo worker’s total job amount to be understated.
Diagnostic check: Set rates as ratio units (e.g., 13:10 for “30% more”), compute total work = solo time × solo rate, then divide by combined rate.
Use when: One person is described as a percent more/less efficient than another and the job time of one person alone is provided.
Boundary: Ignore when efficiencies change over time or when the given quantity is already total work, not time or rate.

Transfer rule: If a phrase like “x less than n” appears, then rewrite it in both plausible algebraic forms and keep only the one consistent with all constraints and answer choices.
Error pattern: I translated comparative wording too quickly and trusted one algebraic reading without checking for ambiguity or consistency.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, list each sentence as an equation/inequality, verify “at least” vs “more than,” and test every derived constraint against the full set of choices.
Use when: Word problems use comparative language, minimum conditions, and answer choices are small integers that should filter interpretations.
Boundary: Ignore this when the statement gives explicit formulas or definitions that remove any wording ambiguity.

Transfer rule: If items with different unit costs are mixed in stated ratios and sold at a profit, then first compute the weighted mean cost using ratio parts, then multiply by the profit factor.
Error pattern: Success came from using proportional weighting instead of a simple average and applying markup after finding the mixture’s base cost.
Diagnostic check: Let total parts equal the sum of ratio terms; compute sum(part × unit cost) ÷ total parts, then verify the result lies between the smallest and largest unit costs before applying profit.
Use when: Use for mixture/alligation-style questions with multiple prices, composition ratios, and a single overall gain or loss percentage.
Boundary: Ignore when quantities are not proportional to the given ratio, or when profit/loss applies to individual components differently, or additional costs/discounts alter the base.

Transfer rule: If a statement compares remaining money to money spent by a fixed difference, then assign variables to spent and remaining and write an equation matching the comparison phrase exactly.
Error pattern: Success comes from translating relational wording into algebra instead of guessing from choices or mixing up “less than” direction.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, verify the equation by substituting your values and checking both total balance and the stated difference condition.
Use when: Apply this to one-variable word problems involving an initial amount, a spent amount, a remaining amount, and a fixed comparison between two quantities.
Boundary: Ignore this when the relationship is multiplicative, percent-based, or involves multiple transactions or changing totals.

Transfer rule: If selecting people while forbidding spouse pairs, then first choose distinct couples represented, then choose one person from each chosen couple.
Error pattern: Success came from structuring the count by constrained groups before counting individual choices, avoiding overcounting and illegal pairings.
Diagnostic check: Verify a one-to-one map: every valid committee corresponds to exactly k distinct couples and one selected member from each, with no committee counted twice.
Use when: Apply to counting problems with grouped entities, one-per-group restrictions, or prohibited pairings within natural pairs/families/teams.
Boundary: Ignore when multiple people may be taken from the same group, or when restrictions depend on cross-group relationships too.

Transfer rule: If a figure is a semicircle and asks for perimeter, then use half the circumference plus the diameter before solving for the radius.
Error pattern: Success came from selecting the full boundary formula instead of confusing arc length alone with perimeter.
Diagnostic check: Write the boundary pieces explicitly, substitute into one equation, and estimate the result to see which option is nearest.
Use when: Apply this to problems involving partial circles, especially when the wording mixes perimeter, arc, and diameter/radius.
Boundary: Ignore this when the quantity asked is only arc length, area, or a full circle’s circumference.

Transfer rule: If asked for a “third proportional” to two values, then set first:second = second:unknown and solve by cross-multiplication.
Error pattern: Success came from translating specialized ratio vocabulary into the standard proportion form instead of guessing from choices.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write a:b = b:x, multiply extremes and means, and verify both ratios match after substitution.
Use when: Apply this on ratio/proportion questions using terms like third proportional, continued proportion, or geometric progression setup.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for an arithmetic relation, another named proportional, or a non-ratio concept.

Transfer rule: If two scale correspondences are given and the relation is linear, then determine the full affine form from both points before converting a new value.
Error pattern: Treated a linear relation as direct proportionality, ignoring the possibility of a nonzero intercept despite inconsistent ratios.
Diagnostic check: Compute the slope from differences, solve for the intercept using one pair, then verify the second pair and only then map the target value.
Use when: A problem states two pairs of equivalent measurements, rates, or temperatures on different linear scales.
Boundary: Ignore when the relation is explicitly proportional through the origin or when more than linear behavior is stated.

Transfer rule: If a word problem gives sequential operations ending in a known result, then translate each step in order into one equation before choosing an option.
Error pattern: Success came from preserving operation order and grouping; common failure is misreading phrases and dropping needed parentheses.
Diagnostic check: Write the expression after each sentence, then expand and reverse-substitute your found value through the original steps to confirm it reproduces the stated result.
Use when: Apply this to single-variable arithmetic/algebra problems with chained actions like multiply, add, then scale, especially in multiple-choice settings.
Boundary: Ignore this when the problem is about counting cases, geometry, data interpretation, or when operation order is explicitly non-sequential.

Transfer rule: If two percentages are each stated relative to the same baseline, then convert both to multipliers and compare with actual/projected.
Error pattern: Success comes from anchoring both changes to one reference value instead of combining percentage changes directly.
Diagnostic check: Set a simple base like 100, compute each scenario from that base, then divide the target quantity by the comparison quantity.
Use when: Relevant in word problems with projected vs actual, increase vs decrease, or any pair of percent changes tied to the same original amount.
Boundary: Ignore this when percentages are chained from different intermediate bases or when the question asks for absolute change rather than a ratio.

Transfer rule: If a moving object fully passes a point, then use its own length/time to get speed; if it fully passes a segment, then add object length and segment length before dividing by speed.
Error pattern: Success comes from modeling “fully pass” with total clearance distance, not just the external object’s length.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write two distances: point-crossing distance = object length; segment-crossing distance = object length + segment length, then verify time = distance/speed.
Use when: Applies to train, conveyor, runner, or vehicle problems about crossing poles, people, bridges, tunnels, or platforms.
Boundary: Ignore when acceleration occurs, partial crossing is asked, or lengths/speeds use inconsistent units.

Transfer rule: If profit is stated as the selling price of some units, then let unit selling price be s, write total SP = total CP + profit, and solve for CP before computing profit%.
Error pattern: Mixed up selling price and cost price for the same units, assuming the profit expression used cost units without deriving the actual relation.
Diagnostic check: Set unit SP = s; form an equation like total SP − referenced SP = total CP; then verify profit% = (SP − CP)/CP with consistent units.
Use when: Quantity-based profit/loss problems compare gain or loss to the selling or cost value of a different number of units.
Boundary: Ignore when profit/loss is directly given as a percent or all compared amounts are already in the same price basis.

Transfer rule: If a sequence has adjacent pairs where the second may be a fixed transform of the first, then test pairwise mappings before using differences.
Error pattern: I chased noisy first-order differences and vague trend language instead of checking simple local operations repeated across terms.
Diagnostic check: Split into consecutive pairs, compute the same operation from each odd term to the next even term, and verify it fits all visible pairs.
Use when: Relevant for short number sequences with alternating-looking terms, especially when some values suggest squares, doubles, halves, or other basic arithmetic links.
Boundary: Ignore when pairwise transforms fail consistently or when position-based recurrences explain more terms with fewer assumptions.

Transfer rule: If buy/sell changes are stated relative to the same reference value, then convert both to multiples of that value and compute profit percent using profit divided by cost.
Error pattern: Success came from anchoring both percentages to one baseline instead of adding or subtracting percent changes directly.
Diagnostic check: Set the reference value to 1, compute cost and selling price as factors, then verify the final percent uses (selling−cost)/cost, not /reference.
Use when: Apply this for profit-loss or markup-discount questions where both adjustments are measured from a common stated value.
Boundary: Ignore this when percentages are chained on different bases, compounded over stages, or one change is defined from cost and the other from selling price.

Transfer rule: If a moving-object timing question involves passing a fixed point, then convert speed to distance-per-second first and use only the object’s own length as distance.
Error pattern: Success came from selecting the correct distance model and doing a unit conversion before arithmetic.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write “fixed point or extended object?” and verify units match; for a fixed point, distance should equal just the object length.
Use when: Apply this to motion problems asking how long a vehicle, train, or runner takes to clear a pole, tree, marker, or observer.
Boundary: Ignore this when both objects have length, relative motion is involved, or acceleration changes speed during the event.

Transfer rule: If testing odd/even in multiple choice, then rewrite each formula unambiguously, compute f(-x), simplify fully, and compare with -f(x) for every option before choosing.
Error pattern: The failure came from notation/parsing ambiguity and stopping after an apparent mismatch instead of verifying each candidate systematically.
Diagnostic check: Expand exponents/grouping explicitly; for each option, make a two-column check of f(-x) and -f(x), then confirm exactly one option fails.
Use when: The problem asks about function parity and options include compressed notation, absolute value, or mixtures of different term types.
Boundary: Ignore this when the domain is not symmetric about zero or the question is not about parity.

Transfer rule: If partnership shares are fractional and one partner changes capital midyear, then convert all capitals to a common integer base and compute capital×time for each interval before taking profit ratios.
Error pattern: Failure came from inconsistent fraction handling and premature decimal conversion, which distorted equivalent capitals and the final ratio.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, rewrite each capital with one LCM denominator, split the year at every change point, total each person’s capital-months, and verify the resulting ratio is fully simplified.
Use when: This applies to profit-sharing, partnership, work-rate, or investment problems where amounts change over different time segments.
Boundary: Ignore this when all contributions stay constant for the whole period or when profit is not proportional to capital multiplied by time.

Transfer rule: If two movers start together and meet, then set their travel times equal and combine their distances to get the total.
Error pattern: Success came from translating a relative-distance statement into variables and enforcing the shared-time condition instead of guessing from speeds alone.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify you used one common time variable or an equation of equal times, and confirm total distance equals the sum of both traveled parts.
Use when: Apply this to meeting-motion word problems with opposite directions, known speeds, and an extra relation between distances already covered.
Boundary: Ignore this when start times differ, there are stops/accelerations, or the relation is about remaining distance rather than distance traveled.

Transfer rule: If a variable is fixed as odd or even, then test any expression containing just that variable before combining parity rules.
Error pattern: Success comes from using invariance: some forms keep a forced parity under all allowed values, while others only guarantee being even.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite givens as 2k or 2k+1 and simplify each choice’s parity; ask “forced odd, forced even, or variable?”
Use when: Apply on integer multiple-choice questions involving odd/even conditions, products, powers, or adding 1 to a constrained variable.
Boundary: Ignore when domains are nonintegers, parity is undefined, or the task depends on magnitude, sign, divisibility beyond 2, or exceptions like zero-specific wording.

Transfer rule: If profit or loss is stated as a fraction of selling price, then convert it to cost price before computing percentage on cost.
Error pattern: Used the wrong base quantity; percentage of loss/profit was taken on selling price instead of the required cost price.
Diagnostic check: Set selling price to a simple value, compute loss/profit, derive cost price, then verify percentage = amount divided by cost price.
Use when: Relevant in profit-and-loss questions where the amount is given relative to selling price, not cost price.
Boundary: Ignore when the question explicitly asks for a percentage on selling price or all quantities already share the same base.

Transfer rule: If actions alternate in a fixed two-step cycle, then compute the net change per full cycle and map any target to cycle endpoints before selecting an answer.
Error pattern: I relied on long step-by-step listing and stopped early instead of abstracting the repeating pattern and checking whether the target appears after a later repeat.
Diagnostic check: Write balances after each full two-day cycle, then add the next positive-step amount; verify whether the target is reached at a cycle end or immediately after the positive day.
Use when: Use this for alternating gain/loss sequences, periodic accumulation, or questions asking when a running total first hits a target.
Boundary: Ignore this when amounts vary irregularly, the cycle length is not fixed, or the question asks for total earned/spent rather than current balance.

Transfer rule: If a word problem asks how much each person gets from a total shared equally, then compute total ÷ number of recipients.
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing equal-sharing structure and choosing division instead of matching tempting leftover numbers from the prompt.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask “Am I finding groups or amount per group?” and verify by multiplying your quotient by the number of recipients to recover the total.
Use when: Apply this to fair-share, per-person, split-evenly, or distributed-among problems with a known total and known number of people or groups.
Boundary: Ignore this when shares are unequal, remainders matter, or the question asks for number of groups rather than amount each.

Transfer rule: If a question gives a per-period cost, a number of periods, and current funds, then compute total needed = rate × periods and subtract current funds.
Error pattern: Success came from translating the story into a two-step arithmetic model instead of comparing choices loosely or using one operation only.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write the equation “extra = (cost each × count) − amount already owned” and verify units stay as money.
Use when: Apply this to word problems about repeated equal spending, saving, or earning across several days, items, or trips.
Boundary: Ignore this when costs vary by period, totals are already given, or the question asks for total spending rather than additional amount.

Transfer rule: If a monic quadratic has integer roots and a fixed positive constant term, then enumerate all distinct integer factor pairs of that constant, including both same-sign cases allowed by the product sign, and map each pair to the middle coefficient via Vieta.
Error pattern: Counted only one sign pattern and missed symmetric coefficient values arising from negative root pairs.
Diagnostic check: List every unordered factor pair of the constant; for each, generate all valid sign assignments matching the product sign, compute the coefficient from the root sum, deduplicate, then count.
Use when: Quadratics ask for how many possible coefficients or sums arise from integer roots with known product.
Boundary: Ignore when roots need not be integers or the constant term/root product is unfixed.

Transfer rule: If a price passes through successive profit/loss changes and the final price is known, then reverse each step using division by its multiplier.
Error pattern: Success comes from keeping cost and selling price roles separate and treating gains/losses multiplicatively, not as additive percentage changes.
Diagnostic check: Write each transaction as new price = old price × (1 ± rate); when moving backward, divide in reverse order and verify by replaying forward.
Use when: Apply this to chained buy-sell or markup-discount problems with several percentage changes on the same item.
Boundary: Ignore this when percentages refer to different bases, include extra fixed amounts, or ask for overall net percentage directly.

Transfer rule: If a total rent is shared by participants with varying quantities over time, then allocate cost in proportion to each participant’s quantity × time contribution over the grand total.
Error pattern: I used an incomplete denominator first, excluding one participant, then started correcting but failed to finish the proportional-share calculation.
Diagnostic check: Compute every participant’s unit-time usage, sum all shares, divide total cost by that sum, then verify one person’s payment plus others would recover the full rent.
Use when: This applies to partnership, rent, labor, grazing, or usage problems where both amount and duration vary across parties.
Boundary: Ignore this when charges are fixed per person, nonproportional, or determined by rates that differ across participants or periods.

Transfer rule: If a probability depends on counting special integers in a range, then enumerate them systematically and verify the count before matching an option.
Error pattern: Miscounting a listed set; the reasoning process was appropriate, but the tally did not match the actual enumeration.
Diagnostic check: After listing candidates, count them twice: once sequentially and once by grouping marks, and confirm none are repeated or skipped.
Use when: Relevant for uniform-selection questions over small integer ranges where the answer is count of qualifying numbers over total outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore when qualification is given by a direct formula, the set is too large for listing, or outcomes are not equally likely.

Transfer rule: If profit shares come from capital-time products, then set full-year partner product and withdrawn partner product in the same order as the stated share ratio before solving.
Error pattern: Used the ratio upside down and failed to sanity-check whether the result fit the answer set.
Diagnostic check: Write capital×time for each person, map left/right profit-ratio terms to the matching person, solve, then verify the result reproduces the given ratio exactly.
Use when: Partnership or work-share questions involve unequal investments and one person enters late or exits early.
Boundary: Ignore when profit is not proportional to capital×time, or when extra conditions like changing capital amounts or multiple intervals are given.

Transfer rule: If a polynomial has only odd-power terms plus a constant, then use g(−x)=2c−g(x), where c is the constant term.
Error pattern: Sign-handling was partly right, but the constant term was reflected incorrectly when converting from the known value at x to the value at −x.
Diagnostic check: Separate the function into odd part and constant; verify odd terms flip sign, constant stays fixed, then compute 2c−given value and compare.
Use when: Apply this for expressions evaluated at opposite inputs, especially polynomials or functions with clear odd/even symmetry plus a standalone constant.
Boundary: Ignore this when even-power terms, nonpolynomial asymmetries, or input shifts/scalings break the simple x↔−x symmetry.

Transfer rule: If counting integers satisfying multiple remainder conditions below a limit, then first combine them into one arithmetic progression and count terms with an inclusive endpoint formula.
Error pattern: Set up the congruences correctly but failed to finish by converting the progression into an exact count under the bound.
Diagnostic check: Find the first valid term and common step, then compute floor((limit-1-first)/step)+1, and verify the last term is below the limit.
Use when: The problem gives simultaneous modular conditions and asks how many positive integers up to a cutoff satisfy them.
Boundary: Ignore this when asked for a specific value, when the range is not bounded above, or when conditions are not periodic congruences.

Transfer rule: If a solid’s corresponding lengths are in ratio a:b, then scale any area measure by a²:b² before comparing.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the asked quantity to its dimension and squaring the linear ratio instead of using it directly or cubing it.
Diagnostic check: Identify the unit type in the formula; if it uses squared length, square the side ratio and verify constants cancel in the ratio.
Use when: The problem compares similar figures or solids and asks for surface area, face area, painted area, or any other 2D measure.
Boundary: Ignore this when the quantity is linear or volumetric, or when the shapes are not similar/corresponding dimensions are unclear.

Transfer rule: If two unit counts are given for the same reference unit, then divide the larger-unit count by the smaller-unit count to get one in terms of the other.
Error pattern: Success came from using an equivalence ratio instead of converting through unrelated formulas or guessing by prefix familiarity.
Diagnostic check: Write “same base unit = count A of unit A = count B of unit B,” then compute count B ÷ count A and verify the result is “unit B per unit A.”
Use when: Relevant in unit-conversion questions that provide two equalities to the same benchmark quantity.
Boundary: Ignore when the equalities are not to the same benchmark or when the relationship is nonlinear.

Transfer rule: If two shapes have equal area and one dimension of the target shape is given, then compute the known area first and isolate the missing dimension with the area formula.
Error pattern: Success came from translating the word statement directly into an equation instead of guessing from answer choices.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, write both area formulas, substitute the known measurements, solve symbolically for the unknown, and verify by plugging back into the target area.
Use when: Apply this on geometry word problems that equate areas across different shapes and ask for one missing side.
Boundary: Ignore this when figures are not stated to have equal area or when scaling, perimeter, or unit conversion is the real focus.

Transfer rule: If a solid must physically fit into a box, then maximize whole-item counts by dimension-by-dimension placement using item extents in possible orientations, not by volume ratio.
Error pattern: Used continuous volume comparison for a discrete packing problem, ignoring diameter, orientation, and leftover unusable space.
Diagnostic check: Compute the item’s full span along each box edge for each orientation, take floor(edge/span), multiply the three counts, and compare orientations.
Use when: Objects are rigid, identical, and placed in rectangular containers, especially cylinders, spheres, or other shapes that waste space between boundaries.
Boundary: Ignore this when the problem explicitly asks only about volume/material, allows deformation, or provides packing-density assumptions.

Transfer rule: If a concentration changes after adding a pure component, then set pure amount over total volume equal to the target concentration and solve.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking both numerator and denominator after the addition instead of changing only one quantity.
Diagnostic check: Compute initial pure amount, define added pure amount, write new pure and new total, then verify the solved value reproduces the target ratio.
Use when: Apply this to mixture or concentration problems where a solution is strengthened by adding undiluted solute.
Boundary: Ignore this when material is removed, diluted with zero-solute liquid, or percentages refer to something other than volume-based composition.

Transfer rule: If a figure is formed by two families of parallel lines, then count each parallelogram by choosing any 2 lines from one family and any 2 from the other, then multiply.
Error pattern: Success comes from mapping a shape-counting diagram to independent pair selections rather than counting visible regions one by one.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify the target shape is uniquely determined by four boundary lines: two from family one and two from family two.
Use when: Apply this to grid-like networks made from exactly two distinct directions of parallel lines and the question asks for total parallelograms.
Boundary: Ignore this when lines are not in two parallel families, shapes are restricted by size/location, or extra diagonals/curves create non-unique boundaries.

Transfer rule: If two bodies fully pass while moving oppositely, then use combined length ÷ crossing time for relative speed, split it by the given speed ratio, then convert units.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling crossing as relative motion and keeping distance, ratio, and unit conversion consistent.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify: crossing distance = sum of lengths; opposite directions means speeds add; ratio parts sum correctly; final unit matches the choices.
Use when: Apply to pass-by or overtake problems involving object lengths, crossing time, and a stated speed ratio or relation.
Boundary: Ignore when lengths are negligible, motion is not along one line, or the question already gives relative speed directly.

Transfer rule: If a straightforward setup yields a value outside all choices, then plug answer choices into the story and test alternate meanings of any transaction phrase before committing.
Error pattern: Over-trusting one algebraic interpretation when wording about taxes, fees, or proceeds may allow more than one money-flow model.
Diagnostic check: Write a one-line cash ledger for each event, compute resulting quantity from each plausible interpretation, and verify the stated quantity change exactly matches.
Use when: Multi-step word problems involve selling, deductions, repurchasing, and a final count difference tied to answer choices.
Boundary: Ignore when quantities are defined unambiguously, no transactional wording is ambiguous, and your solved value cleanly matches a choice.

Transfer rule: If a quantity is a percent of a percent of a whole, then multiply the percentages first and divide the given part by that combined fraction.
Error pattern: Success came from translating nested percentages into a single proportion instead of treating each percentage as applying to the total.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, write “target part = (outer fraction)(inner fraction)(whole)” and verify units; then use the minimum allowed target part for “at least” questions.
Use when: Apply this on multistep percent/allocation problems with nested categories and a request for the smallest or largest possible whole.
Boundary: Ignore this when percentages compare changes over time, overlap between groups, or are not applied sequentially to the same base.

Transfer rule: If a range word like “between” is ambiguous in a multiple-choice sum, then compute both exclusive and inclusive totals before choosing.
Error pattern: Correct method, but language interpretation failed by assuming endpoints were excluded without checking answer-fit conventions.
Diagnostic check: Calculate term count and sum twice—start/end excluded and included—and see which result matches a listed option cleanly.
Use when: Integer-sequence or arithmetic-series questions use natural numbers in a bounded range and wording may or may not include endpoints.
Boundary: Ignore this when the problem explicitly says “strictly between,” “inclusive,” or directly lists the first and last terms.

Transfer rule: If asked for a digit’s place value, then identify its position from right to left and multiply the digit by that place.
Error pattern: Success came from using positional notation instead of matching the digit to its face value or a nearby place.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label places ones-tens-hundreds-thousands from the right, point to the target digit, and compute digit × place unit.
Use when: Relevant for whole-number questions asking for place, place value, expanded form, or value of a specific digit.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for the digit itself, compares numbers without digit value, or uses non-base-ten representations.

Transfer rule: If ages are given in a ratio and a past total is known, then assign ratio multiples, subtract the time gap from each, form one linear equation, and solve the common factor.
Error pattern: Success pattern—translate ratios into algebraic multiples and apply the same time shift consistently to every person before summing.
Diagnostic check: Verify two ways: the past-total equation balances after substitution, and dividing the final ages by the ratio parts gives one identical common factor.
Use when: Relevant for multi-person age problems involving present ratios plus a uniform before/after time statement and a total age condition.
Boundary: Ignore when ratios compare different times, time shifts are unequal, or relationships are non-additive rather than sum-based.

Transfer rule: If one solid is melted into identical new solids, then equate total volume, divide by the count, and solve using the target solid’s formula.
Error pattern: Success came from conserving volume and converting diameter to radius before substitution.
Diagnostic check: Compute source volume, divide by the number of pieces, solve for the target radius, then substitute back to verify the per-piece volume matches exactly.
Use when: Apply for geometry word problems involving reshaping without loss, especially cylinders, spheres, cones, or mixed solids with shared material.
Boundary: Ignore when material is added/removed, dimensions describe surface area, or the quantity sought is not determined by volume conservation.

Transfer rule: If a point is described by distance from a reference point and a side condition, then compute the base distance, scale it, and place the result on the allowed side.
Error pattern: Success came from translating words into absolute-distance steps and using the inequality to choose the correct direction.
Diagnostic check: Find the distance between the two given points, multiply by the stated factor, then verify the candidate is exactly that far from the reference and satisfies the side condition.
Use when: Apply this to number-line or coordinate statements involving “units from,” “twice as far,” or “less/greater than” constraints.
Boundary: Ignore this when the relationship is not about linear distance or when direction is specified directly without needing a side-condition choice.

Transfer rule: If a path has multiple directional moves, then sum all horizontal components and all vertical components before applying the distance formula once.
Error pattern: Chose by nearest option after an inconsistent setup; failed to aggregate same-axis moves and trusted a mismatch.
Diagnostic check: Draw x-y axes, record signed changes for each leg, total each axis, then compute the hypotenuse and confirm it aligns with one choice exactly.
Use when: Relevant for route, displacement, navigation, or vector-style word problems with cardinal directions and a straight-line separation asked.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for total path traveled, timing, or already gives a direct distance without needing component recombination.

Transfer rule: If discounting a future amount under compound interest, then compute the factor carefully and choose the nearest consistent option after a reverse check.
Error pattern: Correct formula selection but inaccurate arithmetic and overreliance on “no exact match,” causing a wrong rejection of the intended choice.
Diagnostic check: Recalculate the power and division, then multiply your present value by the growth factor to see whether it returns the stated future amount within rounding.
Use when: Relevant for finance or aptitude questions involving present value, compound discounting, and answer choices that may reflect rounding or minor print variance.
Boundary: Ignore when the problem specifies simple interest, nonannual compounding details, or requires exact symbolic form rather than approximate numerical selection.

Transfer rule: If a recurrence and one initial value let you express later terms from one free variable, then derive those terms symbolically before judging any “must be true” statement.
Error pattern: I evaluated options too early and favored a broad identity check instead of testing each conditional against the derived formulas.
Diagnostic check: Compute the first few terms in terms of the free variable, substitute any hypothesis from an option, and verify whether the claimed consequence follows exactly.
Use when: The problem gives a recursive sequence, a partial initial condition, and answer choices involving necessary relations or if-then statements.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices depend on external constraints, hidden domains, or require proving behavior beyond the first derivable terms.

Transfer rule: If a question gives principal, annual rate, years, and annual compounding, then compute amount as principal × (1 + rate)^years.
Error pattern: Success came from translating words into the compound-growth structure instead of using simple-interest addition.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify the result by doing year-by-year growth and confirming it matches the formula result.
Use when: Apply this for investment or loan problems asking final amount after multiple periods with stated compounding frequency.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks only interest earned, uses nonannual compounding details, or involves simple interest or withdrawals.

Transfer rule: If dividing a total by a ratio, then sum the ratio parts, compute one unit, and multiply each part; equal ratio terms must produce equal shares.
Error pattern: Success came from applying the ratio-to-unit method instead of guessing from answer choices.
Diagnostic check: Verify the shares add to the original total and that each share divided by its ratio term gives the same unit value.
Use when: This applies to partition problems with a total amount and a stated ratio between two or more shares.
Boundary: Ignore this for percentages, differences-only conditions, or when ratios are implied by extra constraints rather than directly given.

Transfer rule: If a worker is k% more efficient, then multiply rate by 1 + k/100 and divide the original time by that factor.
Error pattern: Success pattern—converted a percent efficiency change into a rate multiplier and applied the inverse relation between rate and completion time.
Diagnostic check: Set the first worker’s rate to 1 unit/day; compute the second rate, then verify time × rate gives the same total work.
Use when: One entity’s completion time is known and another’s efficiency is stated as a percent more or less for the same fixed job.
Boundary: Ignore when the percentage refers to time, output amount, team combinations, changing workloads, or nonconstant rates.

Transfer rule: If a group’s overall average and a subgroup’s average are given, then convert both to totals, subtract, and divide by the remaining count.
Error pattern: Success pattern—used weighted-average decomposition instead of averaging averages directly.
Diagnostic check: Compute total items, subgroup size, overall total, subgroup total, remainder total, then verify remainder count and divide once.
Use when: Relevant for averages split into parts, especially when a fraction of the set has its own average.
Boundary: Ignore when subgroup sizes are unknown, groups overlap, or the question asks for a total/change rather than the other group’s average.

Transfer rule: If a motion problem gives speeds with and without stoppages, then compute running-time fraction as (overall speed)/(running speed), and stoppage per hour = 60 × [1 − that fraction].
Error pattern: Success comes from converting speed comparison into a time-usage ratio, not subtracting speeds as if the difference directly equals stopped time.
Diagnostic check: Assume 1 hour total; find distance from overall speed, divide by running speed to get moving hours, then subtract from 60 minutes.
Use when: Relevant for average-speed questions mixing travel and halt time over the same route or repeated hourly travel pattern.
Boundary: Ignore when speeds apply to different distances, varying road conditions, acceleration phases, or unequal time blocks.

Transfer rule: If a square’s area and a crossing speed are given, then find side = √area, diagonal = side√2, compute time = distance/speed, and convert units before comparing choices.
Error pattern: Success came from chaining geometric formulas with unit conversion in the correct order.
Diagnostic check: Verify √area × √2 for the path, convert distance and speed to compatible units, then check that time × speed reproduces the diagonal.
Use when: The problem involves a square, travel along its diagonal, and a rate in different units than the field dimensions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the path is not the diagonal, the figure is not a square, or speed already matches distance and time units directly.

Transfer rule: If people/machines work together on one job, then convert each completion time to a unit rate, add rates, and invert the total.
Error pattern: Success came from using rates rather than averaging times or adding durations directly.
Diagnostic check: Let total work be 1; compute each rate as 1/time, sum them, take the reciprocal, and verify the result is less than the smallest individual time.
Use when: Apply this to joint-work, filling, or combined-output problems where multiple agents act simultaneously on the same whole task.
Boundary: Ignore this when agents work sequentially, interfere with each other, or output is not additive/constant over time.

Transfer rule: If counting rearrangements of a word, then first count every letter exactly once and compute factorial of that total, adjusting only for repeats.
Error pattern: Miscounted the number of items before applying the permutation formula, causing a wrong factorial and false mismatch with choices.
Diagnostic check: Write the letters in a list, tally the total symbols, mark duplicates if any, then verify the factorial input matches that tally.
Use when: The task asks for permutations, anagrams, or rearrangements of letters, digits, or objects, especially in multiple-choice format.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when order is restricted by positions/rules or when selection is involved rather than arranging all items.

Transfer rule: If comparing investments with different prices or taxes, then convert each to net yield on money invested: coupon × (1 − tax rate if taxable) ÷ market price.
Error pattern: The key pattern is success when all returns are normalized to the same base; failure happens when tax is subtracted incorrectly or yield is judged from coupon alone.
Diagnostic check: Assume a common investment amount, compute annual net cash received from each security, divide by purchase cost, and compare the resulting percentages.
Use when: Use this for bond/stock investment questions involving par vs premium/discount prices, stated coupons, and taxable versus tax-free income.
Boundary: Ignore this when asked about capital gain, redemption value, holding period effects, or non-income objectives.

Transfer rule: If a problem gives both discount% and gain%, then assign marked price and cost price as different bases and relate them through the same selling price.
Error pattern: The failure was using one variable for two distinct reference prices, causing contradictory equations from mixed percentage bases.
Diagnostic check: Before solving, list each percentage with its base; verify discount is from marked price, profit from cost price, and write SP in both forms.
Use when: This applies to price, discount, gain/loss, markup, and “difference between discount and profit” questions with multiple percentages.
Boundary: Ignore this when all percentages are explicitly on the same base or when only one price reference is involved.

Transfer rule: If two ordered lists differ only by one prepended term, then test whether the full list follows a recurrence or transform before assuming simple ordering.
Error pattern: I focused on local placement in an ordered sequence and ignored structure connecting all terms across the lists.
Diagnostic check: Compute successive differences, ratios, or recurrence fits on the known terms; verify which candidate makes one consistent rule hold for every adjacent step.
Use when: A missing entry is inserted at the beginning or middle of an otherwise matching numeric list and answer choices are all plausible values.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt explicitly states plain sorting, counting, or a nonnumeric categorization rule.

Transfer rule: If a circular arrangement forbids one subgroup from all being consecutive, then count all circular seatings and subtract seatings where that subgroup is treated as one block, multiplying by internal permutations.
Error pattern: Success came from using complementary counting with correct circular-symmetry handling instead of trying to count scattered cases directly.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify two counts: total circular arrangements use (n−1)!, and the “all together” case uses (others + 1 block − 1)! × (group size)!.
Use when: Relevant for round-table/permutation problems with a condition about a specified set sitting consecutively or not all together.
Boundary: Ignore when seats are distinct/linear, multiple overlapping restrictions exist, or the subgroup members are not distinct.

Transfer rule: If you compute a percentage change correctly, then convert the result into the answer choice format and place-value system before selecting.
Error pattern: Correct arithmetic but answer-mapping failure: choosing an option without reconciling notation, commas, or equivalent representations.
Diagnostic check: After rounding, rewrite your result exactly as each option would display it, then match by value rather than by first digit or visual similarity.
Use when: Percentage increase/decrease problems with rounding and answer choices shown in unfamiliar grouping, alternate numeral formatting, or large-number abbreviations.
Boundary: Ignore this when no options are given or all choices use one unambiguous, familiar numeric format.

Transfer rule: If a motion problem gives upstream and downstream speeds for the same rower, then compute still-water speed as (upstream + downstream) / 2 after confirming symmetric current effects.
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing a paired-rate structure where opposite current effects cancel when averaged.
Diagnostic check: Write equations base−current = upstream and base+current = downstream; add them to verify 2×base = sum of the two rates.
Use when: Apply to river/boat or wind scenarios with one object moving against and with a uniform flow under unchanged effort.
Boundary: Ignore when times, distances, changing effort, unequal conditions, or nonuniform flow are involved.

Transfer rule: If a problem gives a rate “per N units” and a larger total, then convert totals to the same unit scale and multiply by the number of rate-blocks.
Error pattern: Success came from proportional scaling with consistent units instead of guessing from raw magnitudes.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the total in the denominator’s units, compute total ÷ base-unit count, then multiply by the stated per-block amount; confirm units cancel cleanly.
Use when: The question involves rates, ratios, “for every,” or population counts with million/billion conversions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the relationship is not linear, the rate changes across groups/time, or percentages/probabilities require complements or exclusions.

Transfer rule: If a probability from sequential draws seems not to match choices, then recompute it with combinations and reduce exactly before selecting “none.”
Error pattern: Arithmetic/representation mismatch after a sound setup; the method was fine, but the final fraction-choice comparison was not validated independently.
Diagnostic check: Compute both \(1-\frac{\binom{\text{good}}{2}}{\binom{\text{total}}{2}}\) and \(1-\frac{\text{good}}{\text{total}}\cdot\frac{\text{good}-1}{\text{total}-1}\); simplify and verify they are identical and choice-equivalent.
Use when: Sampling without replacement, “at least one” wording, and multiple-choice options with rational fractions.
Boundary: Ignore when draws are independent/with replacement, or when the event is not naturally handled by a complement.

Transfer rule: If variables must satisfy inequalities and type constraints, then build candidate pairs for each option instead of fixing one convenient value.
Error pattern: Tested arbitrary examples and treated their failure as disproof, rather than searching systematically for any valid construction.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, list parity and smallest feasible cases; try at least two admissible values for each variable and verify all constraints together.
Use when: A multiple-choice question asks what can be possible under number properties like odd/even, prime/composite, and ordering conditions.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for a universal proof, exact computation, or when one counterexample alone is logically sufficient.

Transfer rule: If a train passes a moving person, then compute train length using relative speed × time after converting all speeds to m/s.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling each “passing” event as distance covered at the appropriate relative speed, not mixing platform length with train length.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, write two equations: one for object-plus-train distance, one for train-only distance versus person; verify units and same-direction subtraction.
Use when: Relevant in motion problems involving trains, passing times, platforms, poles, or people moving in the same or opposite direction.
Boundary: Ignore this when acceleration matters, speeds vary, or the event is not a full pass from front entering to rear clearing.

Transfer rule: If a rectangle gives perimeter and a side ratio, then set sides as ratio parts, use 2(L+W)=P to find the scale, then multiply for area.
Error pattern: Success came from converting a ratio into algebraic side expressions and preserving the perimeter factor of 2.
Diagnostic check: Verify the found sides both match the stated ratio and reproduce the perimeter before computing area.
Use when: Apply this to geometry questions with proportional side lengths plus a total boundary measure, asking for actual dimensions or area.
Boundary: Ignore this when the figure is not a rectangle or when the given measure is area, diagonal, or semiperimeter instead of full perimeter.

Transfer rule: If items have preferred categories but actual assignments are capped, then maximize matches by filling each assigned category with as many items that prefer it as capacity allows, using min(prefer, assigned).
Error pattern: Treated one category’s preference count as the whole answer and ignored the other category’s possible correct matches; failed to optimize globally under capacity constraints.
Diagnostic check: Compute preferred counts and assigned counts for every category, add the per-category minima, and verify no reassignment can increase the total.
Use when: A problem gives total items, preference splits, actual allocation splits, and asks for the greatest possible number of “correctly assigned” items.
Boundary: Ignore when assignments are fixed item-by-item, categories interact non-independently, or the question is about minimum rather than maximum matches.

Transfer rule: If counting partitions into equal unlabeled groups with a restriction on two marked people, then count the restricted complement on labeled groups first and divide by symmetry only after checking for double-counting.
Error pattern: Mixed up “a group contains both” with “the partition contains both together somewhere,” causing an incorrect favorable-count setup.
Diagnostic check: State the sample space precisely: are outcomes single subsets or whole partitions? Then test one arrangement and ask whether swapping the two groups creates a new outcome.
Use when: Relevant in combination problems with equal-sized splits, unlabeled groups, and conditions about specified people being together or apart.
Boundary: Ignore when groups are labeled, sizes differ, or the condition targets an ordered assignment rather than an unlabeled partition.

Transfer rule: If a tiling/count problem gives rectangle and tile dimensions in mixed units, then convert all lengths to one unit, divide total area by tile area, and only use an integer result if division is exact.
Error pattern: Success came from applying a unit-consistent area ratio instead of guessing from side counts or premature rounding.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify both areas use the same unit, compute the quotient, and check whether the remainder is zero; if not, reassess assumptions.
Use when: Apply this to paving, flooring, sheet-covering, or brick-count questions with rectangular regions and identical rectangular pieces.
Boundary: Ignore this when gaps, overlap, wastage, thickness, irregular shapes, or specified cutting/packing constraints affect the count.

Transfer rule: If given an average and a difference linking another variable, then rewrite both as linear equations and substitute before evaluating the new average.
Error pattern: Success came from translating words to equations and exploiting cancellation instead of inventing specific values.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, expand the target average symbolically and verify the original variable cancels completely.
Use when: This applies to algebra word problems involving means, sums, and pairwise differences among variables.
Boundary: Ignore this when relationships are nonlinear, weighted, insufficient, or the target expression cannot be reduced by substitution.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for the probability of outcomes from a few independent fair trials, then list the full equiprobable sample space and count favorable cases.
