Error pattern: Success came from systematic enumeration instead of guessing or collapsing distinct sequences into one case.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write all ordered outcomes, verify each is equally likely, then compute favorable ÷ total.
Use when: Apply this to small finite probability tasks involving repeated coin tosses, dice rolls, or other independent symmetric experiments.
Boundary: Ignore this when outcomes are not equally likely, trials are dependent, or the sample space is too large and needs formulas.

Transfer rule: If people move on a loop and must be together again, then compute each lap time (distance ÷ rate) and take the LCM of those times.
Error pattern: Success came from replacing an invalid LCM-of-speeds idea with the shared-event schedule based on return times to the same point.
Diagnostic check: List each runner’s period, verify units are time, then test the candidate by checking each period divides it exactly.
Use when: Relative motion on a circular track or repeating cycle asks when all participants coincide again after starting together.
Boundary: Ignore when the meeting condition is not “same point on a loop” or when speeds change, directions differ, or starts are offset.

Transfer rule: If a word problem gives fixed cost, per-unit cost, target profit, and forecast quantity, then compute required revenue = fixed + (unit cost × quantity) + profit, then divide by quantity.
Error pattern: Success came from translating profit relationships into an equation instead of guessing from choices.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, write profit = revenue − fixed − variable; substitute symbols, solve for unit price, and verify by plugging back in.
Use when: Apply on break-even/target-profit pricing questions with both fixed and variable costs and a stated sales volume.
Boundary: Ignore this when quantity is unknown, prices vary by tier, or taxes/discounts/interest create non-linear revenue or cost.

Transfer rule: If a problem gives cost price and a profit/loss percent, then compute selling price as cost × (1 ± percent/100), using minus for loss and plus for profit.
Error pattern: Success comes from translating percentage change directly into a multiplier instead of guessing from options or mixing up base values.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write CP, mark profit/loss sign, convert the percent to decimal, apply the multiplier once, and verify the result is below CP for loss or above CP for profit.
Use when: Use for single-step price-change questions involving cost price, selling price, discount, markup, profit, or loss percentages.
Boundary: Ignore when percentages are chained, based on selling price instead of cost, or when tax/commission/other adjustments change the base.

Transfer rule: If a solid is built from identical cubes and each cube’s volume is given, then compute total volume and divide by cube volume, checking exact divisibility.
Error pattern: Success pattern—used unit-consistent volume decomposition instead of mixing edge lengths with cube count.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify both quantities are volumes in the same units and confirm total volume ÷ unit volume gives a whole-number count.
Use when: Relevant for packing/tiling questions with rectangular prisms or other solids made from identical blocks where cube size is given by volume.
Boundary: Ignore when dimensions refer to outer shell only, cubes are not identical, gaps are allowed, or the cube information is given by edge length requiring conversion first.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for an average at an earlier time, then shift the total age by (time elapsed × number of people) and divide by the same count.
Error pattern: Success came from treating average as total-sum change over time rather than adjusting one person separately or changing the group size.
Diagnostic check: Compute current total = average × count, subtract elapsed years from every member once, then recompute the average and verify the youngest would be newborn then.
Use when: Apply this to fixed-group age problems where a past moment is defined by one member’s current age or years since an event.
Boundary: Ignore this when people enter/leave the group, ages are nonuniformly measured, or the reference time excludes some members.

Transfer rule: If a count asks for numbers divisible by two values under a limit, then replace the pair with their LCM and use floor((limit−1)/LCM) for a strict “less than” bound.
Error pattern: Success came from reducing a dual-divisibility condition to one periodic step size instead of checking each divisor separately.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, compute the LCM, divide the cutoff by it, then verify strictness by testing whether the cutoff itself is a multiple and adjusting with floor if needed.
Use when: Relevant for counting shared multiples, repeated intervals, or divisibility intersections below or up to a threshold.
Boundary: Ignore when conditions are not pure divisibility counts, ranges are irregular, or extra exclusions/inclusions change the arithmetic progression.

Transfer rule: If a payment is split among workers on one job, then compute each person’s share from contribution = (individual rate) × (time worked), not from completion times alone.
Error pattern: Converted rates correctly but failed to finish the proportional-allocation step from contributions to money.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write each worker’s contribution over the actual joint duration, sum them to 1 whole job, then verify the requested share equals contribution fraction × total payment.
Use when: Work-and-wages problems give solo completion times, a team completion time, and ask for someone’s pay or share.
Boundary: Ignore this when payment is fixed by contract, unequal time worked, or not proportional to work done.

Transfer rule: If one profit is a multiple of another at two selling prices, then write profit as selling price minus cost and equate those expressions by the stated multiple.
Error pattern: Success came from translating comparative-profit wording directly into algebra instead of guessing from options or mixing profit with selling price.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compute the gap between selling prices and verify the higher-profit expression exceeds the lower by exactly one lower-profit amount.
Use when: Apply this to linear profit/loss questions with the same item, fixed cost, and statements like “double,” “triple,” or “x times” profit.
Boundary: Ignore this when cost changes, percentages refer to cost or selling price, or the comparison involves revenue, markup, or loss instead of profit.

Transfer rule: If a subgroup count is given after two nested percentages, then convert the complement if needed and divide by the product of the relevant rates to recover the whole.
Error pattern: Success came from translating layered percentage statements into a single equation instead of combining percentages additively or applying them to the wrong base.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write the chain whole → participating group → stated subgroup, replace each arrow with a decimal multiplier, and verify the known count equals whole × all multipliers.
Use when: This applies to turnout, attendance, sales, or survey problems with “of these” wording and a final subgroup count.
Boundary: Ignore this when percentages refer to different wholes, overlap ambiguously, or absolute counts are compared without nesting.

Transfer rule: If two choice sets partially overlap, then partition items into shared and exclusive groups and count allowed pairs by group before using totals or answer choices.
Error pattern: I abandoned the stated structure and forced a reinterpretation to match an option instead of validating each assumption against the overlap information.
Diagnostic check: Write counts for shared, first-set-only, and second-set-only items; compute valid pairs from that table; confirm any subtraction removes only actually possible forbidden cases.
Use when: Apply this on counting problems with two attributes, overlapping categories, exclusions, or wording like identical, same, except, or every pair.
Boundary: Ignore this when the problem is purely sequential, geometric, or has no overlap/exclusion structure to tabulate.

Transfer rule: If a quantity is rounded to n significant digits, then bound the absolute error by half the place value of the last retained digit and convert that bound to a percentage of the original.
Error pattern: Computing actual rounding difference instead of the maximum possible error for a stated precision question.
Diagnostic check: Identify the last kept place, take 0.5×that unit as error, divide by the original value, multiply by 100, then compare magnitude with choices.
Use when: The prompt asks for percentage error after expressing or rounding a measurement to a given number of significant digits.
Boundary: Ignore when exact observed error is requested, truncation is used, or uncertainty rules are explicitly different.

Transfer rule: If asked for a mean proportional between two positive numbers, then compute the geometric mean by taking the square root of their product.
Error pattern: I confused the target quantity with a different ratio-based formula instead of recalling the standard definition.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify your candidate x satisfies a:x = x:b, equivalently x² = ab, and lies between the two numbers.
Use when: This applies to problems using terms like mean proportional, geometric mean, or continuous proportion between two values.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for arithmetic/harmonic mean or gives a custom formula or nonpositive-domain restriction.

Transfer rule: If a work-rate problem changes both workers and days for the same job, then equate total work as workers × days before comparing with choices.
Error pattern: Success came from using inverse-variation structure correctly and trusting the derived value even when it is absent from the listed options.
Diagnostic check: Write two work expressions for the same job, set them equal, solve, then verify by substituting back into both time scenarios.
Use when: Apply this to fixed-work problems where team size changes and completion time adjusts correspondingly.
Boundary: Ignore this when individual productivity differs, work amount changes, or extra constraints make total work not constant.

Transfer rule: If a random-selection probability can be modeled with or without replacement, then compute both and match the wording and answer format before choosing.
Error pattern: Treated repeated picks as combinations without verifying the problem’s intended dependence structure, so the sample-space model mismatched the options.
Diagnostic check: Calculate the complement under both models—dependent draws and independent draws—and see which one aligns with the provided choices.
Use when: Apply this on urn, bulb, card, or ball questions asking for “at least one” over multiple selections from a finite set.
Boundary: Ignore this when replacement status is explicit, or when order/independence is clearly forced by the wording.

Transfer rule: If draws are independent and a strict order among all results is required, then count distinct-value selections and assign exactly one qualifying ordering per selected set.
Error pattern: Success came from exploiting symmetry of relative rankings instead of enumerating ordered outcomes one by one.
Diagnostic check: Verify ties cannot satisfy the condition, count all ordered outcomes, then confirm each distinct chosen set contributes one favorable permutation out of all possible rank orders.
Use when: Apply to repeated random selections with replacement where comparisons like greater-than/less-than link every draw in a chain.
Boundary: Ignore when outcomes are not equally likely, draws are dependent, or the condition is not a complete strict ordering.

Transfer rule: If combining percentages from groups of unequal sizes, then convert each rate to counts (or use a weighted average) before finding the overall percentage.
Error pattern: Success comes from avoiding a simple average of rates and weighting each subgroup by its size.
Diagnostic check: Compute subgroup totals, multiply each by its rate, add the resulting counts, then divide by the combined total; compare against any unweighted mean you may be tempted to use.
Use when: A problem gives multiple subpopulations, each with its own size and percentage for the same event.
Boundary: Ignore this when all groups are equal-sized or when the asked quantity is a single group’s rate, not a combined rate.

Transfer rule: If expressions show different multipliers times each person’s quantity are equal, then set a common constant and solve each quantity as constant divided by its multiplier before forming the ratio.
Error pattern: Treated equalized products as direct quantities, missing that the underlying amounts are inversely proportional to the given multipliers.
Diagnostic check: Pick a common value for the equal expressions, compute each amount explicitly by division, then verify by plugging back into every equality before using any ratio.
Use when: Relevant in partnership, work, age, or mixture problems with statements like “m times X = n times Y = p times Z.”
Boundary: Ignore when the statement directly gives the quantities’ ratio or when all terms are plain amounts without an equality of scaled products.

Transfer rule: If ages differ by a fixed amount and a future ratio is given, then assign one variable, shift both ages by the same time, and form a single equation.
Error pattern: Success came from translating each statement directly into algebra instead of comparing options or doing mental arithmetic loosely.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, verify the future-year equation uses the same time shift on both people and that substituting your result satisfies both the difference and ratio conditions.
Use when: Apply this to age-word problems involving present/future ages, constant age gaps, and multiplicative comparisons.
Boundary: Ignore this when relationships are not linear time shifts, such as changing rates, non-age contexts, or missing fixed-difference information.

Transfer rule: If lengths use different units, then convert all quantities to one unit before dividing whole by part.
Error pattern: Success came from disciplined unit normalization and checking that the quotient counts discrete equal segments.
Diagnostic check: Write both measures with the same unit, compute total ÷ piece size, and confirm the result is a whole-number count of pieces.
Use when: Apply this to measurement, rate, or partition questions involving cuts, groups, packaging, or repeated equal chunks.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices depend on leftovers, kerf/waste, stretching, rounding rules, or missing conversion information.

Transfer rule: If a percentage of one quantity added to another makes the second become a stated multiple of itself, then set added amount = (new multiple − 1) × second quantity and solve the ratio.
Error pattern: Success came from translating the verbal percent-change relation into one linear equation before comparing quantities.
Diagnostic check: Compute the target increase of the second alone, convert the percent of the first to a fraction, and verify both added amounts match after simplification.
Use when: One amount contributes a percentage of itself to another, and the result is described as the second becoming a fractional multiple of itself.
Boundary: Ignore when the percent applies to the receiving quantity, or when extra steps like repeated changes or totals are involved.

Transfer rule: If a product comes from repeated item weights, then prime-factor the total and map each item's weight to its prime contribution before counting any item.
Error pattern: Success came from converting a multiplicative inventory question into exponent bookkeeping instead of guessing from the answer choices.
Diagnostic check: Factor the total completely, rewrite each item weight into primes, and verify only one nonnegative count fits all prime exponents.
Use when: Apply this to products of several known item values, especially when values are composite and repeated many times.
Boundary: Ignore this when the relationship is additive, probabilistic, or the item values are not fixed constants.

Transfer rule: If a group splits a bill equally after a percent discount on the total, then apply the discount to the total first and divide the reduced amount by the number of people.
Error pattern: Success came from preserving operation order in a percent-change-plus-sharing setup.
Diagnostic check: Compute discounted total as original × (1 − discount rate), then verify per-person share × group size equals that discounted total.
Use when: Totals are shared evenly and a coupon, tax, tip, markup, or discount changes the whole amount before splitting.
Boundary: Ignore this when the percentage applies per person, contributions are unequal, or amounts are changed in multiple conditional stages.

Transfer rule: If a quantity changes at a constant rate and a known fraction takes a known time, then divide the time by that fraction’s numerator to get the time for one equal fractional part.
Error pattern: Success comes from recognizing a direct proportional relationship between equal fractional amounts and time.
Diagnostic check: Verify the setup by multiplying your per-part time by the counted equal parts to reproduce the given total time.
Use when: Apply this to uniform fill/drain/work problems where a stated fraction of one whole is completed in a stated time.
Boundary: Ignore this when the rate varies over time or the process is not proportional to amount completed.

Transfer rule: If ages are linked at different times, then first anchor the person’s current age from a future/past statement and shift every related age to the same reference year before combining.
Error pattern: Success comes from consistent timeline alignment; failures usually mix ages from “now,” “years ago,” and “years ahead” in one equation.
Diagnostic check: Make a mini table with each person’s age at now, past, and future points; verify every condition uses the matching column before doing any sum.
Use when: Use this for age word problems with multiple relatives and phrases like “in ... years” or “... years ago.”
Boundary: Ignore this when quantities are unrelated to time shifts or when a direct present-age equation is already given.

Transfer rule: If a selection question fixes one member and the group size is implied by the context, then subtract that member and choose the remaining slots with combinations, not subsets.
Error pattern: I ignored domain-implied team size and treated the task as choosing any subset, causing a power-set overcount.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, identify total required group size, fixed members, and remaining slots; then verify the count has the form “choose remaining slots from remaining people.”
Use when: This applies to committee, team, squad, or lineup counting problems with mandatory or excluded people.
Boundary: Ignore this when no fixed group size exists or the task truly asks for all possible subsets/selections.

Transfer rule: If two pairwise ratios share one person, then scale them to a common value for that person before forming the full combined ratio.
Error pattern: Success comes from reconciling linked ratios consistently and distributing profit directly in the unified investment ratio.
Diagnostic check: Write both pairwise ratios, find the LCM of the shared person’s parts, rescale both ratios, merge into one three-person ratio, then verify the total parts divide the whole profit sensibly.
Use when: This applies to partnership, investment, work, or mixture questions where shares follow proportional contributions and only pairwise ratios are given.
Boundary: Ignore this when shares depend on unequal time periods, salaries, bonuses, losses, or any rule other than simple proportional distribution.

Transfer rule: If two objects are measured under the same angle/condition, then set up equal corresponding ratios and solve by cross-multiplying.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping corresponding quantities correctly and preserving the same order in both ratios.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, simplify the known ratio, estimate the unknown by scaling, and verify the result changes in the same direction as the related measure.
Use when: Apply this to proportional geometry, similar-figure, scale-factor, rate, or “same conditions” comparison problems.
Boundary: Ignore this when conditions differ, correspondence is unclear, or the relationship is not proportional/linear.

Transfer rule: If a level in a rectangular prism changes, then compute removed volume as base area × change in height, after converting all dimensions to one unit, then apply any unit-rate conversion.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling the situation as a thin rectangular slab and doing unit conversion before multiplying.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify height change is converted to the same length unit, volume units are cubic length, and the final value reflects multiplying by the given per-cubic-unit factor.
Use when: This applies to fill/drain, raise/lower, or layered-volume questions for boxes, pools, tanks, or rooms with constant base area.
Boundary: Ignore this when the container’s cross-section varies with height or when dimensions already represent total volume rather than a level change.

Transfer rule: If a rate is given in degrees per time, then convert total time to that unit, multiply for total degrees, then divide by 360 to get complete rotations.
Error pattern: Success came from consistent unit conversion and treating repeated circular motion as total-angle accumulation.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify units cancel cleanly and independently compute one full-turn time from the rate; confirm the total interval contains that many such periods.
Use when: Apply to clock-hand, wheel, gear, or pointer problems asking for full turns over hours or days.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for position, partial turns, relative motion, or the rate changes during the interval.

Transfer rule: If a river-boat question gives still-water speed and one-way time-distance, then compute one-way ground speed first, derive current by add/subtract, then use time = distance ÷ opposite-direction speed.
Error pattern: Success came from separating still-water speed, stream speed, and ground speed instead of mixing formulas.
Diagnostic check: Verify downstream speed is greater than still-water speed, upstream speed is smaller, and distance equals speed × time in both legs.
Use when: Apply to upstream/downstream motion problems with any two of distance, time, still-water speed, or current-related speed.
Boundary: Ignore when motion is not relative-speed based, or when acceleration, variable current, or nonuniform rates are involved.

Transfer rule: If a work-rate problem changes workers mid-process, then convert everything to worker-days, subtract completed work, and divide the remainder by the new combined rate.
Error pattern: Success came from treating rates as additive and tracking completed versus remaining work instead of averaging times or mixing total time with extra time.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, compute total worker-days, completed worker-days, remaining worker-days, and verify rate × time equals the remaining fraction exactly.
Use when: Apply this to jobs done by identical workers or machines where team size changes after some elapsed time.
Boundary: Ignore this when productivity is nonconstant, workers differ in efficiency, or the question asks for total elapsed time rather than additional time.

Transfer rule: If two values are chosen independently from finite sets, then compute probability as favorable ordered pairs divided by the product of set sizes.
Error pattern: I identified a valid pair but failed to convert the count into the full sample-space fraction consistently.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, write total outcomes = (size of first set)×(size of second set), count all matching pairs, then verify the probability equals count/total and matches one choice.
Use when: Relevant for random selections from listed sets, grids of pairings, or conditions on sums, products, or comparisons.
Boundary: Ignore when choices are dependent, weighted unequally, made without replacement, or when order is explicitly collapsed.

Transfer rule: If ages are given by a past ratio and a present total, then set past ages as k-multiples, add back the time shift to each, and use the total to solve k.
Error pattern: Success came from translating the ratio at the correct time point into linear expressions before using the sum.
Diagnostic check: Verify by plugging the found ages back into both conditions: subtract the stated years and confirm the ratio, then add present ages and confirm the total.
Use when: Apply to age word problems with a shared time shift, a ratio in one time frame, and a sum in another.
Boundary: Ignore when relationships are not proportional, time shifts differ by person, or extra constraints replace a simple total.

Transfer rule: If a ratio includes one quantity that can be found from a total rate, then compute that quantity first and scale by the matching ratio part.
Error pattern: Success came from translating a verbal ratio into part-to-part multiplication after isolating the directly measurable group.
Diagnostic check: Divide the total by the per-item amount, verify divisibility, then confirm the result matches the correct side of the ratio before multiplying by the other side.
Use when: One category has a known per-unit contribution to a total and the categories are linked by a simple ratio.
Boundary: Ignore when the ratio is part-to-whole, rates vary across items, or extra constraints change the proportional relationship.

Transfer rule: If a sequence looks irregular, then first repartition it into fixed-size groups and test each group against external structures like digit counts, dates, or simple transforms.
Error pattern: I guessed from ambiguity instead of systematically checking hidden grouping and representation-based patterns.
Diagnostic check: Insert separators in several plausible ways, write each group’s mapped values, and verify one rule explains all visible terms before choosing.
Use when: Terms are short integers, punctuation or spacing is unclear, and direct arithmetic differences or ratios fail quickly.
Boundary: Ignore this when the sequence already follows a consistent local numeric rule without needing regrouping or reinterpretation.

Transfer rule: If you derive a standalone value from rates, then match that value to the answer choices only after a final option-label check.
Error pattern: Correct computation followed by a transcription or option-selection mismatch between worked result and submitted choice.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, compare the final numeric result in your reasoning with the chosen option’s numeric text; they must be identical.
Use when: Relevant in multiple-choice arithmetic, rate, algebra, or unit-conversion problems where the solved value must be mapped to listed choices.
Boundary: Ignore for open-response tasks or when choices are symbolic and no direct numeric/text match is required.

Transfer rule: If a profit share is partly equal and partly proportional, then simplify the capital ratio first and compute the difference only from the proportional part.  
Error pattern: Mixing up or misreducing the ratio caused the variable setup to fit the wrong weights, making the final total inconsistent.  
Diagnostic check: Before solving, reduce the capital ratio by GCD, note equal distribution creates zero difference, then verify proportional-part difference = given gap.  
Use when: Relevant in partnership or mixture-style distribution problems with a fixed equal share plus a remainder split by investment ratio.  
Boundary: Ignore when the stated gap refers only to one sub-share, or when time, withdrawals, or unequal equal-share groups alter effective ratios.

Transfer rule: If a category threshold includes several groups, then sum exactly those groups and exclude all below-threshold groups.
Error pattern: Success came from translating the wording into a set-membership/addition task and combining only the relevant fractions.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list included categories, convert them to one common denominator, add them, and verify the total stays at or below 1.
Use when: The problem gives fractional parts of a whole across named categories and asks for the share meeting a cutoff such as “at least” or “or higher.”
Boundary: Ignore this when categories overlap, are conditional, or are not parts of the same whole.

Transfer rule: If a sequence seems alternating, then split it into interleaved subsequences by position and test each for its own step pattern before choosing.
Error pattern: I overfit a local up/down difference pattern across adjacent terms instead of checking structure across odd and even positions.
Diagnostic check: Write terms in two lists (1st,3rd,5th...) and (2nd,4th,6th...); verify whether each list follows a simple consistent change.
Use when: Apply this to short number series with zigzag behavior, mixed increases and decreases, or answer choices that fit multiple adjacent-difference stories.
Boundary: Ignore this when the sequence is clearly generated by one direct rule on consecutive terms or by nonnumeric features.

Transfer rule: If two prices are given in a ratio and one exceeds the other by a fixed amount, then assign common-factor variables, equate the difference in parts to the given excess, and scale.
Error pattern: Success pattern—translated the ratio into algebra correctly and used the difference between linked quantities, not the whole amount.
Diagnostic check: Compute the gap in ratio parts, divide the stated excess by that gap to get one part, then rebuild the requested quantity and verify the original difference.
Use when: Relevant for comparison word problems with ratios plus an additive difference between the two quantities.
Boundary: Ignore when the relationship is a sum, product, percentage change, or ratio of totals rather than a direct pairwise difference.

Transfer rule: If a multiple-choice item asks for a combined percentage from several standalone percentages, then first test simple operations on the given values that match answer choices before assuming missing-overlap data.
Error pattern: I over-applied formal set reasoning to a likely puzzle-style arithmetic question and ignored cueing from the answer format.
Diagnostic check: Compute sum, product, average, max, and min of the listed percentages; see whether one result exactly appears among the options.
Use when: Short quantitative MCQs provide only single-category percentages, no intersection data, and all options are simple percentages.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt explicitly asks for exact overlap under standard probability/set assumptions or provides dependence/intersection information.

Transfer rule: If a grouping word problem changes both total and group size, then test divisibility for the original pair and the adjusted pair exactly as stated.
Error pattern: Success came from translating verbal conditions into two arithmetic constraints and checking both instead of trusting only one.
Diagnostic check: Compute total mod original size, then compute adjusted total mod adjusted size; accept only if the first is nonzero and the second is zero.
Use when: Apply this to equal-group or packaging problems with one starting setup that fails and a stated modification that makes division exact.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks only about the revised setup or when “wanted” already implies the original setup worked.

Transfer rule: If consecutive differences form a clear geometric progression with constant ratio, then extend that progression and add the next difference.
Error pattern: Success came from checking second-level structure instead of forcing a direct formula on the terms.
Diagnostic check: Compute adjacent differences; verify at least three consecutive ratios between those differences are identical before extrapolating.
Use when: Apply to integer sequences where first-order changes grow rapidly and the original terms lack an obvious simple arithmetic or geometric rule.
Boundary: Ignore this when equal difference-ratios fail, multiple rules fit equally well, or a simpler term-to-term operation explains every step.

Transfer rule: If two positive integers have a known product and a small known difference, then set the larger as smaller plus the difference and solve the resulting quadratic or factor pair.
Error pattern: Success came from converting a word relation into equations and rejecting any nonpositive root after solving.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, multiply the two candidate integers and subtract them; confirm both original conditions hold exactly.
Use when: This applies to integer word problems giving both a product and an additive gap between two unknowns.
Boundary: Ignore this when values need not be integers or when the relationship is ratio, sum, or divisibility instead of a fixed difference.

Transfer rule: If a price undergoes successive percentage changes on different bases, then convert each to a multiplier and multiply in order before finding net gain/loss from the original base.
Error pattern: Success pattern: avoided adding/subtracting percentages directly and tracked changing bases correctly.
Diagnostic check: Assume an original value of 100, apply each percent change sequentially, then compare the final value to 100 to compute the net percent.
Use when: Relevant for markup, discount, tax, commission, depreciation, or any chained percent-change problem.
Boundary: Ignore when all percentages are explicitly on the same unchanged base or when the task asks only for an intermediate adjusted price.

Transfer rule: If a larger shape is tiled by smaller congruent squares with side lengths that divide evenly, then count per side first and multiply the row and column counts.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the method to a clean tiling problem instead of guessing from options.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compute large side ÷ small side; verify it is an integer, then square that quotient and compare with any area-based result.
Use when: Apply this to square-into-square packing, grid tiling, or equal-size tile counting with aligned edges and no gaps.
Boundary: Ignore this when shapes differ, rotation matters, dimensions do not divide evenly, or packing is irregular/non-grid.

Transfer rule: If distance changes at a constant rate, then compute time as (given time/given distance) × target distance.
Error pattern: Success came from using unit rate and proportional scaling instead of matching unlike quantities in a proportion.
Diagnostic check: Write units on every term; simplify to seconds per unit distance, multiply by the new distance, and confirm the result’s units are seconds.
Use when: This applies to constant-speed or constant-rate word problems with one known time-distance pair and a new distance.
Boundary: Ignore this when the rate is not constant or when the relationship is not directly proportional.

Transfer rule: If summing consecutive integers inclusively via prefix sums, then subtract the sum up to one less than the lower endpoint from the sum up to the upper endpoint.
Error pattern: Off-by-one endpoint handling when converting an inclusive interval into a difference of cumulative sums.
Diagnostic check: Let the lower endpoint be L and upper be U; verify your form is S(U)−S(L−1), then test with adjacent endpoints to ensure both ends are counted.
Use when: A problem asks for the sum of all integers in an inclusive range and gives or suggests a formula for sums from 1 through k.
Boundary: Ignore when endpoints are excluded, order is reversed without relabeling, or the sequence is not consecutive integers.

Transfer rule: If a present ratio and one person’s future age are given, then convert the future age to present first, map it to ratio parts, and scale the other age from the same unit.
Error pattern: Success came from translating a time-shifted statement before using the ratio, avoiding mixing present and future quantities.
Diagnostic check: Compute the known person’s present age by reversing the time change; divide by that person’s ratio part; multiply by the other person’s part; verify both ages keep the original ratio.
Use when: Apply this on age problems with ratios plus “after/before N years” information for one person.
Boundary: Ignore this when the ratio itself changes over time or when extra conditions make a simple proportional model invalid.

Transfer rule: If converting a large whole number to scientific notation, then place the decimal after the first nonzero digit and use the count of places moved as the exponent.
Error pattern: Success came from enforcing the normalized form instead of matching superficial formatting.
Diagnostic check: Verify the coefficient is at least 1 and less than 10, then mentally shift the decimal back by the exponent to see whether the original magnitude returns.
Use when: Apply this to powers-of-ten notation tasks for very large or very small decimals, especially with distracting zeros or oddly formatted choices.
Boundary: Ignore this when the notation is not scientific notation or when units/context require a different representation.

Transfer rule: If finding a GCD of terminating decimals, then scale all values by the same power of ten to integers, take the integer GCD, and scale back.
Error pattern: Success came from using a common scaling framework rather than mixing fraction-denominator shortcuts that can mislead.
Diagnostic check: Count decimal places, choose 10^k for the maximum count, verify each scaled value is an integer, compute the integer GCD, then confirm it divides every original value exactly.
Use when: Apply this to multiple numbers written as terminating decimals where a greatest common measure/divisor is requested.
Boundary: Ignore this for non-terminating decimals, approximate data, or tasks asking for LCM, ratio simplification, or ordinary fraction addition/subtraction.

Transfer rule: If some items are forbidden from a subset of positions, then count all unrestricted assignments and multiply by the probability the restricted items avoid those positions, or equivalently place restricted items first in allowed positions.
Error pattern: Overcounting by choosing unrestricted subsets and permutations that do not enforce a one-to-one placement across all positions.
Diagnostic check: Compute allowed placements for the restricted group as permutations of allowed positions, then place the rest; verify the total is at most the full permutation count.
Use when: Distinct objects fill distinct slots, with a named subgroup barred from a named subset of slots.
Boundary: Ignore when slots or objects are identical, capacities exceed one, or restrictions are conditional/dependent.

Transfer rule: If a counting question asks for ways to complete a form or test, then treat each item as requiring one allowed state from the listed choices unless a blank option is explicitly included.
Error pattern: Misread scope by replacing “complete all items” with “leave all items blank,” ignoring the standard product structure.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the permitted state count per item, verify whether blank is an explicit choice, then multiply equal counts across items.
Use when: Relevant for independent-slot counting problems with repeated answer sets, questionnaires, passwords, or sequences of selections.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt explicitly allows omission, includes a separate blank state, or imposes cross-item constraints.

Transfer rule: If mixing solutions given by part-ratios, then first convert each mixture to per-unit fractions before writing the combined ratio or using alligation.
Error pattern: I added raw numerator and denominator parts as if both containers had the same total size, ignoring different total-part bases.
Diagnostic check: Compute each source’s target-component fraction and verify the desired fraction lies between them; then derive the mix ratio from fraction gaps, not raw parts.
Use when: This applies to mixture, concentration, dilution, alloy, or ingredient problems where each source is itself a ratio of components.
Boundary: Ignore this when the given quantities are already actual amounts on a common scale, not compositions normalized by different totals.

Transfer rule: If a minimum overlap is asked under bounded set sizes and a fixed triple-overlap, then maximize how many of the smaller set can be placed outside the target pair before forcing extra shared members.
Error pattern: I optimized the wrong quantity by using a loose maximum-overlap idea instead of a forcing argument from capacity limits.
Diagnostic check: Set target overlap to 0, then 1, etc., and test feasibility by assigning each set to the largest allowed non-target regions while respecting all lower/upper bounds.
Use when: Relevant for inclusion-exclusion, Venn-diagram, bounded-cardinality, and “minimum/maximum in a specific region” problems with several overlapping sets.
Boundary: Ignore when exact totals/intersections are fully given or when the question is about probability/algebra rather than feasible region counts.

Transfer rule: If a decimal number is built by repeating a shorter block, then factor it as block × repunit/power-sum before testing divisibility.
Error pattern: Stopped at separate divisibility checks of pieces instead of exploiting the repeated-structure factorization that guarantees a common factor.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the number as (first block)×10101… or equivalent; verify by expansion, then inspect forced factors of that multiplier.
Use when: The digits form an exact repeated pattern, especially a 1- or 2-digit block repeated multiple times in base 10.
Boundary: Ignore when the pattern is not an exact repetition or when the question depends on variable-specific divisibility beyond the structural multiplier.

Transfer rule: If workers and outputs scale together over the same time, then reduce to one worker’s rate before choosing a time.  
Error pattern: I matched equal counts to a faster completion time instead of preserving the given duration for each worker’s single output.  
Diagnostic check: Compute rate as outputs per worker per day; then invert that unit rate to get days for one worker to make one output.  
Use when: Applies to constant-rate work problems with multiple agents, identical productivity, and a question asking for one agent’s time for one item.  
Boundary: Ignore when agents differ, cooperation changes efficiency, setup delays matter, or production is not proportional over time.

Transfer rule: If a worker’s full-job time is given, then compute any partial-job time by multiplying that time by the fraction of work, then add phase times.
Error pattern: Treated the full-job time as the time for a half-job; phase-based rate problems fail when work fractions are not converted into times correctly.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, write each phase as “time = work ÷ rate” and verify the first phase uses only the stated fraction, not the whole.
Use when: The work is completed in stages, especially when extra identical workers join after a stated portion is done.
Boundary: Ignore when the given time already refers to the partial task or when rates vary by stage.

Transfer rule: If a cylinder is inscribed in a sphere, then relate sphere radius to cylinder radius and half-height with \(R^2=r^2+(h/2)^2\) before using any area formula.
Error pattern: I assumed a direct equality between cylinder height and sphere diameter instead of enforcing the cross-sectional right-triangle constraint.
Diagnostic check: Draw the central cross-section, mark radius, half-height, and sphere radius, and verify they form a right triangle that matches the given ratio.
Use when: A solid is fitted inside another curved solid and only dimension ratios are given, especially for sphere-cylinder or cone-sphere geometry.
Boundary: Ignore this when the embedding relation is explicitly given by equal heights/diameters or when the figure is not inscribed/coaxial.

Transfer rule: If a factorial-divisibility result from prime-exponent counting is not among the choices, then recheck the transcription, base conversion, and whether the question asks for a prime-power or composite-power exponent.
Error pattern: Mechanical use of a correct method without a final consistency check against the answer format or source statement.
Diagnostic check: Compute the prime valuation, convert carefully to the target base, then verify the resulting integer appears in the options; if not, audit symbols, copied terms, and arithmetic.
Use when: The problem asks for the greatest exponent of a prime or composite power dividing a factorial and provides multiple-choice answers.
Boundary: Ignore this when answers are open-response or when no transcription/choice validation is possible.

Transfer rule: If a random-draw guarantee asks for at least k of each type, then use the worst case: total items minus the largest possible stash that still leaves some type below k, then add one.
Error pattern: Success came from setting counts with ratios first; the risk is stopping at totals and not converting the guarantee into an adversarial “missing one type” count.
Diagnostic check: Compute each type count, then for each type calculate “all other types + (k−1) of this type”; take the maximum and add 1, then convert to cost.
Use when: Relevant for unequal category counts, random dispensing, and wording like “minimum required to guarantee.”
Boundary: Ignore when draws are chosen, replacement occurs, or probability rather than certainty is asked.

Transfer rule: If two percentages apply across different bases or years, then convert each to a multiplicative factor and compare by forming a ratio of the resulting amounts.
Error pattern: Success comes from chaining percent changes multiplicatively; failure comes from adding or subtracting percentages that refer to different quantities.
Diagnostic check: Define a simple base value for the original whole, compute both actual amounts symbolically or numerically, cancel common factors, then convert the ratio to a percent.
Use when: The question asks what percent one quantity is of another after a rate change, markup, salary change, or savings/spending fraction shift.
Boundary: Ignore this when all percentages refer to the same unchanged base and the task is only a direct percent computation.

Transfer rule: If notation uses adjacent parentheses with exponents/signs, then first infer the symbolic pattern and solve for the missing exponent by rewriting all terms in a common base.
Error pattern: I treated compact algebraic notation as ordinary arithmetic steps, ignoring structure and exponent laws.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, parse each symbol group, translate it consistently, and verify whether exponent rules make both sides match without decimal approximations.
Use when: Relevant in multiple-choice algebra items with repeated grouped forms, hidden exponents, or compressed notation designed for pattern recognition.
Boundary: Ignore this when the expression is plainly standard arithmetic with explicit operators and no ambiguous grouped notation.

Transfer rule: If a problem compares monthly interest under different annual rates, then convert each annual rate to a monthly rate and solve with payment = principal × rate.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking units consistently and scaling the target payment before solving for the new principal.
Diagnostic check: Compute old principal from the given monthly payment, increase the payment by the stated percent, then divide by the new monthly rate; verify the new principal is larger when payment rises and rate falls.
Use when: Relevant for simple-interest or nominal-rate multiple-choice questions involving monthly payouts, percent change in income, and a changed annual rate.
Boundary: Ignore this when compounding, fees, taxes, unequal time periods, or nonmonthly payment conventions are involved.

Transfer rule: If a group’s average changes after replacing some members, then convert the average change into total-sum change and equate old total minus removed values plus added values to the new total.
Error pattern: Success pattern—used total-sum invariance under replacement instead of trying to infer the original average directly.
Diagnostic check: Compute change in total as (group size × average change), then verify added-sum − removed-sum equals that amount before taking any requested average.
Use when: Relevant in average problems involving fixed group size, substitutions, and known ages or scores of removed members.
Boundary: Ignore when group size also changes without full accounting, or when the question depends on median, ratio, or weighted categories rather than simple averages.

Transfer rule: If you compute a conversion result, then separately match that exact result to the choice list before selecting a letter.
Error pattern: Correct calculation but answer-selection transcription mismatch between worked result and chosen option.
Diagnostic check: After solving, point to the computed value and verify the marked choice contains the same value and unit, digit for digit.
Use when: Multiple-choice unit conversions or any problem where you derive a numeric result and must map it to a listed option.
Boundary: Ignore when the response is open-ended with no options, or when options differ only by reasoning rather than by final value.

Transfer rule: If a rate question mixes distance and time units, then convert both to the target units first and compute speed = distance ÷ time.
Error pattern: Success came from disciplined unit normalization before arithmetic, avoiding mismatched-unit division.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, write distance in kilometers, time in hours, divide, and confirm the result’s unit is km/h.
Use when: Apply this to motion or work-rate multiple-choice problems with meters/minutes, seconds/hours, or other mixed units.
Boundary: Ignore this when units already match the requested rate or when the task asks for a non-rate quantity.

Transfer rule: If asked for the least value formed by distinct positive terms from a set, then add the smallest distinct allowed terms first and verify all constraints.
Error pattern: Success came from constructive minimization rather than testing choices one by one.
Diagnostic check: List the allowed terms in ascending order, select the first required number of distinct valid terms, sum them, then confirm no smaller total can satisfy the rules.
Use when: Relevant for “least/smallest” questions with sums of distinct members from a restricted class.
Boundary: Ignore when repetition is allowed, terms may be nonpositive, or the task asks about possibility rather than minimum.

Transfer rule: If comparing averages of evenly spaced inclusive integer ranges, then use each range’s midpoint and subtract the midpoints.
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing an arithmetic-sequence shortcut instead of summing terms or comparing counts.
Diagnostic check: Compute first-plus-last for each range, halve to get each midpoint, then verify both ranges have the same step size.
Use when: Apply this to consecutive integers or any arithmetic progression where only the difference between two set averages is asked.
Boundary: Ignore this when spacing is irregular, values are weighted, endpoints are excluded asymmetrically, or the sets are not arithmetic sequences.

Transfer rule: If maximizing a middle value in an ordered integer list with fixed total and one endpoint fixed, then minimize all values below it and set the next higher value to the smallest allowed value above it.
Error pattern: Ignored ordering/positivity constraints on every variable and optimized one term using an incomplete sum relation.
Diagnostic check: Compute the total, assign the lower terms their minimum legal values, force the adjacent upper term to its minimum legal value, then verify strict order and positivity for all entries.
Use when: Ordered distinct integers, fixed mean or sum, one extreme given, and the goal is the largest possible median or interior term.
Boundary: Ignore when variables need not be distinct/ordered, are not integers, or no extremum under a fixed total is requested.

Transfer rule: If a word problem says a percent of a number is increased or decreased by a fixed amount, then write an equation with the percent applied before the add/subtract step.
Error pattern: Success came from translating the sentence in the correct operation order and isolating the variable systematically.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, substitute your candidate back into the verbal statement and verify both the percent calculation and the final result exactly match.
Use when: This applies to one-variable percent problems mixing a percentage of an unknown with a constant change and an equality.
Boundary: Ignore this when quantities are compared multiplicatively only, involve successive percentages, or the unknown is not the original whole.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what fraction of a small set lies within k standard deviations of a given mean, then first compute the inclusive interval mean ± k·SD and count members in it.
Error pattern: Arithmetic/interpretation slip: converting counts to percentages incorrectly and misclassifying values relative to the interval.
Diagnostic check: For n items, translate the percent into an exact count target, mark each item as inside/outside the inclusive bounds, and verify the inside count matches the target.
Use when: A multiple-choice set is tested against a mean-and-standard-deviation band, especially with small discrete lists and phrases like “exactly.”
Boundary: Ignore when the reference mean/SD belongs to a different dataset than the counted set or when “within” is explicitly defined as exclusive.

Transfer rule: If a rate question gives separate intervals, then compute average rate as total quantity divided by total time, not by picking a listed choice from intuition.
Error pattern: Success came from aggregating across intervals before dividing, instead of confusing average speed with one interval’s speed or an unweighted mean in unequal durations.
Diagnostic check: Write two sums explicitly: total distance and total time; then verify units reduce to distance per time.
Use when: Apply this to motion or work problems with multiple segments, changing rates, or speeds stated over distinct time blocks.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for a midpoint, median, or a simple average of values rather than an overall rate.

Transfer rule: If mixtures have different volumes and concentrations, then compute each part’s amount by volume × fraction before combining, then divide by total volume.
Error pattern: Treated concentration fractions as if each came from one equal-sized unit, ignoring the stated quantities being mixed.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list each container’s volume, multiply by the target-component fraction, sum those amounts, and verify the result is between the smallest and largest given fractions.
Use when: Weighted-average, mixture, concentration, percent-content, or combined-rate problems where groups contribute unequal amounts.
Boundary: Ignore when all groups have equal size or the question asks only for an unweighted average or a single container’s composition.

Transfer rule: If two unknown quantities are each written as “total minus a constant,” then express both algebraically and apply every given inequality before checking choices.
Error pattern: Success came from forming the linear expressions; risk was drifting after the algebra and nearly ignoring a strict positivity condition.
Diagnostic check: Compute each individual amount, require each be at least 1, compute their sum, enforce the sum constraint, then intersect all resulting bounds.
Use when: Word problems define several amounts relative to the same variable and include both individual minimums and a combined comparison.
Boundary: Ignore this when quantities are not all tied to one common variable or when conditions are not simple linear inequalities.

Transfer rule: If individual and combined completion times are given, then convert each time to a work rate, subtract known individual rate from combined rate, and invert the remainder.
Error pattern: Success pattern: modeling “days to finish” as “work per day” and combining contributors additively before converting back to time.
Diagnostic check: Set total work to 1; compute rates as reciprocals, verify combined rate exceeds each individual rate, then invert the unknown rate and check the result is slower than the team.
Use when: Relevant for shared-work, filling, or speed problems where multiple agents contribute simultaneously to one fixed job.
Boundary: Ignore when workers interfere, rates vary over time, tasks are not identical/additive, or the question asks for rate rather than completion time.

Transfer rule: If asked for the sum of the first n natural numbers, then compute n(n+1)/2 before comparing choices.
Error pattern: Success came from recalling the standard closed-form formula and carrying out straightforward arithmetic carefully.
Diagnostic check: Substitute the given count into n(n+1)/2, simplify stepwise, and verify the result is about n²/2 for reasonableness.
Use when: This applies to problems asking for a consecutive sum starting at 1 and ending at a positive integer.
Boundary: Ignore this when the sequence skips terms, starts elsewhere, includes negatives, or is not an arithmetic run of consecutive integers.

Transfer rule: If a linear equation has an added unknown, then isolate it by subtracting the known addend from the total and compare the result against every choice.
Error pattern: Success pattern: direct inverse-operation arithmetic plus explicit option verification prevents being trapped by nearby distractors.
Diagnostic check: Recompute the subtraction digit by digit, then substitute the result back into the original equation; if it fits but no option matches, choose the catch-all choice.
Use when: Relevant for single-step algebra questions with one unknown and multiple-choice answers, especially when several choices are close numerically.
Boundary: Ignore when the equation needs more than one algebraic step, contains hidden constraints, or lacks a catch-all option.

Transfer rule: If motion is downstream or aided by a current, then add the current speed to still-water speed before computing time = distance ÷ effective speed.
Error pattern: Success came from selecting the correct relative-speed operation first, then applying the basic distance-rate-time relationship consistently.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, write effective speed explicitly, check the units match, and verify distance divided by that speed gives a plausible travel time.
Use when: Relevant in river/boat, wind, conveyor, or any rate problem where an external flow helps or opposes motion.
Boundary: Ignore this when no assisting/opposing flow exists, or when the given rate is already the net ground-speed.

Transfer rule: If repeated independent trials require exact counts of several mutually exclusive outcomes, then use a multinomial count times the product of category probabilities.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping a word problem to multinomial structure instead of treating categories separately or counting only one ordering.
Diagnostic check: First infer any missing category probability from “exactly one occurs,” then verify counts sum to trials, compute arrangements with factorials, and multiply by probability powers.
Use when: Apply this to fixed-length independent experiments with three or more exclusive outcomes and a requirement for exact frequencies of each.
Boundary: Ignore this when order matters directly, trials are dependent, probabilities change by trial, or the question asks for at least/at most counts.

Transfer rule: If a straightforward calculation yields an answer absent from all choices, then stop and reparse the wording for hidden interpretation traps before selecting.
Error pattern: I applied the most literal unit-based computation and ignored strong evidence from the answer set that the prompt likely encoded a different counting model.
Diagnostic check: Compute the direct result, compare with choices, then list at least two alternate readings of “per cut/per piece/per segment” and see whether one consistently maps to a choice.
Use when: Multi-choice word problems with unit conversions, repeated actions, and answer options that conflict with the first-pass arithmetic.
Boundary: Ignore this when the problem is open-response or when the direct calculation matches a choice cleanly.

Transfer rule: If added values are both near the current mean and balanced around it, then prefer them as the pair most likely to reduce standard deviation.
Error pattern: Success came from focusing on spread from the center rather than chasing changes in the mean alone.
Diagnostic check: For each pair, estimate its average and each value’s distance from the current mean; favor the pair with the smallest distances and the most symmetry.
Use when: This applies to questions about how adding a few numbers affects standard deviation of an existing set.
Boundary: Ignore this shortcut when sample sizes, exact variance formulas, or large mean shifts are required to compare close cases.

Transfer rule: If a largest circle fits exactly inside a square, then set the circle’s diameter equal to the square’s side, halve for radius, and apply πr².
Error pattern: Success came from mapping an inscribed-figure condition to the governing dimension before calculating.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Is this inscribed or circumscribed?” then verify the chosen diameter/radius touches the intended boundaries exactly.
Use when: Use for geometry items about biggest/smallest circles in squares or other shapes where fit determines diameter.
Boundary: Ignore when the circle is outside the shape, dimensions refer to diagonals, or the problem gives area ratios or non-maximal placement.

Transfer rule: If an expression could denote exponents, then rewrite it explicitly with parentheses/powers before doing any algebra.
Error pattern: Misread notation by treating exponential terms as linear terms, leading to invalid simplification.
Diagnostic check: Before combining terms, ask whether variable occurrences are in exponents; if yes, test by rewriting in a common base and checking answer choices by substitution.
Use when: Relevant for equations with adjacent numbers/variables, superscript-like formatting, shifted exponents, or answer sets suggesting simple fractional roots.
Boundary: Ignore when notation is unambiguously linear and no variable appears as an exponent or power.

Transfer rule: If total pay combines a fixed amount and a percent-based part, then subtract the fixed amount from the target and divide by the commission rate.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating additive and multiplicative components instead of applying the percentage to the whole target income.
Diagnostic check: Define variables and verify with an equation of the form total = base + rate×amount; substitute your result back to confirm it reproduces the target.
Use when: This fits wage, pricing, or revenue questions with a guaranteed amount plus a percentage of some unknown quantity.
Boundary: Ignore this when percentages are chained, based on profit/difference, or when no fixed additive component exists.

Transfer rule: If counting multiples in a stated interval, then first decide whether the endpoints are included, convert endpoints to quotient indices, and count only interior terms when “between” excludes ends.
Error pattern: Misread interval language and included boundary multiples, causing an off-by-two counting error despite a valid sequence-count method.
Diagnostic check: Replace the interval with quotient bounds; list whether lower and upper endpoint multiples are allowed, then verify count = last index − first index + 1 after any endpoint exclusions.
Use when: Applies to counting divisible numbers, arithmetic-sequence terms, or integer values inside ranges with words like between, from, inclusive, exclusive, at least, or less than.
Boundary: Ignore when the problem explicitly includes both endpoints or asks for multiples up to/through limits without ambiguous interval wording.

Transfer rule: If two linked rotating objects share the same tangential speed, then compare rotation rates by the inverse of their radii or diameters.
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing an inverse proportionality instead of matching rotation rate directly to size.
Diagnostic check: Write speed = circumference × revolutions per time; cancel the common tangential speed and verify the rate ratio flips the size ratio.
Use when: Apply this to gears, wheels, pulleys, or circles moving together at the rim with equal linear speed.
Boundary: Ignore this when slipping occurs, tangential speeds differ, or the quantities compared are not rotational rates about circular paths.

Transfer rule: If an expression mixes subtraction and division, then compute the division first and only afterward combine terms.
Error pattern: Success came from correctly applying operation precedence instead of reading left-to-right.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the expression with implied grouping from precedence, evaluate each high-priority operation, then compare units/magnitude before choosing.
Use when: Relevant for arithmetic expressions containing more than one basic operation, especially with decimals that may tempt shortcut reading.
Boundary: Ignore this when grouping symbols explicitly override precedence or when the task is not numerical expression evaluation.

Transfer rule: If a quantity grows linearly and one later value is a fractional increase over an earlier value, then write both times as start + rate·time and solve directly before matching choices.
Error pattern: Correct model, but an algebra/arithmetic slip after clearing fractions changed the rate.
Diagnostic check: Expand both sides, clear denominators, then isolate the rate and substitute it back into both time-point expressions to verify the stated multiplicative relationship exactly.
Use when: Arithmetic-sequence or constant-rate growth problems compare two times using phrases like “fraction taller,” “percent more,” or “times as much.”
Boundary: Ignore when growth is not constant, the comparison is additive rather than multiplicative, or the quantities are not tied to equally spaced time steps.

Transfer rule: If a paving problem asks for the minimum count of whole equal square slabs, then first scale all dimensions to integers, find their greatest common measure, and divide each dimension by it before multiplying.
Error pattern: Success comes from optimizing tile size first; failure comes from using area alone or skipping a common-unit conversion.
Diagnostic check: Verify the chosen square side divides both dimensions exactly, then confirm count = (length/side) × (width/side).
Use when: Apply this to rectangular covering problems with equal whole square tiles and a minimum-number requirement.
Boundary: Ignore this when tiles need not be square, cuts are allowed, or dimensions are not for a full rectangle.

Transfer rule: If asked for a product’s unit digit, then replace each factor by its last digit and multiply while reducing to the last digit after each step.
Error pattern: Success came from using modular arithmetic on ones-place digits instead of full multiplication.
Diagnostic check: Write the sequence of last digits only, compute cumulatively mod 10, and look for any step creating a terminal zero.
Use when: This applies to integer multiplication questions asking for a final ones digit or last-digit pattern.
Boundary: Ignore this for sums, non-integer factors, or questions needing more than the ones place.

Transfer rule: If distributing distinct items into fixed labeled recipients with equal bundle sizes, then multiply successive combinations for each recipient and divide only by within-bundle permutations, not by recipient permutations.
Error pattern: The key success pattern is separating labeled-group assignment from unlabeled-group overcounting; confusion arises when treating distinct recipients as interchangeable.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, ask: “Would swapping two recipients with the same bundle create a different valid outcome?” If yes, do not divide by recipient factorial.
Use when: Apply for counting allocations of distinct objects into specified people or boxes with exact quotas per recipient.
Boundary: Ignore when recipients are truly unlabeled, bundle order matters, or not all objects are distributed under fixed equal-size quotas.

Transfer rule: If an event names both a source selected at random and an outcome within that source, then multiply the source-selection probability by the conditional outcome probability.
Error pattern: I answered only the within-source chance and ignored the earlier random-choice stage, dropping a required factor.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, list every stochastic step in order, assign each probability, and verify the event description is matched by their product or sum.
Use when: Apply this to multistage probability setups involving a randomly chosen container, group, path, or case before drawing or observing.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks only for a conditional probability inside a specified source with no prior random-selection stage.

Transfer rule: If one quantity is asked as a percent of another after separate percent changes from the same baseline, then convert both to baseline multipliers and divide actual by projected.
Error pattern: Success came from using one common reference point instead of comparing percent changes directly.
Diagnostic check: Let last year equal 100, compute both resulting amounts, then verify the requested percent is (target/reference)×100, not a difference.
Use when: This applies to word problems with projected vs actual values, increases/decreases, and a final “what percent of” comparison.
Boundary: Ignore this when the percentages are sequential on the same evolving quantity or when the question asks for percent change rather than percent of.

Transfer rule: If a mixture gives two part percentages and asks “how many more,” then compute the percent difference and apply it to the total.
Error pattern: Success came from translating percentages into quantities and subtracting parts, rather than comparing answer choices loosely.
Diagnostic check: Verify the part percentages sum to the whole, compute each part or their percentage gap, then check larger part minus smaller part equals the requested excess.
Use when: Relevant for percent-of-total mixture, category split, or composition problems asking for amount difference between components.
Boundary: Ignore when asking for ratios, totals after change, concentration comparisons, or when percentages refer to different bases.

Transfer rule: If a problem asks for a percent of a fraction, then convert the percent to a decimal or fraction and multiply directly.
Error pattern: Success came from correct representation conversion and straightforward multiplication without overcomplicating the arithmetic.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, estimate whether the percent is above or below 100%; the result should be respectively larger or smaller than the original quantity.
Use when: Apply this on percent-of-value questions, especially when one factor is a fraction, decimal, or mixed numeric form.
Boundary: Ignore this when the wording implies percent change, discounts, ratios between percents, or asks for comparison rather than direct multiplication.

Transfer rule: If two category percentages and their overlap are given, then compute “at least one” as sum minus overlap, and subtract from the whole for “neither.”
Error pattern: Success pattern—recognized an overlap-counting setup and applied inclusion–exclusion instead of adding categories directly.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, verify the overlap is subtracted once, the union stays within the total, and “neither” equals total minus union.
Use when: Relevant for percentage/count problems involving two groups, shared members, and a request for union, overlap, or outside both groups.
Boundary: Ignore when groups are mutually exclusive, more than two sets require extended formulas, or values are conditional rather than whole-class totals.

Transfer rule: If a division problem says the division is exact and one divisor was mistakenly used, then first reconstruct the dividend as mistaken divisor × obtained quotient, then divide by the intended divisor.
Error pattern: Success came from preserving the invariant dividend rather than comparing quotients directly.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, write D = d_wrong × q_wrong; then verify D ÷ d_right is an integer and matches an option.
Use when: Apply this to exact-division correction problems involving a wrong divisor, wrong quotient, or swapped division inputs.
Boundary: Ignore this when there is a remainder, rounding, or the mistaken operation is not simple division with the same dividend.

Transfer rule: If a total is given for multiple identical items after a percent discount, then divide by the item count first or include the count in the equation before undoing the discount.
Error pattern: Treated a group total as the price of one item; omitted the multiplicative factor for quantity.
Diagnostic check: Define a per-item variable, write “discounted total = quantity × discounted per-item price,” then verify the resulting original total matches the given total after applying the discount.
Use when: Word problems mention several identical objects, one shared final amount, and a percentage change from listed price.
Boundary: Ignore when prices differ by item, the final amount is already per item, or quantity is explicitly one.

Transfer rule: If a fixed budget buys one quantity at one unit price and a different quantity after a per-item price change, then set the two total-cost expressions equal.
Error pattern: Success pattern: modeling “exactly enough” as one constant budget and linking both scenarios with the same total.
Diagnostic check: Define unit price p and budget B; write B=qp and B=r(p−d) or B=r(p+d), solve p, then substitute back and verify both scenarios.
Use when: Apply to word problems with unchanged total money, changed unit price, and changed number of items purchased.
Boundary: Ignore when the total budget also changes, quantities are ranges/maximums, or extra fees, taxes, or discounts alter total cost separately.

Transfer rule: If selections are made from disjoint groups for separate roles, then count each group independently with combinations/permutations as needed and multiply.
Error pattern: Success came from decomposing a compound counting task into independent subcounts and matching order sensitivity to each role type.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, list each selection step, mark “ordered” or “identical,” compute each count separately, then verify no candidate can appear in more than one step.
Use when: Apply this on counting problems with multiple departments/categories, separate eligibility pools, and a final team formed by combining choices.
Boundary: Ignore this when pools overlap, constraints link choices, or arrangements across positions matter beyond simple independent selection.

Transfer rule: If one process alone and the combined process times are given, then convert both to per-unit rates and subtract slower net from faster single-process rate to isolate the opposing rate.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling work problems with rates rather than manipulating times directly.
Diagnostic check: Write unit fractions for each hourly rate, verify combined rate is smaller than the filling rate, subtract, then invert only the isolated leak rate.
Use when: Relevant for fill-empty, work-rest, speed-current, or any situation with one helpful and one opposing process acting together.
Boundary: Ignore when processes are not simultaneous, rates change over time, or quantities are not linear in time.

Transfer rule: If pay includes fixed cash plus a noncash item and service is partial, then equate the partial-service share of the full package to the actual mixed payment received.
Error pattern: Treated a lump-sum item inconsistently across methods instead of keeping one algebraic model for cash and in-kind compensation.
Diagnostic check: Define one variable for the item, write total annual compensation as cash-plus-item, multiply that whole total by time served, and verify the resulting item value is nonnegative.
Use when: Compensation problems mix salary and goods/benefits, and the worker leaves before completing the full term.
Boundary: Ignore when payment terms are nonlinear, item value changes over time, or bonuses/penalties depend on completion.

Transfer rule: If a word problem gives a total group and then names a subgroup separately, then test whether the subgroup is already included before summing allocations.
Error pattern: Double-counting from treating overlapping categories as disjoint when the wording may describe a subset of the total.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the entities as set relations; ask “Does this second label add new people, or just reclassify some of the total?” and compute both interpretations briefly.
Use when: Counts are given for one broad group plus another labeled group, and payouts are based on the same reference quantity.
Boundary: Ignore when the text explicitly says the groups are separate, additional, or non-overlapping.

Transfer rule: If operators are redefined, then first rewrite the entire expression with each symbol’s substituted meaning before calculating.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating translation from evaluation and resisting the urge to compute using the printed symbols.
Diagnostic check: Make a four-symbol mapping list, rewrite every operator once, then verify no original special symbols remain before applying normal precedence.
Use when: This fits arithmetic or logic questions where symbols, signs, or words are assigned nonstandard meanings.
Boundary: Ignore this when symbols keep their usual meanings or when the task asks for algebraic properties rather than direct evaluation.

Transfer rule: If a motion problem gives step-count ratio and step-length equivalence, then compute speed as (steps per same time) × (length per step) for each side before simplifying.
Error pattern: Success came from separating frequency from stride length and combining them multiplicatively instead of comparing counts alone.
Diagnostic check: Write speed_A/speed_B = (count_A/count_B) × (stride_A/stride_B); derive stride ratio from the equivalence statement, substitute, and cancel units.
Use when: Apply this to walking, running, gears, or work-rate questions mixing event frequency with per-event size or distance.
Boundary: Ignore this when all compared units are already speeds/rates on the same basis, so no per-event conversion is needed.

Transfer rule: If you start with some items and then obtain more from an external source, then add the two amounts unless wording says some were lost, given away, or used.
