Error pattern: I treated an acquisition event as a removal event by keying on a verb without tracking direction of ownership.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing an operation, restate each quantity as "owned before," "gained," or "lost"; if both quantities end up under your possession, addition is required.
Use when: This applies to word problems about collecting, receiving, picking, finding, or taking items where possession may shift.
Boundary: Ignore this check when the action explicitly removes items from your total or asks for a difference or remainder.

Transfer rule: If asked for an average annual increase over years, then compute (final − initial) ÷ (later year − earlier year) and match the closest option.
Error pattern: Success came from separating total change from time span instead of confusing average increase with an endpoint or total increase.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify units as “quantity per year,” and estimate whether change ÷ years is near 1 rather than near the total change or tiny decimals.
Use when: Apply to word problems comparing two dates and two quantities, especially with multiple-choice approximations.
Boundary: Ignore this when growth is compounded, rates vary by interval, or the question asks for percent change, ratio, or median.

Transfer rule: If two movers travel in the same direction with a staggered start, then compute catch-up time as initial lead distance divided by relative speed.
Error pattern: Success comes from translating the delay into a distance gap first, then using speed difference rather than comparing total distances separately.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, calculate head-start distance = earlier speed × delay, relative speed = faster − slower, and verify units give time.
Use when: Apply this to constant-speed pursuit problems with one traveler starting later on the same path and asking when the later traveler catches up.
Boundary: Ignore this when speeds vary, paths differ, directions oppose, or acceleration/extra stops change the gap over time.

Transfer rule: If a finite series can end early, then count sequences that end on the final required win and multiply by all symmetric winners, or compute the full-length case and subtract from 1.
Error pattern: Counted one side’s winning paths only and used invalid combinatorial counts that ignored the “last game must clinch” constraint.
Diagnostic check: For each possible series length k, verify the champion has exactly one fewer required wins in the first k−1 games, wins game k, then double for either champion.
Use when: Two symmetric competitors play repeated independent games until one reaches a target number of wins.
Boundary: Ignore when teams are unequal, games are dependent, ties/extra outcomes exist, or the series is not stop-on-clinch.

Transfer rule: If a word problem describes money transfers, then define post-transfer amounts first and translate “left with” and “will have” into equations from those updated amounts.
Error pattern: Misreading relational phrasing after a transfer, especially attaching the multiplier to the wrong post-transfer expression or person.
Diagnostic check: For each sentence, write ordered pairs before and after transfer, then verify the equation uses the after-state on both sides and preserves total money.
Use when: Two-person quantity problems involve giving/taking amounts and comparative phrases like twice, thrice, more than, or left with.
Boundary: Ignore this when comparisons are about original amounts only or when totals change through spending, earning, or external additions.

Transfer rule: If one person is before another and a count is “between” them, then place them in order and use earlier-position = later-position − between − 1.
Error pattern: Treated overlapping counts as separate blocks and ignored that “before the later person” already includes the earlier person and the in-between group.
Diagnostic check: Convert statements to positions from the front, compute both positions, then total = earlier person’s position + people after earlier person; verify no person/group is counted twice.
Use when: Relative-order word problems with “before,” “after,” and “between” involving two named positions in a single line.
Boundary: Ignore when counts refer to different events, multiple lines/groups, or changing membership rather than one fixed ordering.

Transfer rule: If discounts begin only after stated quantity thresholds, then split the total into ordered tiers and price each tier separately before summing.
Error pattern: Success came from respecting piecewise conditions instead of applying one discount rate to all units or stacking rates incorrectly.
Diagnostic check: Write threshold cutoffs, compute units in each bracket, verify bracket counts add to the total, then apply each bracket’s discounted unit price once.
Use when: Relevant for bulk-pricing, tax brackets, commissions, shipping bands, or any schedule where rates change after cumulative amounts.
Boundary: Ignore this when one rate applies uniformly to every unit or when the problem explicitly says later discounts also apply retroactively.

Transfer rule: If given pairwise completion times and asked for all together, then convert each time to a rate, add the pairwise rates, and divide by 2 to get the total individual rate.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling work as rates and using symmetry instead of solving for each person separately.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write the three pair-rate equations, sum them, confirm each individual rate appears exactly twice, then invert the final combined rate.
Use when: Apply to work-time, pipe, or speed problems that provide sums of two contributors and ask for the combined effect of all contributors.
Boundary: Ignore when contributions are not constant, pairings overlap unequally, or the task asks for an individual rather than the full group.

Transfer rule: If two travelers cover the same route in different total times, then time to the midpoint is half of each traveler’s own full-route time.
Error pattern: Misread a full-trip time as a midpoint time, effectively doubling the faster traveler’s midpoint time.
Diagnostic check: Let the route be length 1; compute each speed as 1/(full time), then compute midpoint times as 0.5/speed and compare.
Use when: One-dimensional motion problems give each person’s time for the entire distance and ask about a halfway point or equal fraction of the route.
Boundary: Ignore when the target point is not a fixed fraction of the route or when speeds change during travel.

Transfer rule: If adding terminating decimals, then align places and perform full column addition, carrying across the decimal point if needed.  
Error pattern: Success came from using exact place-value addition instead of estimating or matching an option prematurely.  
Diagnostic check: Write equal-length decimals, add right to left, then remove only trailing zeros and confirm the result matches digit-by-digit.  
Use when: This applies to arithmetic with decimals, especially when sums may look equivalent under different formatting.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is not exact decimal addition, such as rounding, estimation, fractions without conversion, or conceptual comparisons.

Transfer rule: If you compute a value from scientific notation, then separately match that exact numeral to the option before selecting.
Error pattern: Correct computation but answer-selection mismatch; the reasoning succeeded, the final option mapping failed.
Diagnostic check: Write the expanded number, count its digits/zeros, then compare it character-by-character with the chosen option text.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice items requiring conversion between scientific notation and standard decimal form.
Boundary: Ignore when no options are provided or when the task asks only for the computed value, not an option label.

Transfer rule: If a base is one less than the modulus, then replace it by −1 modulo that modulus before taking powers.
Error pattern: Success came from spotting a near-modulus simplification and handling odd/even exponent parity correctly in modular arithmetic.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the base as modulus−1, compute the power as (−1)^n using parity, add remaining terms modulo the modulus, then convert any negative residue to a standard remainder.
Use when: Apply this to remainder problems with powers, especially when a term is very close to the divisor and the expression includes addition or subtraction.
Boundary: Ignore this shortcut when the base is not congruent to ±1 or another simple residue, or when the modulus changes across terms.

Transfer rule: If an age problem gives a fixed age difference and a future ratio, then assign variables, write both future ages explicitly, solve the linear equation, and only then answer the requested time shift.
Error pattern: Success comes from translating each statement into algebra without mixing present and future ages.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify one equation uses the unchanged difference and another correctly adds the same years to both people before applying the ratio.
Use when: Use for word problems about two ages with “older than,” “in/future years,” and multiplicative comparisons.
Boundary: Ignore when relationships are not linear age statements or when rates, averages, or more than two timelines are involved.

Transfer rule: If a fixed fraction of a mixture is removed and replaced, then track ingredient amount removed from the original and solve the replacement concentration from the final total.
Error pattern: Success comes from conserving total mass and separating “amount of ingredient added” from “percent of whole after replacement.”
Diagnostic check: Assume a convenient total (like 100), subtract the ingredient in the removed portion, compute the final ingredient amount, then divide the needed added ingredient by the replacement amount.
Use when: A mixture/solution problem gives initial concentration, fraction replaced, and final concentration with unchanged total quantity.
Boundary: Ignore this when total quantity changes overall, multiple ingredients interact nonlinearly, or percentages are not by the same base.

Transfer rule: If combining group averages, then convert each mixed-number average to an improper fraction, multiply by its group size, sum totals, and divide by total count.
Error pattern: Arithmetic setup was right, but mixed-number-to-fraction conversion was executed incorrectly, creating a wrong weighted average.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify each conversion by reversing it: improper fraction ÷ denominator should reproduce the original whole number and fractional part.
Use when: This applies to multi-group average problems, especially when averages are mixed numbers and counts differ across groups.
Boundary: Ignore this when all groups have equal counts or when totals are given directly without needing mixed-number conversion.

Transfer rule: If two movers start at different times, then compute each traveler’s total distance from their own start, including any head-start segment, before comparing.
Error pattern: I correctly found the shared-travel phase but compared only the simultaneous portions, dropping the earlier traveler’s initial distance.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, write total distance for each as “head start + during-overlap travel,” then subtract and verify the totals sum to the original separation.
Use when: Apply this to meet-up, catch-up, or opposite-direction motion problems with staggered start times and a final comparison of distances.
Boundary: Ignore this when all travelers start together or when the question asks only about overlap-phase distance, speed, or meeting time.

Transfer rule: If an object must fully clear another object, then use total distance = moving length + obstacle length, and convert speed to consistent units before time = distance/speed.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the physical event to the full-clearance distance and maintaining unit consistency throughout.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, write the event endpoints explicitly, sum all required lengths, convert rate to base units, then estimate whether the resulting time is plausible.
Use when: Apply this to crossing, overtaking, or passing problems involving lengths of moving bodies and fixed structures.
Boundary: Ignore this when only a point crossing time is asked or when speed already matches the distance unit.

Transfer rule: If a simple-interest question gives principal, final amount, and time, then compute interest as amount minus principal and rate as (interest × 100) / (principal × time).
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the wording directly to the simple-interest relationship instead of guessing from answer choices.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, verify units and recompute by substitution: principal × rate × time / 100 should equal the interest you first calculated.
Use when: Apply this to straightforward simple-interest problems with one unknown rate and no compounding, installments, or changing balances.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when interest is compound, rates vary over time, or fees/partial payments alter the net amount.

Transfer rule: If containers have different capacities, then convert each fill level to a common base volume before adding and only then divide by the target container’s capacity.
Error pattern: Success came from proportional-volume reasoning instead of averaging or combining fill fractions directly.
Diagnostic check: Set the smaller capacity to 1 unit; compute each actual amount, add transferred volume, then verify the final fraction is total volume divided by the receiving capacity.
Use when: One vessel’s capacity is given relative to another and liquid is transferred or combined.
Boundary: Ignore when capacities are equal already, or when the question asks about concentration/composition rather than total fill level.

Transfer rule: If one moving object fully crosses another object, then use total relative distance = sum of both lengths before computing speed.
Error pattern: Treated a “passing” event like passing a point, ignoring the stationary object’s own length in the distance covered.
Diagnostic check: Sketch start and finish positions; confirm the mover’s front clears the far end and its rear starts behind the near end, then count every segment traversed.
Use when: Relevant for trains, vehicles, or bodies completely overtaking, crossing, or clearing another extended object, platform, tunnel, or person.
Boundary: Ignore when the obstacle is effectively a point, or the wording asks about reaching a marker rather than fully passing an object.

Transfer rule: If a two-year same-rate problem gives both simple and compound interest, then use CI−SI as the second-year interest-on-interest and solve before testing options.
Error pattern: Success comes from using the two-year relation directly; failure comes from heavy algebra substitution instead of exploiting the small difference term.
Diagnostic check: Compute d = CI−SI; set d = P(r/100)^2 and SI = 2Pr/100, eliminate r or use r = 200d/SI, then verify the resulting principal reproduces both totals.
Use when: Apply to fixed-principal, same-rate, exactly two-year comparisons between simple and compound interest.
Boundary: Ignore when time is not two years, rates vary, compounding frequency differs, or amounts rather than interest values are given.

Transfer rule: If consecutive terms are all produced by the same ratio, then extend the sequence by applying that identical ratio once more.
Error pattern: Success came from checking the step-by-step transformation instead of guessing from absolute values or option familiarity.
Diagnostic check: Compute each adjacent quotient; if they match consistently, use that quotient on the last term before choosing.
Use when: Apply this to ordered sequences of numbers, especially when values shrink or become fractional and an arithmetic difference is not constant.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when quotients vary, multiple operations alternate, or another clear structure outranks a constant-ratio pattern.

Transfer rule: If two example words define a letter→digit substitution, then infer each shared letter’s digit and encode the new word position by position.
Error pattern: Treated a solvable mapping puzzle as underdetermined instead of extracting all letter assignments from overlapping examples.
Diagnostic check: Write the distinct letters from the examples, assign known digits from each code, verify every letter in the target word is mapped, then compare only those candidate strings.
Use when: Short coding/decoding multiple-choice items provide at least two examples and the target word uses only letters appearing in those examples.
Boundary: Ignore when the code depends on position, arithmetic on whole words, repeated-letter behavior, or any rule beyond simple fixed substitution.

Transfer rule: If present worth and true discount are given, then compute banker’s gain using BG = (TD²)/(PW), not by introducing unknown rate or time.
Error pattern: Started correctly by finding the future amount, but then shifted to an incomplete method and failed to finish a direct identity.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list known discount identities and verify one uses only the given quantities; then substitute and simplify fully.
Use when: Relevant in simple-discount questions involving present worth, true discount, banker’s discount, and banker’s gain with missing rate/time.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the problem gives interest rate or time explicitly and asks for a quantity better found from first-principles formulas.

Transfer rule: If a final price includes a stated percent increase on an original amount, then divide by \(1+\text{rate}\) to recover the original.
Error pattern: Success comes from translating “more than” into a multiplier on the base, not subtracting the percent from the final amount.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write final = original × multiplier; verify the multiplier is greater than 1 for markup and recompute by inverse division.
Use when: Apply this to percent markup, profit, tax, commission, or any wording where a charged/selling amount is based on an increased base.
Boundary: Ignore this when the percent is a discount, a percent of the final amount, or when multiple sequential changes are involved.

Transfer rule: If a symbol is defined as a product from 1 through an integer, then treat later occurrences with that symbol as factorial-like values, not ordinary addition or exponents.
Error pattern: Ignoring a custom notation definition and reverting to familiar arithmetic, causing the entire range to be misread.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each endpoint using the given definition, then test divisibility by a small factor already included in the product before judging primality.
Use when: A problem introduces special notation or factorial-style products and asks about primality, divisibility, or counts in an interval.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the notation is standard arithmetic or when the numbers are explicitly expanded already.

Transfer rule: If counts are cumulative by visit number, then total revenue = all customers’ first-visit charge + each later-visit tier counted once at the repeat-visit charge.
Error pattern: Double-counting nested groups by treating people with more visits as separate from, rather than included within, lower-tier repeaters.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write visit tiers as cumulative sets and verify tier totals sum to total visits, not total people in disjoint buckets.
Use when: A problem gives totals plus how many reached a second, third, or later occurrence with different prices after the first.
Boundary: Ignore when categories are explicitly disjoint or when pricing resets independently per event, item, or person-group.

Transfer rule: If a quantity grows at “x% more than” another annual rate, then add the rates first and apply compound growth for each year.
Error pattern: Success came from translating comparative percentage wording into one effective yearly rate and compounding instead of using simple addition over time.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compute effective annual rate = base rate + extra rate, then verify future value with start × (1 + rate)^years.
Use when: This fits word problems about prices, wages, populations, or costs changing yearly relative to inflation or another stated annual rate.
Boundary: Ignore this when rates vary by year, the increase is absolute not percentage-based, or the problem specifies simple growth instead of compounding.

Transfer rule: If an object passes a fixed point completely, then convert speed to m/s and compute length = speed × time.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the scenario to a direct distance-rate-time model after proper unit conversion.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify the time is for clearing a point, convert km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6, then multiply by seconds.
Use when: Apply this to motion problems where a moving object's full length is inferred from the time to pass a stationary marker.
Boundary: Ignore this when another object's length matters, acceleration occurs, or time refers to meeting, overtaking, or crossing a span.

Transfer rule: If a grouping size changes but the total quantity stays fixed, then compute total = old group size × old group count, then new count = total ÷ new group size.
Error pattern: Success comes from conserving the total and using inverse proportionality between group size and number of groups.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write the two-step equation chain and verify units cancel: items/row × rows = items, then items ÷ items/row = rows.
Use when: Apply to row-column, packing, teams, or any rearrangement problem where one arrangement reveals a fixed total.
Boundary: Ignore when totals change, leftovers/remainders are allowed, or rates/time variables are mixed in.

Transfer rule: If items are first grouped into equal bundles, then compute the number of bundles and use arrangements/permutations only among those bundles, not combinations of original items.
Error pattern: Treated a two-stage word problem as a subset-selection problem and ignored the “every possible arrangement” cue.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the task as units and actions: count final units, decide whether order matters, compute arrangement count, then multiply by time per move.
Use when: The problem forms identical groups first, then asks about all possible ways to place, order, or send those groups.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks only how many groups can be made or when order is explicitly irrelevant.

Transfer rule: If identical workers complete one job together, then compute total worker-hours and divide by the new worker count.
Error pattern: Arithmetic/result-mapping slip after correct rate setup; the reasoning was right but the selected option/conclusion was mismatched.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, calculate workers × time for the original case, divide by new workers, then verify the chosen option matches that exact time.
Use when: Applies to constant-rate, identical-agent work problems where only the number of workers changes and the total job stays fixed.
Boundary: Ignore when workers differ in speed, efficiency changes with team size, or setup/overhead means output is not proportional.

Transfer rule: If a work problem gives normal time and slower combined time due to a leak/drain, then convert both to rates and subtract: leak rate = normal fill rate − net fill rate.
Error pattern: Success comes from modeling additive/subtractive rates instead of comparing times directly.
Diagnostic check: Compute 1/t_fast and 1/t_slow, verify the leak/drain rate is positive and smaller than the fill rate, then invert that leak rate to get emptying time.
Use when: Apply to tank, pipe, pump, or work-rate questions with one agent helping and another opposing.
Boundary: Ignore when times are for separate stages, changing rates, or non-opposing processes.

Transfer rule: If a total cost is split across item groups and one group’s average is known, then compute that group’s total, subtract from the grand total, and divide by the remaining group’s count.
Error pattern: Success pattern—used sequential decomposition instead of mixing averages across unequal group sizes.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify units with: known-average × known-count = known-group total; grand total − known-group total = other-group total; other-group total ÷ other-count = target average.
Use when: Relevant in purchase, mixture, or grouped-average problems with counts, one subgroup average, and an overall total.
Boundary: Ignore when totals are not additive, averages are weighted by something else, or prices/rates vary within the target subgroup.

Transfer rule: If multiple agents work simultaneously on one job, then convert each completion time to a per-unit rate, sum the rates, and invert once at the end.
Error pattern: Success comes from modeling work problems with rates instead of averaging times or adding durations directly.
Diagnostic check: Write each rate as “job per hour,” add using a common denominator, then verify the total rate exceeds each individual rate and the final time is shorter than the fastest single time.
Use when: Apply this to fill/work scenarios where several independent contributors act together on the same whole task.
Boundary: Ignore this when contributors interfere, switch on/off at different times, or rates vary over time.

Transfer rule: If an equation appears to yield multiple valid values but the format expects one, then recheck notation/parentheses and test each candidate under the original expression before choosing.
Error pattern: I stopped after a generic power-to-1 rule and ignored ambiguity plus the mismatch between derived solutions and a single-choice format.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the equation exactly with explicit grouping, substitute every plausible candidate back into that exact form, and reject any value not uniquely consistent.
Use when: Apply this on exponent problems with ambiguous formatting, identities like powers equaling 1, or answer sets suggesting only one admissible result.
Boundary: Ignore this when notation is fully explicit and the problem explicitly allows multiple solutions.

Transfer rule: If a trip has multiple speed segments with known times, then compute each segment’s distance, sum distances, and divide by total time.
Error pattern: Success came from using the weighted-average-by-time method instead of averaging the speeds directly.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write distance = rate × time for every segment, add all distances, add all times, and verify units cancel to distance/time.
Use when: This applies to travel or work-rate questions split into parts with different rates and explicit durations.
Boundary: Ignore this when all segments cover equal distances or when the question asks for something other than an overall average rate.

Transfer rule: If a component is added to a mixture and a target percentage is specified, then write component/total before and after, set (old component + added)/(old total + added) = target, and solve.
Error pattern: Success comes from tracking both numerator and denominator changes instead of adjusting percentages directly.
Diagnostic check: Compute the initial component amount from the starting percent, define one variable for added amount, solve the ratio equation, then verify the resulting fraction equals the target.
Use when: Percent-composition mixture problems where adding or removing one ingredient changes the overall concentration.
Boundary: Ignore this when amounts are fixed, no mixture total changes, or the task asks only for the current composition.

Transfer rule: If motion is with a current or tailwind, then add the flow speed to the object’s still-medium speed before computing time = distance/speed.
Error pattern: Success came from correctly classifying the situation and using the proper combined-speed formula instead of subtracting or mixing formulas.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write “direction?”, compute effective speed separately, then divide distance by that speed and verify the time-speed product returns the distance.
Use when: Apply this to one-dimensional rate problems involving boats, swimmers, aircraft, conveyors, or any travel aided by a moving medium.
Boundary: Ignore this when no medium effect exists, when speed already includes the medium, or when rates vary over time or by segment.

Transfer rule: If equal-magnitude percent increase and decrease occur in sequence, then convert them to multipliers and multiply, not subtract percentages.
Error pattern: Success came from using compounded relative change instead of assuming opposite percents cancel linearly.
Diagnostic check: Let the starting value be 1; compute the final expression as (1+r)(1−r), set it equal to the stated net-change multiplier, and solve.
Use when: Apply this to multi-step percent-change, growth/decline, revenue, price, population, or discount problems with changing bases.
Boundary: Ignore this when all changes are measured from the same original base or when the problem gives absolute amounts, not percentages.

Transfer rule: If a selection must include all available items from one source, then treat that source as fixed and count only the remaining choices from the other source with combinations.
Error pattern: Success came from separating mandatory picks from optional picks instead of combining all items into one pool.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark each group as “forced” or “choose,” compute each count, and verify the total equals the required final size.
Use when: This applies to counting problems with multiple sources or categories and wording like must include, at least, exactly, or remaining items.
Boundary: Ignore this when order matters, repetition is allowed, or the “must” condition is not actually fixed membership.

Transfer rule: If one new result changes an average by a stated amount, then set old average = new average minus the change and compare totals before vs. after adding one item.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing the count before the added item from the total count after it.
Diagnostic check: Define a pre-addition count variable, write old total = old average × count, then verify new total divided by count+1 equals the stated new average.
Use when: A single added score, sale, or payment changes an average and the question asks for the number of items.
Boundary: Ignore when multiple items are added, removed, or weighted differently, or when the average change is not caused by exactly one new item.

Transfer rule: If a compound inequality is split into parts, then combine the results by intersection only, keeping the shared restrictions unchanged.
Error pattern: Sign/direction confusion when merging inequalities turned a stronger upper bound into an unrelated two-sided interval.
Diagnostic check: After solving each piece, pick a test value from your combined claim; if it fails any original part, the merge is wrong.
Use when: Chained inequalities, multiple inequalities on the same variable, or answer choices compare “must be true” statements from derived bounds.
Boundary: Ignore when conditions are joined by “or,” involve different variables, or require existence rather than simultaneous truth.

Transfer rule: If a boundary length is stated as a fraction of the enclosed area for a circle, then set circumference equal to that fraction times area and cancel shared factors before solving.
Error pattern: Success came from translating words directly into an equation and simplifying structurally instead of testing choices.
Diagnostic check: Write the relation symbolically, substitute the circle formulas, divide by common constants and one radius factor, then verify the remaining variable has length units.
Use when: Apply for geometry word problems linking perimeter/circumference and area of the same figure by a proportional statement.
Boundary: Ignore when the figure is not the same on both sides, dimensions are inconsistent by context, or extra scaling/conversion details are present.

Transfer rule: If a ratio links two quantities and a difference is given, then express both as the same ratio multiple and use subtraction on the parts.
Error pattern: Success came from translating ratio and difference into one consistent equation instead of guessing from answer choices.
Diagnostic check: Let quantities be k-scaled ratio parts; subtract the smaller part from the larger and verify the result matches the stated difference before choosing.
Use when: Apply this to word problems with two categories, a fixed ratio between them, and a stated amount by which one exceeds or trails the other.
Boundary: Ignore this when the relationship is not proportional, involves changing totals over time, or compares more than two quantities.

Transfer rule: If minimizing one ticket type in a two-price total, then solve the linear Diophantine equation with modular arithmetic and choose the smallest positive valid count, not zero when the item must be included.
Error pattern: I searched sequentially and accepted an endpoint case, missing the integer-congruence constraint and the implicit requirement that both ticket types can appear.
Diagnostic check: Compute the count modulo the other price, list the smallest valid counts, and verify whether zero is allowed by the wording before converting count to dollars.
Use when: A fixed total is made from two unit prices and the question asks for a minimum or maximum spend on one category.
Boundary: Ignore this when quantities need not be integers, only one category may be used, or inclusion/exclusion conditions are explicitly different.

Transfer rule: If a seller pays a commission based on the final listed price, then set listed_price − commission_rate·listed_price equal to cost plus desired profit.
Error pattern: I treated the percentage as a simple markup on cost and ignored that the fee is taken from the selling price.
Diagnostic check: Write a net-revenue equation, solve algebraically for the listed price, then substitute back to verify net received matches target proceeds.
Use when: Pricing problems mention commissions, platform fees, or taxes calculated as a percent of the customer-facing price.
Boundary: Ignore this when the percentage is explicitly applied only to cost, not to the final charged amount.

Transfer rule: If a container is partially filled, then compute wetted area as base area plus only the submerged portions of each interior wall.  
Error pattern: Success came from decomposing a 3D surface into all distinct wet faces and summing them without adding any dry or top surface.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list every interior face, mark “wet” or “dry,” write one area expression per wet face, then verify units and count symmetry pairs once.  
Use when: Apply this to rectangular tanks, cisterns, boxes, or prisms where liquid depth is given and a wet or exposed surface area is asked.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for volume, total outer area, open-top area, or when walls are slanted/curved and need different geometry.

Transfer rule: If a percentage describes a complement group and that group’s subcounts are fully listed, then sum the subcounts and divide by the complement percentage to get the whole.
Error pattern: Success came from translating part-to-whole language into one equation instead of mixing subgroup details with the target total.
Diagnostic check: Identify the referenced group, confirm its pieces are exhaustive and disjoint, add them, then verify part ÷ whole-percent gives a sensible whole.
Use when: A problem gives a total percentage for one category and concrete counts for all members in that category split by subtypes.
Boundary: Ignore this when subgroup counts overlap, omit cases, or the percentage refers to a different base population.

Transfer rule: If two totals differ by exactly one identical item while another item is unchanged, then subtract the totals to get that item’s unit price, then scale to the asked quantity.
Error pattern: Success comes from noticing matched terms and using elimination instead of solving the whole system.
Diagnostic check: Write both purchase equations, confirm one term has the same coefficient, subtract line-by-line, and verify the result’s units before multiplying.
Use when: Relevant in bundle-pricing or linear-combination word problems where two transactions share at least one common item.
Boundary: Ignore when quantities of all items change without a shared fixed term, or when prices are nonlinear, discounted, taxed differently, or bundled inconsistently.

Transfer rule: If a geometry word problem gives dimensions via ratios and your solved measure is a decimal in a base unit, then test equivalent common subunits before rejecting all choices.
Error pattern: Correct algebra but premature answer selection failure from ignoring implied unit conversion or answer-scale mismatch.
Diagnostic check: Compute the target quantity symbolically, compare its magnitude to the choice format, then convert through standard metric scales and see whether one form aligns cleanly.
Use when: Ratio-based dimension problems, volume/area contexts, and multiple-choice answers that are whole numbers while your result is a neat decimal.
Boundary: Ignore this when units are explicitly fixed in the answer choices or when conversion would violate the stated measurement system.

Transfer rule: If a fraction’s parts change by percentages, then convert each change to a multiplier and divide the given result by those multipliers to recover the original ratio.
Error pattern: Success pattern: treating “increased by p%” as original × (1 + p/100), not as adding raw percent values to numerator or denominator.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write both transformed parts explicitly, form the new/original ratio factor, and verify by reapplying the percentage changes to your candidate.
Use when: Relevant for fraction, ratio, or proportion problems where numerator and denominator are changed by different percentages.
Boundary: Ignore when percentages apply to the whole fraction/value at once, or when changes are absolute amounts rather than percent multipliers.

Transfer rule: If two travelers cover the same distance with speeds in ratio a:b and one takes Δ longer, then set times as b:a and solve the extra-time difference from a common multiplier.
Error pattern: Success came from using inverse proportionality between speed and time for fixed distance, rather than comparing raw speeds directly.
Diagnostic check: Let times be kb and ka; compute the time gap k|b−a|, set it equal to the given delay, solve k, then recover the required time.
Use when: Apply this to equal-distance rate problems giving a speed ratio and an absolute difference in arrival times.
Boundary: Ignore this when distances differ, rates vary during travel, or the given difference is in speed or distance instead of time.

Transfer rule: If quantities are linked by “twice/half” statements plus an average or total, then convert all values to one variable before comparing choices.
Error pattern: Success comes from preserving directional ratio language and reducing the system consistently instead of mixing substitutions or reversing relationships.
Diagnostic check: Write both relations symbolically, derive the total from the average, solve for one variable, then verify the ordered triple satisfies each original phrase.
Use when: Apply this to word problems with ordered quantities, multiplicative comparisons, and a given mean or sum.
Boundary: Ignore this when relationships are additive, unordered, or when the task asks only for a direct estimate rather than exact values.

Transfer rule: If your computed work/rate answer is not among the choices, then reread the timeline and recompute each phase from the original wording before trusting the algebra.
Error pattern: Correct equation setup can still fail when you skip an end-to-end consistency check against all given answer choices.
Diagnostic check: Compute solo rate, remaining work, and joint rate separately; then plug your result back into the second phase and also compare it to the available choices.
Use when: Multi-stage work problems with one worker starting alone, another joining later, and fixed total output.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is not a staged rate/work setup or when answers are not multiple-choice.

Transfer rule: If total selling price of one quantity equals total cost price of another, then convert both to per-item values by dividing by their quantities before comparing.
Error pattern: Success came from using unit-rate normalization instead of comparing unequal totals directly.
Diagnostic check: Set one item’s cost to 1 unit, compute implied per-item selling price from the given equality, then evaluate (SP−CP)/CP × 100 and sign.
Use when: Relevant in profit-loss, ratio, or pricing problems where prices for different numbers of items are equated.
Boundary: Ignore this when quantities differ because of discounts, mixed item types, or extra fixed charges not proportional per item.

Transfer rule: If two equal-length movers fully pass, then use total length as twice one length and compute it from relative speed × given passing time before changing scenarios.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling crossing with relative motion and preserving the same total distance while only changing relative speed.
Diagnostic check: Verify three items: relative speed is difference for same direction, sum for opposite direction, and crossing distance equals combined lengths.
Use when: Apply this to pass-by problems involving two moving objects, stated speeds, a crossing time in one setup, and a new time asked in another setup.
Boundary: Ignore when lengths differ but are unspecified, motion is not along one line, or the event is not full crossing.

Transfer rule: If a statement says profit is p% of cost, then set profit = p/100 × cost and selling price = cost + profit, not p/100 added as the whole selling price.
Error pattern: Misreading “profit as a percent of cost” as “selling price as a percent of cost,” causing every later step to be anchored to the wrong base.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, plug in a simple cost like 100, compute profit and selling price directly from the wording, then verify selling price exceeds profit by exactly the cost.
Use when: Apply this on markup, margin, discount, commission, or percentage-of-base problems where multiple quantities are compared.
Boundary: Ignore this when the statement already defines selling price directly or asks only for a ratio without any base-quantity wording.

Transfer rule: If combining group averages, then convert each mixed-number average to an improper fraction, multiply by its group count, sum totals, and divide by the total count.
Error pattern: Arithmetic conversion slip—miswriting a mixed number as the wrong improper fraction, which corrupts an otherwise correct weighted-average method.
Diagnostic check: Before finalizing, recompute each mixed number with whole×denominator + numerator, then verify each day’s total by reversing: total ÷ count must recover that day’s average.
Use when: Relevant for multi-group average problems with different group sizes, especially when averages are fractions or mixed numbers.
Boundary: Ignore when all groups have equal size or when the question asks for a simple unweighted mean of listed values.

Transfer rule: If an age problem mixes past and future statements, then define present-age variables and convert each sentence into a time-shifted linear equation before comparing options.
Error pattern: Success came from preserving equal time shifts on both people and simplifying the future “exceeds by” statement into a fixed age difference.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, verify each equation by plugging in the implied age gap and ensuring both transformed statements hold at the stated times.
Use when: Apply this to two-person age word problems involving “years ago,” “years hence,” multiplicative ages, and a requested present-age ratio.
Boundary: Ignore this when ages are not the unknowns or when relationships are non-linear, probabilistic, or about changing rates rather than fixed differences.

Transfer rule: If your computed result is absent from all choices, then pause and re-read for hidden constraints, alternative sample spaces, or wording mismatches before declaring the options wrong.
Error pattern: Correct local counting but overconfident interpretation lock-in; failure was not validating assumptions against the multiple-choice structure.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, list the assumed sample space, event definition, and symmetry model, then ask “Could any standard reinterpretation change the denominator or favorable count?”
Use when: Apply this on discrete probability/counting questions, especially with dice/cards and when a clean calculation yields a value outside the answer set.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is open-response or explicitly confirms the sample space and assumptions with no ambiguity.

Transfer rule: If a profit-comparison problem gives unit cost plus quantities and selling prices for separate groups, then compute profit per unit for each group and multiply before comparing totals.
Error pattern: Success comes from separating per-unit profit from total profit and not mixing inventory totals with sold quantities.
Diagnostic check: Write two expressions in the form (selling price − cost) × quantity sold, evaluate both, then subtract in the asked direction.
Use when: Apply this to word problems about gross profit, markup, or earnings across different time periods, batches, or customer groups.
Boundary: Ignore this when costs vary within a group, overhead/fixed costs are included, or the question asks for revenue rather than profit.
